Beushening: It involves cross ploughing the young crop, 4-6 weeks after sowing with a light country plough in 5-10 cm standing water, ones or twice. Purpose behind this to control weeds, optimize crop stand and provide soil aeration. Puddling: It is a process of destruction of soil aggregates by mechanical force in soils with excessive moisture content. Puddling destroys the soil structure which hampers root penetration and the development of the succeeding upland crops grown in rotation with rice. Puddling increases the bulk densityof soil about from 1.4 to 1.7 g/cc. It is done with a puddler.

Catch crops: These are gown as substitute for the main crop that has failed on account of unfavorable condition. a. Square system: • Simplest and widely adopted /popular method • In this method R x R and P x P distances are kept similar' • The plants are planted exactly at right angle at each corner. Overview a. Square system: Key Points Simplest and widely adopted /popular method In this method R x R and P x P distances are kept similar' The plants are planted exactly at right angle at each corner. Number of plants/ha = 10,000 m2/x2 Where, x2= R x R/P x P. b. Rectangular system: More plants can be planted as compare to square system. Keeping more space between row to row and plant to plant distance is kept comparatively less. Number of plants = 10,000 m2/X x Y. c. Hexagonal or equilateral triangle system: It accommodated 15% more plants than square system. The plants are planted at the corner of equilateral triangle. This is very intense method of planting and difficult to layout. Requires fertile land. d. Quincunx system/diagonal/filler system: Most suitable in highly fertile soil. This method is similar to square system but an additional 'filler' plant is planted in the center of square. Alm

a. Black tip: Due to deficiency of boron. Overview a. Black tip: Due to deficiency of boron. Key Points Near brick kilns distal end of affected fruits get turned black and become hardened. Class: Mainly two classes of insect -pest that is agricultural importance are below: 1. Class: Hexapoda/Insecta Body is divided into three viz, head, thorax and abdomen. Eg. Insects are 97% of total population of the phylum arthropod. What is insect: The insects are tracheate arthropods in which the body is divided in to head, thorax and abdomen. A single pair of antennae is present and the head bears a pair of mandibles and two pairs of maxillae, the second pair fused medially to form the labium. The thorax carries three pairs of legs and usually one or two pairs of wings. The abdomen is devoid of ambulatory appendages and the genital opening is situated near the posterior end of the body. The colour blindness is another example of sex linkage in humans. Sons from the marriage between colour blind man and normal woman will be normal, but daughters will carry such genes in heterozygous condition. Marriage of such carrier girl with colour blind boy will yield children in which both male and female children will be colour blind each in 50% cases.

Compounding is the procedure for finding the future value of a present sum given the interest rate and frequency of compounding. Definition, formula and annuity - Since, capital expenditure involves cash and benefits over time, it is necessary to adjust for the time value of money for conducting a meaningful investment analysis. - Such adjustment of time value of money is made through compounding and discounting technique. - Compounding: Compounding is the procedure to find the future value of a present sum, given the earning power (interest rate) of money and the frequency of compounding. - The future value of money is the value of an investment on a particular date in the future. - This is based on the assumption that the investment will earn interest which is reinvested at the end of each year to also earn interest. - The future value includes the original investment, the interest it earns and interest on the accumulated interest. - Compounding is the process used to determine costs and returns at the end of planning horizon. - The procedure of finding future value of present sum

section: Treatment of Seeds at the Time of Soaking for Sprouting
text: Treat seeds in a solution containing Carbendazim, Pyroquilon, or Tricyclozole at 2g/lit of water for 1 kg of seed, soaking for 2 hrs, followed by sprouting and sowing in a nursery bed. (a) Wet Seed Treatment Treat the seeds in Carbendazim or Pyroquilon or Tricyclozole solution at 2g/lit of water for 1 kg of seed. Soak the seeds in the solution for 2 hrs. Drain the solution, sprout the seeds and sow in the nursery bed. It gives protection to the seedlings up to 40 days from seedlings disease such as blast and it is better than dry seed treatment. (b) Seed Treatment with Azospirillum Three packets (600 g/ha) of Azospirillum culture are mixed with sufficient water, wherein seeds are soaked overnight before sowing in the nursery bed. The bacterial suspension after decanting may be poured over the nursery area itself.

Seeds are soaked for 10 hours, then drained to remove excess water. Preparation The seeds should not be soaked in running water, which removes the minerals and nutrients. Soaking and Sprouting Keep the soaked seeds in a gunny bag in a dark room. Cover with extra gunnies for 24 hours. Avoiding Heat The seeds should not be covered with thick material, which develops heat and reduces the aeration.

section: Preparation of Nursery for Sowing: Dry, Wet and Dapog Method
text: The preparation of a nursery for sowing involves creating raised beds using the dry or wet and Dapog method. Dry Method 5-8 m long, 1.2 m wide and 0.30 m raised bed s are prepared and dry seeds are sown, frequent water is done to germinate the seed. Apply 1.0:0.50:0.50Kg NPK/100 m Dapog Method 5-8 m long ,1.2 m wide and 0 .30 m raised beds are prepared sedds are broadcast @1.0 kg /m thus 40-45 m area is sufficient to raised nursery for one ha area.

Apply 2.5:1.50:1.50kg NPK/45 m. When seedlings are 2-3 leaf stage at 12-14 DAS, pull out and transplant into main field. Wet Method About 800 m area for planting one ha is required. Raise the nursery near the water source Pre-Transplant Care Apply 1 t of FYM or compost to nursery and spread the manure uniformly. Before ploughing, allow water to a depth of 2.5 cm. Post-Transplant Care Apply 1.0:0.50:0.50 kg NPK/100 m area before last puddling. After 10 DAS, topdress 1.0 kg N/100 m area. Water Management For water management in nursery, first drain the water 18–24 hrs after sowing and allow enough water to saturate the soil from 3–5 day. From 5 day onwards, increase the quantity of water to a depth of 1.5 cm depending on the height of seedlings.

Apply pre-emergence herbicides at specific rates to control weeds in nurseries. Keep thin film of water at the time of herbicide application and should not drain the water after application.

Puddle and level the fields after applying basal fertilizers, then seedlings are dibbled at specific spacings for early, medium, and late duration varieties. The process of transforming rough rice into polished rice through various steps including parboiling, curing, milling, and polishing. Parboiling Rough rice is soaked, steamed, and redried before milling. Advantages of Parboiling Easy dehusking Low incidence of pests and diseases Curing Steaming for 15–20 minutes is sufficient to bring satisfactory curing effect. Milling Rice milling involves the removal of husks and bran from rough rice to produce polished rice. Polishing Removal of very fine bran (often called whitening) 2–3 times.

Direct seeding involves applying the recommended seed rate, nutrient management, and water management practices for optimal crop growth. Seeds and Sowing The seed rate is 60, 70 and 80 kg/ha for fine medium and coarse rice but now under modern technique only 25-30 kg seed/ha. Sprouted seeds are sown in lines using drum seeder. It is more economical and labour saving. Nutrient Management Application of 100: 60: 40 kg of N, P2O5 and K2O respectively 50% N should be applied at 20 DAS and the remaining 25% N each at maximum tillering and panicle initiation stage. Classification is largely based on the character of the kernels. Flint Corn (Zea mays indurate) Starchy endosperm enclosed with hard hammy endosperm. Kernel size is large with flat bottom and round at the top, high proportion of starch, colour may be white or yellow, mostly grown in India. Dent Corn (Z. mays indentata) Maize kernels have both soft and hard starches. The hard starch extends on the sides and the soft starch is in the centre and extends to the top of the kernel. Pop Corn (Z. mays averta) Kernel size is small. Hard and corneous endosperm is present. After heating the pressure built up within the kernel suddenly results in an explosion of the grain is turned inside out. Sweet Corn (Z. mays saccharata) The kernals are translucent, horny and more wrinkled when dry. Presence of recessive gene “su” (sunken-1, sunken-2) break the conversion sugar to starch in endosperm that results in sweet taste of kernels.

Flour corn resembles flint corn in appearance and ear characteristics, with grains composed of soft starch and little or no dent. Characteristics It has a waxy appearance and gummy starch due to amylopectin. Origin Waxy corn is originally from Mexico and Central America.

Sorghum is one of the major food crops of the world, particularly Africa and Asia. Uses of Sorghum It is used in various forms, similar to rice as cooked food, malted, flour for dosai and making chapatti or rotti, popped, semolina etc. Nutritional Content 10–12% protein 72.6% carbohydrate 3% fat 1.6% mineral Growth and Drought Tolerance It has the capacity to withstand drought or excess moisture (92% of sorghum is grown under rainfed). It comes up well even in marginal soil under moisture stress. Undesirable Qualities High amount of Niacin interface with the synthesis of Tryptophane Leucine: iso-leucine ratio (3.4) causes nutritional disorder 'Pellagara' Oxalic acid affects absorption of Ca and metabolism of Ca Sorghum Poisoning It contains ‘cynogenic glucoside’ called ‘Dhurin’. This glucoside is converted into HCN in the stomach of ruminants, causing bloating and death. Sorghum Injury Sorghum stubbles/roots have high C: N ratio (50:1), causing temporary immobilization of soil ‘N’ and affecting succeeding crops.

A short day C4 plant, commonly grown in warm weather conditions. Classification Modified and simple classification based on spikelet type by Harlen and De-Wet (1971). Climate Short day C4 plant Long day condition delays flowering and maturity Warm weather plant, grown even at 1500 m from MSL Optimum rainfall of 300-400 mm Temperature Requirements Minimum temperature: 8-10°C Optimum temperature: 26-29°C Maximum temperature: 35-40°C Soil Suitability Grown under a variety of soils, with clay loam or loamy texture having good water retention being best suited. Area, Production and Productivity World production: 147 m.t. India's staple food crop in north Karnataka, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, and Rajasthan. India's total production: 11.08 m.t. India's productivity: 950 kg/ha.

Average and well distributed rainfall of 300-400 mm is optimum for rainfed sorghum. Field Preparation Field preparation: Field has to be prepared well in advance taking advantage of early showers. FYM @) 12.5 t/ha is applied at last ploughing. Chiselling is recommended to break hardpan once in three years. Varieties Local: Varsha, MAU 1, MAU 2 AICSIP developed 15 sorghum composite varieties (CSV 1 to CSV 15) and 18 hybrids (CSH 1 to CSH 18) Varieties (continued) CSH 1, CSH 6 and CSH 9 produce grain yield of 3.0 t/ha, while CSH 15 and CSH 18 produce grain yield of 4.3 t/ha. Seed Rate The seed rate is 12-15 kg/ha.

Seed treatment is done with Azospirillum and phosphobacteria each 3 pockets (600 gm). Sowing The seeds are sown before onset of monsoon at 5 cm depth with seed cum fertilizer drill or by seed drill or by country plough. Pre monsoon sowing/dry seeding i.e., sowing a week or 2 weeks before on set of monsoon is followed. Spacing 45×15 cm (1,80,000 plants/ha) 60/30×15 cm for intercropping and paired row system Manuring Application of FYM or compost at 12.5 t/ha during last ploughing is recommended. Growth stages There are five growth stages.

The growth stages of sorghum, from seedling to maturity. Growth Stages Seedling stage: 1–15 days Vegetative stage (Grand growth): 16–40 days Flowering/Reproductive stage: 41–65 days Maturity: 66–95 days Ripening: 96–105 days Weed Management Keeping the sorghum fields free of weeds from 2 weeks after germination till 5 weeks is good. If sufficient moisture is available, spraying atrazine 50%WP @ 1kg ai/ha as pre-emergence within three days of sowing followed by one hand weeding/inter cultural operation may be done. Striga Management Post emergence application of 2,4-D Na salt at 2.0 kg/ha at 25–30 DAS Intercropping with red gram Crop rotation with trap crops like cotton, sunflower, groundnut, cowpea, etc., which induce germination of weed seeds, but they are not themselves parasitized Heavy application of N and FYM and flooding the field Spraying Urea 10% solution on 25–30 DAS Using germination stimulants like Strigol and ethylene gas

Sorghum is often grown in combination with other crops, such as red gram, soybean, green gram, cowpea, black gram, to optimize yields. Thinning Thinning should be completed 10–15 days after emergence leaving one plant per hill. Harvesting and Threshing Most of the high yielding varieties and hybrids mature in about 100–115 days. The right stage for harvest is, when the grain becomes hard having less than 25% moisture.

The process of harvesting crops, including cutting or removing the plant material, allowing it to dry, and threshing the grain. Harvesting Methods Harvesting is done by cutting the entire plant or removing the ear heads first and cutting down the plants later. Harvesting is allowed to dry for 2–5 days. Threshing and Drying Threshing is done with the help of thresher or beating the ear heads. The threshed grain is dried in the sun for a week to bring the moisture content to 10–12% for safe storage. Yield Grain Yield (t/ha) 2–3 t/ha Dry Stover Yield (t/ha) 8–10 t/ha

Sorghum raised by either direct seeding or transplanting, with advantages including reduced main field duration and controlled shoot fly attacks. Advantages of Irrigated Transplanted Crop Main field duration is reduced by 10 days; shoot fly attacks will be economically controlled in the nursery; seedlings which show chlorotic and downy mildew symptoms can be eliminated; optimum population can be maintained as only healthy seedlings are used and seed rate is reduced by 2.5 kg/ha. Varieties CSV 1 to CSV 15: grain yield of 3.5-4 t/ha, in 110-115 days CO 25: grain yield of 6.0 t/ha, straw yield of 17.5 t/ha, in 115–120 days CO 26: grain yield of 6.0 t/ha, straw yield of 19.0 t/ha, in 105–110 days BSR 1: grain yield of 6-6.5 t/ha, straw yield of 9.6 t/ha, in 105–110 days Hybrids CSH 1 to CSH 18: grain yield of 4.5-5.0 t/ha, in 100-110 days CSH 5: grain yield of 4.5 t/ha, straw yield of 12.5 t/ha, in 100 days COH 4: grain yield of 6.5 t/ha, straw yield of 20.0 t/ha, in 105–110 days COH 5: grain yield of 6.8 t/ha, straw yield of 19.0 t/ha, in 100 days Seed Rate Direct sowing: 10 kg/ha; tran

A nursery is required for planting one ha, about 7.5 cent (300 m2) area near the water source. Preparation For planting one ha, about 7.5 cent (300 m2) nursery area is required, near the water source. Application of 750 kg of FYM or compost for 7.5 cent nursery is done and another 500 kg for covering the seeds after sowing is used. Raised Beds Forming raised beds of 2 m × 1.5 m with 30 cm spacing to a depth of 15 cm is done. Seed Treatment Carbendazim/captan/thiram @ 2 g/kg of seed (24 hours before sowing) 2% KHPO for 6 hours and shade dried for 5 hours 3 pockets of Azospirillum (600 g/ha) using rice kanji as binder

section: Sowing, Transplanting, and Irrigation in Agriculture
text: The process of sowing seeds, transplanting seedlings, and irrigating crops is a crucial part of agricultural practices. Sowing Forming rills using fingers, broad casting the seeds and covering with 500 kg of FYM is done. Irrigation Immediately after sowing 3rd day 7th day 12th day 17th day Transplanting Age of seedling is 15-18 days. The seedlings are dipped in Azospirillum solution for 15-30 minutes.

The field is prepared by ploughing with an iron plough once and twice with a country plough, followed by chiseling to overcome sub soil hard pan. Preparation of Main Field The field is prepared by ploughing with an iron plough once and twice with a country plough, followed by chiseling to overcome sub soil hard pan. Chiseling for Alfisol Soil chiseling the field at 0.5 m interval to a depth of 40 cm on both the direction of the field followed by disc ploughing once and cultivator ploughing twice Application of Organic Amendments Application of 12.5 t FYM or compost/ha with 2 kg of Azospirillum (10 pockets/ha) is recommended. Formation of Ridges and Furrows Ridges are formed at 45 cm apart Furrows are also formed at 45 cm apart

The process of applying fertilizers to crops in an efficient and effective manner. General Recommendations If soil test recommendation is not available, the blanket recommendation of 90:45:45 kg NPK/ha is recommended. For direct seeded crop, the blanket recommendation of 90:45:45 kg NPK/ha is followed. Application Timing 50% N and entire P and K should be applied basally before planting for transplanted crops. Remaining 50%N is applied on 15 DAS for transplanted crops. 50% N, and entire P and K should be applied basally and the remaining 50% N on 25–30 DAS for direct seeded crops. Micronutrient Application For Zn deficient soils, 25 kg ZnSO4/ha is applied at the time of sowing/transplanting. If Zn deficiency is noticed, ZnSO4 at 0.5% concentration is sprayed. Micronutrient Application (continued) For Fe deficient soils, 50 kg FeSO4 is applied at sowing or at planting. If Fe deficiency is noticed, FeSO4 at 1% concentration is sprayed. Spacing and Thinning The spacing is 45 × 15 cm (1,48,000 plants/ha) for both direct and transplanted crop. For raising intercrop and paired row system,

Sorghum is slow growing in the early stage and is adversely affected by weed competition. Pre-emergence Herbicide Application Pre-emergence herbicide Atrazine 50 WP at 500 g/ha (atrazine 0.25 kg/ha) on 3 DAS using high volume sprayer followed by one hand weeding on 30–35 DAS is recommended. Pulse Crop as InterCrop If pulse crop is raised as intercrop, do not use atrazine. Hand Weeding for Transplanted and Direct Seeded Crops Two hand weeding on 15–20 DAS and 35–40 DAS for direct seeded crop Two hoeing and weeding on 10 and 30–35 DAS for transplanted crop Water Management Total water requirement is 450–500 mm. Irrigation at 50% depletion of available soil moisture or 0.6 IW/CPE ratio is sufficient. Critical Stages of Water Stress One week before flowering One week after flowering Irrigation Scheduling For normal condition, 8 irrigations are to be given i.e. on 1st day, 4th day, 15th, 28th, 40th, 53th, 64th, 76th and 88th days. Harvesting and Processing When the crop matures, leaves turn yellow and the grains are hard and firm and moisture content will be less than 25%. At this stage,

The sorghum crop is intercropped with Cowpea, Soybean, Black gram and green gram. A stable food crop used by about 100 million people in rural areas of India and Sub Saharan Africa. Uses of Pearl Millet Roti or Chapatti, porridges, cooked grains, fried preparations, fermented products, beer, pancakes, fodder, and as pasture grass. Nutritional Content High protein (12.6%) High fat (5%) High fibre (1.2%) 60–70% of Carbohydrate Rich in Ca, Vitamin Riboflavin and Carotenoides Cultivation and Varieties Pennesitum glaucum Cultivated species for grain Pennesitum purpurea Forage species

Pearl millet is a crop grown in Africa, India, Pakistan, China, Sudan, and Egypt. Area, Production and Distribution It is largely grown in India. The important pearl millet producing countries are India, Africa, Pakistan, China, Sudan and Egypt. In India, it is cultivated in an area of 10 m.ha with a production of 7.9 m.t and productivity of 791 kg/ha. Area under cultivation is high in Rajasthan, followed by Maharashtra, Gujarat and Uttar Pradesh. The production is more in Rajasthan, followed by Maharastra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and Uttar Pradesh. Stages seedling stage (1–18 days) Tillering stage (19–35 days) Flowering phase (36–55 days) Maturity phase (56–85 days) Climate It is a rapid growing, warm weather crop and it has resistance for drought. The best temperature is between 20 and 28°C. It can withstand even desiccation. It is highly suitable for the areas having rainfall ranges from 400–750 mm. Rainfall during vegetative phase is highly favourable, while rainfall at flowering is not conducive, as it washes off the pollen and there is a poor seed setting. The crop grows better in

A type of pearl millet grown in India, sensitive to water logging and acidic soil. Soil Grown in a wide variety of soils, but sensitive to water logging. Grows well in well drained sandy loams. Time of sowing kharif (rainfed-June–October) winter (rainfed–November-February) summer (rain fed–March-June) Hybrids Many hybrids have been developed, including HB-3 and PHB 14, which are the best with a yield potential of 6.0 t/ha. Composite WCC 75 95 days Irrigated crop yields 3.0 t and rainfed crop yields 2.0 t/ha Planting methods Direct seeding either broadcasting or sowing behind country plough. (a) Raising seedling in the Nursery and transplanting. (b) Direct sowing.

section: A. Seed Rate and Seed Treatment
text: The seed rate for direct sowing is 5 kg/ha and for transplanting, it is 3.75 kg/ha. Seed Treatment Seed treatment is done with fungicides-captan or thiram 2 g/kg of seed, followed by Azospirillum seed treatment (3 pockets or 600 g/ha seed rate). Ergot Affected Seeds Remove using salt solution (1 kg of NaCl in 10 lit of water), to prevent primary infections and shade dried.

section: Field Preparation for Both Irrigated and Rainfed Crop
text: Deep ploughing with Iron plough and country plough is to be done twice to bring fine tilth. Land Shaping For irrigated crop (transplanting), either ridges and furrows at 45 cm apart or beds of convenient size depending upon the water availability are formed. For rainfed crop, flat sowing is followed. Transplanting Pull out of the seedlings is recommended when age of seedling is 15–18 days. Transplant single seedling at spacing of 45 × 15 cm (similar row spacing is adopted for rainfed crop also) with 3-5 cm depth. Direct Sown Crop Soaking the seed in 2% potassium chloride or 3% NaCl for 6 hours followed by shade drying for 5 hours is done. Seed rate is 5 kg/ha. Fertilizer Management Irrigated crop: Hybrids 80-100 : 40-50 : 40 kg N : PO : KO/ha. Varieties 80 : 40 : 40 kg N : PO : KO/ha. Rainfed crop: 60 : 30 : 30 kg N : PO : KO/ha. Water Management It is a highly drought tolerant crop and water requirement is 300–350 mm. Irrigation at available soil moisture of 50% or optimum IW/CPE ratio 0.4 is sufficient.

Three irrigations can be recommended for panicle initiation, flag leaf and flowering in addition to sowing irrigation. Thinning and Gap Filling In the direct sown crop, after 1st weeding at the time of irrigation, gap filling and thinning is done to a spacing of 15 cm between plants. In rainfed crop, thinning should be done 10-15 DAS. Weed Management Crop weed competition is up to 35 days. Pre-emergence application of atrazine at 500 g/ha followed by hand weeding on 30–35 days after transplanting or sowing. Cropping System 1.Bajra – Barley Intercropping system in North India 2. Bajra – Wheat 3.Bajra + Groundnut 4. Bajra – Gram 5.Bajra – Black gram 6. Bajra – Pea 7. Bajra + Green gram 8. Bajra – Potato 9. Bajra + Castor 10. Bajra + Cowpea Harvesting and Threshing The grains are separated either by beating the ear heads by sticks or by trampling by bullocks. If mechanical thresher is available, thresh it or spread it and drag a stoneroller over it.

The small millets have potentiality to grow even under adverse ecological condition and very poor agro-climate regions where main food crops cannot be grown. Types of Small Millets The five small millets are: 1. Finger millet (Ragi mandua): Eleusine coracana 2. Italian millet (Thenai, Kakun, Fox tail): Setaria italica 3. Kodo millet (Varagu): Paspalum scrobiculatum 4. Proso millet (Panivaragu, Cheena): Panicum millaceum 5. Barnyard millet (Kudiraivali, Sawan): Echinochloa frumentacea 6. Little millet (Samai): Panicum milliare List of Small Millets Finger millet Italian millet Kodo millet Proso millet Barnyard millet Little millet

It is a staple food crop in many hilly regions of the country, grown both for grain and forage. Cultivation and Uses It is cultivated mainly in Asia and Africa. It is grown both for grain and forage. In Northern hills, grains are eaten in the form of chapaties and in South India, grain flour is used for preparing gruel, cakes or unleavened bread, puddings, porridges, sweets etc. Nutritional Value Grains contain 9.2% protein, 1.29% fat, 76.32% carbohydrates, 2.24% minerals 3% ash and 0.33% Ca. Health Benefits It is good for persons suffering from diabetes. Green straw is suitable for making silage. Production and Area In India, it is cultivated in an area of 19.1 lakh ha with a production 27.62 lakh tonns The production is high in Karnataka, followed by Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh, Orissa, and Andhra Pradesh Soil and Climate It is grown in wide variety of soils and it thrives well in well-drained loam or clay loam. It tolerates salinity better than other cereals.

Ragi is cultivated in three seasons namely kharif, rabi and summer. Varieties VR 708 VL 352 GPU 45 RAU 3 VL 348 VL 149 GPU 28 GPU67 GPU85 RAU 8 BM 2 A404 Seed Rate and Sowing 10 kg/ha seed sown at spacing 25 cm with 2.5 cm depth. Main Field Preparation and Planting The field is ploughed thoroughly to get a fine tilth with mould board plough. FYM or compost at 12.5 t/ha is incorporated. Application of NPK Application of NPK is done as per soil test or a blanket recommendation of 60:30:30 of NPK kg/ha is recommended. Water Management Depending upon the duration of the crop (80, 100 and 120 days) and stage of the crop, irrigations may be given. Weed Management Application of Butachlor 2.5 l/ha or Fluchloralin 2 l/ha or pendimethalin 2.5 l/ha as pre-emergence with 600 liters of water. Cropping System Ragi is intercropped with legumes like field beans, cowpea, and fodder sorghum or occasionally with other millets. Pest and Disease Management To control mosaic virus, spraying Monocrotophos 36 WSC 0.05%

Control of blast involves spraying carbendazim, while harvesting is done in two stages due to non-uniform maturity. Blast Control Spraying of carbendazim 500 g/ha is recommended to control blast. If necessary, 2 and 3 spray may be given at 15 days interval after 1 spray. Root Aphid Control To control root aphids, dimethioate at 3 ml is mixed with 1 of water and drenching is done. Harvesting First harvest: ear head of main shoot and 50% of ear heads turn brown. Cutting, drying, threshing, and cleaning are done. Second harvest: seven days after first harvest. All ear heads including green ones are cut with sickles first, then straw is harvested. Curing Harvested heads are cured by heaping in shade for one day without drying to make greener ear heads mature. Then drying, threshing, and cleaning are done.

Italian millet is a type of grain that contains 12.3% protein, 4.7% fat, 60.6% carbohydrates, and 3.2% ash. Cultivation and Uses Italian millet is generally grown as a rainfed crop. Grain flour is used in the form of chapaties, and grains are fed to cage birds. Distribution and Importance Cultivated in India, China, Eastern Europe, Southern parts of former USSR, African, and American countries. Important crop in China, providing approximately 15–17% of the total food consumed. Soil and Climate Requirements Italian millet can grow in poor soils but requires fairly fertile soils for good yields. It thrives best on rich, well-drained loam soils and grows successfully with 50–75 cm rainfall. Varieties Maturity duration Grain yield (q/ha) Stover yield (q/ha) Short durarion MS 4872 65-70 12-15 MS 4884 65-70 12-15 BR 7 65-70 12-15

A highly drought tolerant crop that can be grown in areas with scanty and erratic rainfall, known for its coarse food grains and nutritional benefits. Characteristics It has a coarsest food grain covered with a horny seed coat, which should be removed before cooking. Immature and molded grains are poisonous. Nutritional Value 8.3% protein 1.4% fat 65.6% carbohydrates 2.9% ash Growth Requirements It thrives best on well drained sandy loam to loamy soils and requires rainfall of 400–500 mm. Varieties Short durarion JK13, 41, 65, 76, 155, 439 Medium durarion: GPUK,Pali, Didari, Niwas No 1 Distribution and Climate It is grown mostly in Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Uttar Pradesh. It makes rapid growth in warm and dry climate.

section: Common Millet (Panivaragu, Cheena, Proso millet): Panicum millaceum
text: The common millet offers better prospects for intensive cultivation in dry land areas and evades drought by its quick maturity. Nutritional Content Grain contains 12.5% protein, 1.1% fat, 68.9% carbohydrate, 2.2% crude fibre and 3.4% ash. Uses cooked grain flour for making chapaties perched grains poultry feed Origin and Distribution It is grown extensively in India, Japan, China, Egypt, Arabia and Western Europe. In India, it is largely grown in Madhya Pradesh, Eastern Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka. Soil and Climate Well drained loam or sandy loam, free of kankar and rich in organic matter is ideal for cultivation of common millet. It can be grown both in rich and poor soils having variable texture ranging between sandy loam and clays of black cotton soils.

A crop that can be grown in areas with scanty rainfall and can withstand water stagnation to a certain extent. Varieties RAU 2, Ko 4 and Arjun (75-80) SIA 326, SIA 2593, 3085, PS 4 (80-85) Maturity Duration and Yield Grain yield (q/ha) 10-12 Stover yield (q/ha) 20-25 Medium Maturity Duration SIA 326, SIA 2593, 3085, PS 4 (25-32)

A drought-resistant crop used in making rice pudding, consumed by poor class people, and as feed for cage birds. Characteristics Grains contain 6.2% protein, 9.8% crude fibre, 65.5% carbohydrates, and 4.4% ash. Uses Used in making rice pudding Consumed by poor class people Brewed for beer Cultivation Soil requirements Suitable soils Light soils including red loams, alluvial and black cotton soils Rich, well-drained loam soils Varieties Maturity duration: VL 172, Medium durarion: VL 207, RAU 3, RAU9 85-90. Stover yield (q/ha): 80-85, 15-18. Grain yield (q/ha): 12-15, 30-32.

Green gram is an excellent source of high-quality protein, near about 24%. Features of Green Gram Moong is consumed as whole grains as well as dal, sprouted whole moong is used in South India. In sprouted moong ascorbic acid (Vitamin-C) is synthesized and the amount of riboflavin and thiamine also increased. Benefits of Green Gram Being a leguminous crop, it can fix atmospheric N, it is also used as green manuring crop and helps in preventing soil erosion. Being a short duration crop it fits well in any crop rotation. Uses of Green Gram After picking of pods, it may be used as green fodder or as green manure. The husk of the seed can be used as cattle feed. Production and Area Contributes 14% in total pulses area Contributes 7% in total pulses production Origin and Cultivation Green gram is the native of India and Central Asia. In India moong is grown in almost all the states. It is grown in about 3.1 Mha with the total production of about 1.1 Mt of grain.

Greengram is widely cultivated in various parts of the world, including southern Asia and Africa. Geographical Distribution Greengram is widely cultivated in India, Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Pakistan, China, Fiji, Australia, America and Africa. It is also grown to a lesser extent in many parts of Africa and the USA, especially Oklahoma. Area Under Cultivation The area under this crop is around 3.2 million hectares with the production of 0.95 million tones and a productivity of 304 kg/ha. Regional Distribution in India Rajasthan (799.5 ha) Maharashtra (546 ha) Production by State in India Maharashtra (193.3 t) Andhra Pradesh (166.7 t) Botanical Description Small herbaceous plant growing to a height of 30-100 cm. The leaves are trifoliate with long petioles; the leaflet being large, ovate and entire.

Moong is considered to be the hardiest of all pulse crops. Climate and Elevation Moong requires a hot climate and can tolerate drought to a great extent. It can be grown from sea level to an elevation of 2000 metres. Seasons Kharif season in north India Summer season in north India Rabi season crop in south and south west Soil Requirements A well-drained loamy to sandy loam soil is best suited for moong cultivation. Saline and alkaline conditions should be avoided.

Moong varieties suitable for different seasons and regions in India. Characteristics of Moong Varieties Moong varieties have different maturity periods, yield potentials, and resistance to diseases. Variety Details Samrat: matures in 60-65 days, suitable for summer and Kharif season with a yield potential of 12-15 q ha. Pusa Vishal: matures in 65-70 days, suitable for summer and Kharif season with a yield potential of 12-15 q ha. Asha: suitable for irrigated condition in Kharif season, resistant to yellow mosaic virus, matures in 75-80 days, and yield potential is 12-15 q ha. Narendra moong 1: matures in 65-70 days, susceptible to yellow mosaic virus, and yield potential is 12-15 q ha. Pant moong 1: matures in 75 days in Kharif and 65 days in summer, resistant to yellow mosaic virus, and yield potential is 10-12 q ha. Pant moong 2: matures in 65-70 days in Kharif and 60-65 days in summer, resistant to yellow mosaic virus, and yield potential is 10-12 q ha. Pant moong 3: matures in 75-85 days and is suitable for growing in Kharif season, moderately resistant to yellow mosaic virus, an

Greengram and moongbean farming involves the cultivation of these two crops, which are commonly grown together in North India. Cropping Systems Maize-Wheat-Greengram Potato-Wheat-Greengram Greengram-wheat Greengram-potato Field Preparation A thorough land levelling is must for quick drainage. The crop requires fine seedbed preparation. Time of Sowing Kharif: Second fortnight of June to first fortnight of July Rabi: October to November Summer: Middle of March to middle of April Seed Rate and Spacing During Kharif season 12-15 kg seed per hectare should be sown in 45 cm apart, while during Rabi and summer seasons 20 kg seed per hectare should be sown in rows 30 cm apart. Seed Treatment Before sowing seed should be treated with Thiram or Carbendazim (Bavistin) at the rate of 2.5 g/kg of seed. Rhizobium Culture Rhizobium culture is a must to get a bumper crop, as it helps in the development of nodules on the roots which are beneficial for fixing atmospheric nitrogen in the soil. Manures and Fertilizers Greengram is generally raised on the residual fertility of soil. In case of light soil

section: Zinc Sulphate and Elemental Sulphur for Higher Yields
text: Application of 20 kg/ha each of zinc sulphate and elemental sulphur is essential for higher yields. Water Management For rainy season crop, irrigation is not needed but drainage is very important. For Rabi and summer five to six irrigations may be given. The first irrigation should be given about 20-25 days after sowing. The subsequent irrigations should be given at an interval of 12-15 days and irrigation should be stopped after 40-45 days of sowing. Weed Control Two weedings at 20 days interval from 25 days after sowing keep the field free from harmful weeds. Chemicals like Fluchloralin (Basalin) 1kg a.i. per hectare in 800- 1000 litres of water may be applied as pre-planting spray. Diseases Important diseases are yellow mosaic, mosaic mottle, leaf crinkle, leaf curl, seed and seedling rot, cercospora leaf spot, anthracnose and charcoal rot. The symptoms and control measures are given below-

Symptoms of Yellow mosaic virus appear with a month of sowing, causing leaf lamina to become yellow and scattered round spots. Control Measures Grow resistant varieties like Asha, Pant moong-4, Narendra moong-1 etc. Spraying of Oxydemeton methyl (Metasystox) (0.1%) + Melathion (0.1%) at 10 days interval is very effective.

Leaf margin shows upward rolling, become deformed, irregular light green areas appeared alternating with normal green in leaf surface. Symptoms Leaf margin shows upward rolling, become deformed, irregular light green areas appeared alternating with normal green in leaf surface. Control measures: Grow resistant/tolerant varieties, Spraying of Oxydemeton methyl (Metasystox) (0.1%) + Melathion (0.1%) at 10 days interval is very effective. Leaf Crinkle Symptoms appear first in third leaf after 3-4 weeks of sowing. Leaves become enlarge followed by crinkling Control measures: Rogue out disease plant as soon as they appear.

A viral disease characterized by curling of leaf margins downwards, reddish-brown discoloration on the under surface of leaves, and chlorosis around lateral veins. Symptoms It is a viral disease; chlorosis appear around the lateral vein near the leaf margin of young plants. The affected leaves show curling of margins downwards while the veins on the under surface of the leaf show reddish-brown discoloration. Control Measures Spraying of Oxydemeton methyl (Metasystox) (0.1%) + Melathion (0.1%) at 10 days interval is very effective.

Caused by two species of cercospora fungus, small round spots with violet red in colour may be observed. Control Measures Spraying of Mabcozeb 75 WP at the rate of 2 kg in 1000 litre of water per hectare at 10 days interval is very effective.

Diseased by fungus Colletorichum capsici, characterized by dark brown circular spot that increases in size with concentric ridges and ash color. Symptoms Diseased is caused by fungus Colletorichum capsici, dark brown circular spot appears initially, later the spots increase in size by developing concentric ridges and the colour turns into ash colour. Control measures Spraying of Mabcozeb 75 WP at the rate of 2 kg in 1000 litre of water per hectare at 10 days interval

Diseased is caused by a fungus Macrophomina phaseoli, characterized by rotting of roots and stems of the plant. Symptoms Affected parts of the plant turn into reddish-brown to black in colour. Control measures 1. Diseases can be controlled by treating the seed with Brassicol (0.25%) before sowing.

The pod borer is a destructive insect pest that damages crops at the time of pod formation, feeding on foliage and grains within pods. Characteristics Polyphagous in nature. Damage Damages crops at the time of pod formation, feeding on foliage and grains within pods.

The adult moths of these caterpillars lay eggs in large clusters and the young larvae congregated. Control Dusting by 2% Methyl parathion dust at the rate of 25-30 kg ha can be effective to control this disease. Spraying of Endosulfan 1.5 litres in 1000 litres of water can also be efficient. Control Basal application of Phorate (Thimet) 10% granules at the rate of 10 kg per hectare is very effective. Spraying of monocrotophos 36EC at the rate of ml/Litre of water can also be done.

Blackgram is a pulse crop rich in protein and phosphoric acid, used for various culinary preparations and as a green manuring crop. Uses of Black Gram It is used for preparation of 'bari' (spiced ball) which makes a delicious curry. It is the chief constituent of 'Papad.' Its husked dal is ground into a fine paste and allowed to ferment and then the fermented dal is mixed with equal quantity of rice flour to make 'dosa' and 'idli'. The dal of black gram is also used in the preparation of ‘halwa' and 'imarti'. Health Benefits Excessive use of black gram causes flatulence which can, however be prevented by adding little as a foetida, pepper and ginger in the culinary preparations. It should not be taken by those who are easily predisposed to rheumatic diseases and urinary calculi as it contains oxalic acid in high concentration. Cultivation and Uses It fits well as 'catch crop’. It is also an important crop for cultivating as ‘paira crop’ in paddy. The green plant (i.e., used as fodder) is very nutritive and it is very useful to milch cow specially. Environmental Benefits Black gram ha

Black gram is a native of India as seen from Vedic literature. History Black gram is a native of India as is seen from Vedic literature. There is mention of urd seed in Vedic texts such as Kautilya’s “Arthasastra” and “Charak Samhita”. According to Zokovskij (1962) urd originated in India from Phaseolus sublobatus (wild progenitor).

Blackgram occupies 2.97 million ha and contributes 1.25 million tonnes to pulse production with a productivity of 419 kg/ha. Regional Distribution The area under blackgram is highest in UP (539 ha) followed by Maharashtra (480 ha). The production under this crop is highest in Andhra Pradesh (251 tonnes) followed by UP (239 tonnes). Cultivation Patterns mainly as kharif crop almost in all states in northern plains, also cultivated during spring as a catch crop in southern and south-eastern region, cultivated in rice fallows during rabi

Vigna mungo is subdivided into two sub-species: Vigna mungo var. niger and Vigna mungo var. viridis. Characteristics of Sub-Species Vigna mungo var. niger includes varieties with early maturity and black, bold seeds. Vigna mungo var. viridis includes varieties with longer maturity period, small size seeds, and green colour.

It requires warm and humid conditions during growing season. Optimum Temperature The optimum temperature for growth ranges from 25-35C. Temperature Tolerance However, it can tolerate temperature up to 42C. Weather Conditions Heavy rains and cloudy weather at the time of germination are harmful. Heavy rains and cloudy weather during flowering stage are harmful. Day Length Short days are conducive for higher productivity.

Blackgram is best suited on well drained loams or slightly heavy clay loam soils with neutral pH. Optimal Soil Conditions Well drained loams or slightly heavy clay loam soils with neutral pH are best suited. Salt Tolerance and Saline Soils Due to its salt tolerance, it can be grown in moderate saline and alkali soils.

The field should be levelled and free from weeds, with land preparation involving 1-2 deep ploughing followed by 2-3 harrowing and planking. Importance of Field Preparation The crop does not require fine tilth but the field should be levelled and free from weeds. Land Preparation Process 1-2 deep ploughing 2-3 harrowing and planking Cropping in Rice Its utera cropping in rice involves no land preparation, as seeds are broadcast in standing crop of rice.

The sowing time for different crop seasons varies depending on the climatic condition. Seasonal Sowing Times The sowing time for different crop seasons are: (i)Kharif: Onset of monsoon in later part of June and early part of July. (ii)Rabi: October to November. (iii) Pre-Kharif or zaid : Last week of February to first week of April.

The seed rate and spacing of a crop vary depending on the season, with different rates required for kharif, other seasons, and utera cropping. General Guidelines In kharif, the crop is sown in rows 30-45 cm apart due to vigorous plant growth, while in other seasons, a narrow row of 20-30 cm is recommended. The plants are thinned to a spacing of 5-10 cm after germination and establishment. Seed Rate 15-20 kg/ha in kharif Double the seed rate of kharif for other seasons 30-50 kg/ha for utera cropping Optimum Population and Seeding Depth The optimum population is 4 lakh/ha in kharif, and 10 lakh/ha in spring and summer seasons. The optimum seeding depth is 4-6 cm.

Seed should be treated with specific chemicals or microorganisms before sowing to prevent disease incidence. Chemical Seed Treatments Seed should be treated with Agrosan GN or Emison-6 or Carbendazim 50% (Bavistin) or Mancozeb 75% WP (Dithane M-45, Indofil M-45 etc.) @ 3.0 g or Trichoderma viridi @ 5 g per kg of seed before sowing to prevent the incidence of diseases. Microbial Seed Inoculation Seed should be inoculated with Rhizobium culture for better nodulation and nitrogen fixation.

Black gram can be grown in various cropping systems, including rotations with other crops like rice, potato, maize, sorghum, wheat, pigeon pea, mustard, mungbean, and as an intercrop with sugarcane and sorghum. Importance of Black Gram Cropping Systems Black gram can be grown in various cropping systems, including rotations with other crops like rice, potato, maize, sorghum, wheat, pigeon pea, mustard, mungbean, and as an intercrop with sugarcane and sorghum. Rotations with Black Gram Paddy - Potato - Black gram Maize -Potato-Black gram Sorghum-Black gram-Wheat Maize-Toria -Black gram Maize -Wheat-Black gram Pigeonpea -Black gram-Wheat Maize-Mustard- Black gram Black gram -Toria -Wheat- Mungbean Mixed/ Intercropping of Black Gram Black gram can be grown mixed with other traditional crops like sorghum, maize, pearlmillet, pigeonpea during Kharif Season.

Black gram has a slow growth during its first 75-90 days. Benefits of Black Gram This space could otherwise be occupied by weeds causing some problem to crop. In case of paired row planting, two rows are made closer and thus this extra space is provided in between two pairs of rows. Inter Cropping with Sugarcane Black gram may be inter cropped with spring planted Sugarcane.

A variety is a specific type or cultivar of a plant species, distinguished by its unique characteristics. B-76 (Kalindi) Plant is dwarf and bushy. Pods are hairy and seed are bold and black in colour. Mature in 80-85 days with yield 15-20 q/ha. This variety is suitable for sowing from end of February to early July in West Bengal. HPU-6 Mature in 100-120 days with yield of 10-12 q/ha. It is a suitable variety for growing in Kangra and Kulu Valleys of Himachal Pradesh. Krishna The variety gives average yield of 8-10 q/ha in 90-100 days maturity period. Seed are bold and black in colour. Kulu-4 Maturity period is 120 days. Average yield is 8-10 q/ha. It is a suitable variety for cultivation in Kulu Valley in Himacba1pradesh. Mash-48 It is a semi dwarf variety with average yield of 15-20 q/ha. It is resistant to drought. Plants are spreading type. Maturity day is 85-90 days. It is susceptible to viral disease. Naveen Maturity period is 90-95 days. Seed are yellowish green in colour. Average yield is 10-12 q/ha. It is a suitable variety for cultivation in North Bihar as a catch crop betwe

Apply 20 kg nitrogen with 40-60 kg PO/ha. Seed Treatment Seed treatment with rhizobium helps in better nitrogen fixation. Seed treatment with PSB improves phosphorous availability to the plants. Fertilizer Application Drill fertilizers 5-7 cm below seed at sowing time. Application of S @ 20 kg/ha and Mo 0.5 kg/ha is beneficial. Inter cropping Fertilizer applied to main crop may also meet its requirement when raised as intercrop.

Irrigation in black gram depends upon the amount and distribution of rainfall during the growing season. Requirements for Irrigation In the absence of rains, irrigation should be given at flowering and pod filling stage. Irrigation Schedules 3-5 irrigations at 15-20 days interval Under irrigated conditions of rabi, spring and summer seasons

The management of weeds in agricultural settings is crucial to ensure crop health and productivity. Importance of Weed Control The short stature of crop in sole stands provides scope for intense weed competition. Initial 30-40 days after sowing is critical period of crop-weed competition. Recommended Weed Control Methods Two hand weeding at 20-25 and 30-40 days after sowing Pre-plant incorporation of fluchloralin or pre-emergence application of pendimethalin or alachlor @ 1 kg/ha

Spraying the crop with specific chemicals at certain concentrations can help manage diseases. Cercospora Leaf Scope Angular, brown or red colour spots with grey or brown centre and radish purple border are formed on leaves, stalks and pods. Treatment for Cercospora Leaf Scope Spray the crop with Blitox -50 or Indofil M -45 @ 1.5 to 2.0 Kg/ha in 500 l of water. Bacterial Leaf Scope Symptoms appear as water soaked dots on the under surface of the leaf which remain small in size and the surrounding tissues becomes necrotic. Treatment for Bacterial Leaf Scope Spray the crop with copper oxychloride @ 1.52 to 2.0 Kg in 500 l of water.

Affected plants show yellow and green areas on leaves, badly affected leaves turn completely yellow, and reduce yields considerably. Control Measures To control this disease, treat the seed with thiram @4 g/kg seed. Pest Management Hairy caterpillars Flea beetles Jassids White fly

Pigeonpea is the second most important pulse crop in the country. Uses of Pigeonpea It is consumed extensively as dal, as it is rich in protein (21%), iron and iodine. It is also rich in essential amino acids like lycine, tyrocene, cystine and arginine. Other Uses of Pigeonpea The pod husk and seed husk are used as feed for cattle. The dry sticks are used for thatching and fuel purpose. Environmental Benefits of Pigeonpea Pigeonpea being a legume possesses valuable property as restorer of nitrogen in soil. The plants shed large number of leaves, which add organic matter to soil.

India is believed to be the center of origin and diversity of pigeonpea. Geographical Distribution The closest wild relative of pigeonpea (Atylosia canifolia) was found in India and Australia. The centre of origin is the eastern part of peninsular India, including the state of Orissa, where the closest wild relatives (Cajanus cajanifolia) occur in tropical deciduous woodlands. Domestication From India it was domesticated to East Africa and West Africa. There was first encountered by Europeans, so it obtained the name Congo Pea. By means of the slave trade, it came to the American continent, probably in the 17th century.

Pigeonpea is grown in over 50 tropical countries, mainly in Africa, Asia, and the Americas. Main Producing Countries India Myanmar Malawi Uganda Kenya Tanzania Nepal Congo Haiti Major Regions of Cultivation Pigeonpea is mainly grown in Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. Early-Maturing Varieties In Punjab and Haryana, early-maturing varieties are grown, which escape frost.

A type of legume that comprises two varieties: Cajanus indicus var. bicolor (arhar) and Cajanus indicus var. flavus (tur). Characteristics of Cajanus indicus var. bicolor (Arhar) Late-maturing, tall and bushy perennial types with dark coloured pods containing 4 to 5 seeds. Characteristics of Cajanus indicus var. flavus (Tur) Early maturing, relatively short stature varieties with yellow flowers and plain pods containing 2-3 seeds.

Pigeonpea can be grown in a wide range of climatic conditions, including tropical and subtropical areas with temperatures between 20°-40°C. Optimum Conditions Moist and humid conditions during the vegetative phase and dry conditions during the reproductive phase are suitable for successful raising of pigeonpea. Limitations Cannot withstand water logging Cannot withstand frost Photoperiod and Light Intensity Pigeonpea is a short-day plant with a critical photoperiod of 13 hours. Low light intensity at pod formation is harmful.

Pigeonpea can be grown on a wide range of soils, but sandy loam to clay loams are ideal. Ideal Soil Conditions The soil should be deep, well drained and free from soluble salts. Soil pH Range 5.5-8.0 pH range of 5.5-8.0 successfully Limitations Due to Soil Acidity It cannot tolerate soil acidity owing to aluminium toxicity.

Pigeonpea can be intercropped or sown mixed with a number of other crops, such as sorghum, maize, rice, groundnut, sesame, urdbean, greengram, cowpea, ragi and soybean, and an additional yield may be obtained. Cropping System Details There is a possibility of raising early maturing pigeonpea as a summer crop with intercrop of greengram or cowpea. In this cropping system, pigeonpea may be sown in mid-April keeping a row-to-row distance of 75-90 cm, intercropped with 2-3 rows of greengram. Harvest Timing Greengram becomes ready for harvest by the end of June (65-70 DAS).

A clod and weed-free seed-bed for proper germination and establishment of seedlings is achieved by opening the soil through soil-turning plough or disc harrow followed by the cross-harrowing or ploughing with desi plough on or before the onset of monsoon. Importance of Field Preparation Thorough levelling is essential for quick drainage and also to avoid water logging. Sowing pigeonpea on a ridge and furrow planting is preferred to overcome water logging. Methods of Field Preparation soil-turning plough or disc harrow cross-harrowing ploughing with desi plough

Seed should be sown behind the plough or with the help of seed drill in rows. Row Spacing The row spacing in kharif varies from 40-60 cm in short and medium duration varieties to 60-90 cm in long duration varieties. In rabi season, the crop is grown in 30 cm rows. Thinning After germination, the seedlings are thinned to maintain an intra-row spacing of 15-20 cm. Optimum Population 60,000-1,00,000 in kharif 1.5-3.0 lakh/ha in rabi

Seed should be treated with thiram @ 2.5 g/kg seed, Rhizobium culture, or Trichoderma harzianum before sowing. Inoculation Methods Seed inoculation with Trichoderma harzianum alone or serial inoculation of T. harzianum, followed by Rhizobium may significantly reduce wilt incidence, enhance nodulation and root/shoot growth. Effectiveness of Inoculations Trichoderma harzianum + Rhizobium was ineffective

The sowing time for pigeonpea should be adjusted to avoid rains and frost at flowering and reproductive stages. Regional Sowing Times For early rabi planting in Bihar, eastern Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, September sowing is ideal. The rabi cultivation of pigeonpea in rice fallows is increasingly popular, and is sown immediately after rice harvest in southern India. Specific Sowing Times by Region Haryana: mid-March to mid-June (T-21) Uttar Pradesh and northern Rajasthan: mid of June to July end, second fortnight of June Bihar, eastern Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal: September Southern India: immediately after rice harvest Ist week of July (UPAS-120) First fortnight of April for double cropping (medium-early varieties) Late Pigeonpea Sowing The late pigeonpea is sown with the onset of monsoon, preferably by first week of July.

The recommended fertilizer dose is 15-20 kg N and 40-60 kg PO/ha. Seed Treatment Seed treatment with Rhizobium culture is beneficial. Fertilizer Dose 15-20 kg N/ha 40-60 kg PO/ha Convenient Application 100 kg diammonium phosphate is applied per hectare area. PSB Culture Use of PSB culture improves the available phosphorus status in the soil. Top-Dressing for Waterlogging 50 kg N/ha

Long duration pigeonpea with deep root system can withstand drought, while short duration cultivars require irrigation. Importance of Irrigation The critical stages for irrigation are branching, flowering and pod filling. Water Requirements 20-25 cm water to produce a tonne of grain. Irrigation at Critical Stages At times of prolonged drought, irrigation at flowering and pod filling stages is highly rewarding in Kharif.

Keeping crops free from weeds during critical periods is important for weed control. Critical Periods of Weed Competition The initial 7-8 weeks period of crop sowing to branching stage is critical, while in short duration varieties it is the first 4-6 weeks. Dominant Weed Species Trinthema monogyna Cyprus rotundus Amaranthus viridis Phylanthus niruri Sorghum halepense Cynodon dactylon Commelina bengalensis L. Euphorbia parviflora L. Celosia argentena L. Amaranthus spinosus L. Echinochloa colona L. Digitaria sanguinalis Dactyloctenium aegyptium L. Ageratum conyzoides L. Eclipta alba L. Portulaca oleracea L. Weed Control Methods Hand-weeding at 25 and 45 days after sowing Application of weedicide immediately after sowing Pre-plant incorporation of fluchloralin @ 1kg/ha Pre-emergence application of pendimethalin 1kg/ha Hand-weeding or mechanical hoeing at 6-8 weeks after sowing with herbicides more effective

Control measures for various plant diseases include treating seeds with thiram, using resistant varieties, crop rotation, removing excess water, and ensuring proper aeration. Causes of Diseases Various plant diseases are caused by viruses, mites, and fungi. Types of Diseases Wilt: The plant remains green and show wilting. Removal of roots shows browning of the xylum which curtail the uptake of nutrients. Sterility mosaic: This is caused by virus. The virus is transmitted by mites which results in malformation of flowers and no pods will be formed. Phytophthora stem blight: Brown colour spots will appear on the stem and the rotting will start at these spots and plant becomes week and fall down. Control Measures Before sowing, seed should be treated with thiram @ 2.5 g/kg seed. Use of resistant varieties is best in disease-prone areas. Use crop rotation. Remove the excess rain or irrigation water. There should be proper aeration in the field.

Pod borer is the major insect in North India. Control Measures For its control, spray monocrotophos 36 SL@750 ml/ha or 187.5 ml cypermethrin 25 EC or 300 ml fenvalerate 20 EC or 537.5 ml deltamethrin 2.8 EC in 750 liters of water per hactare at 50 % pod formation stage.

The process of separating seeds from their pods, typically involving threshing, winnowing, and drying to achieve a suitable moisture content. Threshing Ground and bundled. These are taken to threshing floor and staked upright, dried for a few days and shaken vigorously to separate pods. Winnowing The resultant material, i.e. pods and dry leaves, is beaten with sticks or is trampled by bullocks. The seeds and husk are separated by winnowing. Drying Threshed and cleaned produce should be further sun dried to reduce the moisture content to 10-11%.

The groundnut is a legume crop that belongs to the family Leguminosae/Fabaceae, resistant to soil erosion and useful as a rotational crop. Characteristics of Groundnuts Groundnut cake is chief oil cake feed to animals (7-8% N, 1.5% P2O5 and 1.2% K2O) and also used as manure. Nutritional Value of Groundnuts rich in nutrients, providing over 30 essential nutrients and phytonutrients good source of niacin, folate, fiber, magnesium, vitamin E, manganese and phosphorus

Groundnut is a native of Brazil, South America. History of Spread The crop has spread from Brazil to Peru, Argentina and Ghana, from where it was introduced by the Portuguese into Africa from where it was introduced into Jamaica, Cuba, West Indies islands and North America. Global Expansion from Mexico across the Pacific to Philippines then spread to China, India, Malaysia and Indonesia

Groundnut is grown in almost all tropical and subtropical countries of the world. Important Groundnut Growing Countries China India USA Nigeria Indonesia Myanmar Sudan Global Production Statistics Area (Mha) Production (Mt) 24.7 34.4 7.3 7.8 1.9 2.6 Productivity by State Tamil Nadu has the highest productivity (1630 kg ha), followed by Gujarat (1360 kg ha).

Groundnuts have been divided into two groups: the erect or bunch type and the trailing or spreading type. Characteristics of Groundnut Types Morphologically groundnuts have been divided into two groups. The erect or bunch type-include Arachis hypogaea subspecies fastigiata. Pods in erect type are borne in bunch close to the base of plant. Erect types are normally short duration. Seeds have no dormancy and sometimes the first form pod may sprout before harvest if conditions are suitable. This is due to presence of water-soluble auxins. Characteristics of Groundnut Types The trailing or spreading type-include Arachis hypogaea subspecies procumbens. Pods are spreading so harvesting is difficult. Comparatively it is longer duration crop than bunch type.

Groundnut is grown in the tropics and subtropical countries, lying between 45ºN and 35ºS, and up to an altitude of 1000 m. Ideal Climate Conditions The arid and semi-arid regions with 500-700 mm rainfall during crop growth period are ideal for ground production. The crop can be grown successfully in places receiving a maximum rainfall of 1250 mm. Climate Limitations The groundnut, however, cannot withstand frost, long and severe drought or water stagnation. Soil Temperature Requirements It seems that plant will grow best when the mean temperature is from 24-33ºC. During ripening period, it requires about a month of warm and dry weather.

Groundnut thrives best in well-drained sandy and sandy loam soils, with pH between 6.0-6.5. Optimal Soil Conditions Groundnut is grown on a wide variety of soil types but, thrives best in well-drained sandy and sandy loam soils, as light soil helps in easy penetration of pegs. Heavy and stiff clays are not desirable for groundnut cultivation as pod development is hampered in those soils. Soil pH Groundnut gives good yields in the soils with pH between 6.0-6.5.

Groundnut is grown in rotation with various crops, including wheat, lentil, chickpea, pea, barley, pearl millet, maize, sorghum, castor, cotton, and safflower. Common Cropping Systems The most common cropping systems are: Groundnut-wheat/barley/ chickpea/field pea / lentil. Regional Variations Sorghum is grown after harvest of groundnut in Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra.

Deep ploughing should be avoided for groundnut due to difficulties in harvesting, but a combination of soil turning plough followed by two harrowings can achieve good surface tilth up to 12-18 cm depth. Preparation Deep ploughing should be avoided for groundnut due to difficulties in harvesting, but a combination of soil turning plough followed by two harrowings can achieve good surface tilth up to 12-18 cm depth.

Seeds should be shelled by hand one week before sowing to prevent damage, and treated with a fungicide to check for diseases. Preparation of Seeds Pods should be shelled by hand one week before sowing. Hand shelling ensures little damage to seeds. Pods shelled long before sowing time are liable to suffer from loss of viability and storage damages. Seed Treatment with Fungicides Treat the selected kernels with 5 g of Thiram or Captan or Ceresan per kg of kernels so as to check various seed and soil borne diseases. Inoculation with Rhizobium Culture Seed should be inoculated with proper strain of Rhizobium culture particularly in those places where groundnut is to be grown for the first time.

section: Seed Rate, Spacing and Sowing Method
text: Seed rate depends upon the growth habit of variety and seed weight for obtaining good yields. General Guidelines Seed rate can vary according to the region also. In bunch types, the row-to-row distance is kept 30-40 cm and in spreading types 45-60 cm. Seeding Requirements 80-100 kg of seeds per hectare for bunch types 60-80 kg for spreading types Plant-to-Plant Distance Plant to plant distance would be 15 and 20-22.5 cm for bunch and spreading types respectively. Sowing Methods Seed drill Behind the country plough Hand dibbling Tractor-mounted groundnut planter Sowing Depth The depth of sowing should be 5 cm.

The time when a rainfed crop is sown, typically in the last week of June to first week of July for most crops, but can vary depending on irrigation conditions or region. General Sowing Time The time when a rainfed crop is sown, typically in the last week of June to first week of July for most crops, but can vary depending on irrigation conditions or region. Regional Variations Southern states: November-December (groundnut) Gujrat, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh: Second fortnight of January to first fortnight of February (summer groundnut)

Moongphali is a type of crop that contains 53% oil and has a shelling percentage of 78%. Varieties RS-1 Chitra Amber PG. NO.1 Moongphali No. 145 BG-1 & BG-2 Kopergaon No.1 TMV-6 Characteristics Seeds size Medium Oil percentage 53% Shelling percentage 78% Oil percentage 48% Shelling percentage 72% Yield potential 15-20 quintals per hectare

Groundnut needs more phosphorous, sulphur, calcium, and nitrogen for its growth. Nutrient Requirements Groundnut needs more phosphorous, sulphur, calcium, and nitrogen for its growth. Nitrogen Requirement can be partially met by seed inoculation with efficient strains of rhizobium

section: Maintaining Organic Carbon in Soil for Good Yields
text: A desirable level of organic carbon in the soil (0.3-0.7%) must be maintained to ensure overall health of soil and continued good yields. Fertilizer Application Apply 15 kg N, 50 kg P2O5 and 25 kg ZnSO4/ha at the time of sowing. Phosphorus should be applied preferably through single super phosphate; it provides sulphur in addition to phosphorous. Fertilizer Placement The fertilizers should be placed at the time of sowing about 4-5 cm in the side of the seed and 4-5 cm below the seed level. Calcium and Yield Calcium too has pronounced effect on proper development of pods and kernels. Use of gypsum @ 100-150 kg/ha at the time of field preparation can add to the yield.

Groundnut does not require irrigation as a rainy season crop, but care should be taken to ensure the soil is friable and has sufficient moisture content. Importance of Irrigation in Groundnut Cultivation Irrigations are necessary in southern part of country where groundnut grown in Rabi season too, three to four irrigations are necessary. Critical Stages for Irrigation Flowering Pegging Last Irrigation Before Harvesting The last irrigation before harvesting will facilitate the full recovery of pods from the soil.

Irrigation at 25% depletion of available soil moisture throughout the growth period results in high pod yield. Optimal Irrigation Schedules Irrigation at 25% depletion of available soil moisture from pegging to early pod development and at 50% DASM at other stages appears to be ideal for high water use efficiency. IW/CPE Ratio for High Water Use Efficiency An IW/CPE ratio of 1.0 at moisture sensitive stages and 0.6 during other stages leads to high water use efficiency.

A reduction of 20-45% in yield due to weeds has been recorded. Recommended Weed Control Measures Two weedings 20 and 45 (days after sowing) DAS are recommended. No weeding or intercultural operation should be done after pegging has commenced; pegs have started moving undergrounds. Earthing Up Earthing up can be done in bunch and semi spreading types to facilitate maximum penetration of pegs. Pre-Emergence Application Pre- emergence application of Pendimethalin @ 1 kg a.i./ha along with 2 inter-cultures at 30 and 45 DAS have been recommended in irrigated conditions. Fluchloralin (Basalin) at the rate of 1 kg a.i. per hectare dissolved in 800-1000 litres of water can also be used as pre-planting incorporation.

The management of diseases in groundnut crops. Tikka Disease or Leaf Spot Cercospora arachidicola and Cercospora personatum cause Tikka disease, appearing 3-4 weeks after sowing. Spots on leaves are circular to irregular, surrounded by a yellow halo, and can be reddish brown to black on the upper surface and smooth and light brown on the lower surface. Collar Rot and Seed Rot Aspergillus niger causes collar rot and seed rot. Symptoms include rotting of seeds, soft rot of hypocotyls, and post emergence collar rot of seedlings. Treatment involves using Thiram or Captan on healthy seeds. Sclerotium Rot Sclerotium rolfsii causes sclerotium rot, characterized by white thread-like fungal growth and yellow to brown leaves. Soil application of Brassicol before sowing is beneficial. Charcoal Rot Microphomina phaseoli causes charcoal rot, marked by a red-brown water-soaked lesion on the stem of infected plants. Spraying Brassicol before sowing is effective. Rust Puccinia arachidis causes rust, characterized by red pustules on leaves that turn dark brown. Treatment involves spraying Zineb as so

White-grub, a menace in the light soils of Rajasthan, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and Haryana can be controlled effectively by treating seed with Chlorpyriphos 20 EC or Quinalphos 25 EC@ 15 ml/kg of seeds. Control Measures White grubs live in soil and remain active from July

Controlling pests such as aphids, jassids, thrips, moths, and leaf minor using various methods including spraying pesticides. Pest Control Methods Using light traps to destroy moths may control leaf minor. Carbaryl 50 WP 0.02% spray is most economical. Spraying Pesticides Spray 500 ml malathion 50EC in 500 lt. of water per hectare

A carcinogenic substance produced by mould such as Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus in kernels during post harvest processing and storage. Prevention and Control Measures It is desirable to store groundnuts in gunny bags as pods rather than kernels. The gunny bags are stacked in a store-room over planks in tiers comprising not more than ten in each in such a way that air keeps circulating. Detoxification Methods Filtration at oil mills Exposure to sunlight for an hour (removes nearly 90% of aflatoxin) Chemicals such as chloride, peroxide, sodium bisulphate

Soybean is an important pulse crop rich in food value. Characteristics and Uses of Soybean It is a cheapest, richest and easiest source of best quality protein and fat. It is more considered as oilseed crop owing to its multiplicity of uses as food and industrial products, it is called a ‘wonder crop or miracle crop’. It is the number one oilseed crop of the world which contains 40% protein and 20% oil. Nutritional Value of Soybean Soybean protein is rich in the valuable amino acid lysines (5%) in which most of the cereals are deficient. The seeds contain good quality protein rich in lysine and oil is having considerable amount of essential fatty acids (Omega-6 and Omega-3). It also contains phytochemicals known as isoflvines which protect human body against chronic diseases such as cancer, diabetes, osteoporosis and blood pressure. Benefits of Soybean for Soil Fertility Soybean, being leguminous crop, improves the soil fertility by fixing atmospheric nitrogen and also through leaf fall at maturity. Culinary Uses of Soybean bread kachori pastries high-protein food for children food f

Soybean is reported to have been originated in Eastern Asia, especially in China around 2800 B.C. History of Soybean Origin The wild ancestor of the soybean is Glycine soja (previously called G. ussuriensis), a slender twining vine legume native to central China and Korea. Spread of Soybeans Japan other countries Introduction to India In India, the cultivation of soybean was first started at Nagpur (1822).

The United States of America have become the world leading producer of soybeans. Key Producers USA Brazil Argentina China India Global Production Share These countries represent more than 90% of global soybean production.
