Avoid excessively dense plant populations. Use mechanical or manual intercultivation. Apply balanced NPK; excessive nitrogen may increase crop succulence. Manage irrigation and drainage to avoid pest and disease build-up. Use intercropping. Use crop rotation.

Loss of soil productivity or a process that lowers current or potential soil capacity to produce. Source figures About 32.7% of the total geographical area is stated as degraded. Total geographical area: 328.73 million ha. About 65% of land degradation occurs through water and wind erosion. Net sown area: 141.89 million ha. Types and area Water erosion: 57.16 mha. Wind erosion: 10.46 mha. Ravines: 2.68 mha. Salt affected: 6.32 mha. Water logging: 3.20 mha. Mines and quarry wastes: 0.25 mha. Shifting cultivation: 2.35 mha. Degraded forest: 24.9 mha. Special problems: 0.09 mha. Total listed degraded area: 107.43 mha.

Soil degradation is classified in the source as physical, chemical and biological degradation. Physical degradation Soil erosion. Soil slips. Soil slides. Mud flow. Water logging. Chemical degradation Soil salinity. Soil sodicity. Soil acidity. Biological degradation Loss of soil organic matter. Associated with high temperature and low water content.

Human, environmental and management pressures that reduce land quality. Factors Extensive and frequent cropping. Excessive fertilizer use. Shifting cultivation without adequate recovery. Poor irrigation practices. Over-extraction of groundwater. Conversion of forest and agricultural land to other uses. Urban encroachment. Deforestation and illegal felling. Overgrazing and excessive fuel-wood collection. Industrial and mining activities without adequate preventive measures. Human and livestock pressure. Frequent drought or monsoon failure.

Detachment of soil particles from the parent soil body. Types Wind erosion. Water erosion. Wave erosion. Wave erosion Caused by combined action of wind and water. Occurs mainly along canal and river banks. Can be controlled by lining canals. Basic relationship Erosion = f(erosivity) × (erodibility). Erosivity is the potential ability of rain to cause erosion. Erodibility is soil vulnerability to erosion based on inherent properties.

section: Factors and Losses Due to Soil Erosion
text: Rainfall, vegetation and soil properties control erosion and its effects. Factors Rainfall amount, intensity, duration and distribution affect runoff and erosion. Vegetative cover intercepts rainfall and reduces erosion. Topography affects runoff and particle transport. Increasing slope generally increases erosion. Major losses Loss of rainwater from fields. Loss of fertile topsoil. Loss of plant nutrients. Siltation of reservoirs and reduced storage capacity. Source figures Soil loss is stated as 16.35 t/ha annually. Permissible limit is stated as 11 t/ha.

Water erosion is described through sheet, rill and gully stages; USLE is used to predict soil loss. Stages Sheet erosion: uniform removal of a thin topsoil layer. Rill erosion: small channels formed by runoff. Gully erosion: advanced rill stage with deep and wide channels. USLE A = R K L S C P. A = predicted soil loss. R = rainfall and runoff factor. K = soil erodibility. L = slope length. S = slope gradient. C = soil cover and management. P = erosion-control practice.

Wind-driven movement of soil particles through saltation, suspension and surface creep. Particle movement Saltation: bouncing of fine particles around 0.1–0.5 mm. Suspension: movement of very fine particles or dust below 0.1 mm. Surface creep: movement of particles above 0.5 mm and below 1.0 mm along the surface. Factors Wind velocity is a major factor. The source states wind velocity above 5–6 m/s is undesirable. Soil texture, structure, cohesiveness, bulk density, organic matter, moisture and surface roughness affect erosion. Vegetative cover reduces erosion. Wind erosion equation E = I R K F C W D B. E = soil loss by wind erosion. I = soil cloudiness factor. R = surface cover factor. K = surface roughness factor. F = soil textural class factor. C = local wind factor. W = field width factor. D = wind direction factor. B = wind barrier factor.

A sustainable-agriculture approach focused on efficient use and conservation of limited natural resources. Need Green Revolution increased food production, but sustainability is now a major concern. Limited land and water resources require continuous productivity improvement. Poor resource management and excessive agrochemicals threaten sustainability. Impacts include biodiversity loss, land and water degradation, pollution and climatic changes. Water-resource pressures Limited expansion of irrigation potential. Non-judicious use of water. Poor irrigation-project efficiency, stated as only 30–40%. Conveyance losses. Diversion of agricultural water to non-agricultural uses. Increasing groundwater pollution.

Resource-conservation strategies for maintaining agricultural productivity and ecological balance. Biological diversity Maintain essential ecological processes. Preserve genetic diversity. Ensure sustainable use of species and ecosystems. Diversification Use crop diversification. Integrate dairy, fisheries, poultry, horticulture and forestry. Reduce monoculture effects. Improve soil health and resource use. Support nutrient recycling. Reduce risk and uncertainty. Improved systems Integrated intensive farming system uses farm-grown biological inputs and nutrient recycling. Precision farming improves input-use efficiency. Use soil-test-based fertilizer application. Use land leveling and micro-irrigation. Include legumes in crop rotations. Other measures Use organic farming. Reclaim degraded land. Use integrated water management. Use bio-intensive integrated pest management.

An agricultural system dependent on substantial external inputs such as hybrid seed, fertilizers, pesticides, machinery and irrigation. Development Developed in response to rising food demand. Green Revolution emphasized higher harvest per unit area and increased cropping seasons. High-yielding hybrid varieties required new production practices. Input dependence Chemical fertilizers were used heavily because hybrid varieties were nutrient sensitive. Pesticides were needed because new crops were susceptible to pests and diseases. Weedicides or manual weeding were needed because dwarf hybrids competed poorly with weeds. Mechanization became an integral component. New crops required more water and improved irrigation. Sustainability issue Many external resources were not recycled. The system depended on regular external inputs for high yields. Stopping inputs could make the system unproductive.

Benefits attributed in the source to high external input agriculture. Advantages Rapid increase in agricultural production. Improved food availability. Reduction of some nutrition-related problems. Improved varieties can give yields in a short period. Mechanization helps address labour shortages. Higher income and profit margins. Higher land productivity. Improved market facilities.

Environmental, economic and social problems associated in the source with high external input agriculture. Major disadvantages Reduced biodiversity can disturb environmental balance. Machinery may increase soil erosion through constant furrowing. Dependence on imported machinery, fertilizers, pesticides and hybrid seed. Pesticides can kill natural enemies as well as target pests. Agrochemicals can affect soil pH, CEC, structure, texture and soil organisms. High capital requirements can disadvantage capital-poor farmers. Traditional varieties and indigenous knowledge may decline. Farmers may face environmental, social and economic problems.

Shortcomings identified by the source in planning and long-term effects of Green Revolution practices. Economic and ecological issues Surplus production could contribute to lower commodity prices. Long-term dependence on pesticides and chemical fertilizers was not fully anticipated. Quick crop response encouraged artificial-manure use without awareness of long-term effects. The source states that 40–50% of applied nitrogen may be wasted in tropical countries. Nitrogen losses increase with high rainfall, drought, erosion and low organic matter. Continuous NPK use may create micronutrient deficiencies. Nitrous oxide contributes to atmospheric and ozone-related concerns. Pesticide issues Pesticide poisoning can affect people. Repeated use can lead to pest resistance. Pesticides can kill natural enemies. Pesticides can contaminate water, air, soil and food. Pesticides can enter food chains and food webs.

section: Low External Input and Sustainable Agriculture (LEISA)
text: An integrated agricultural system designed to maintain optimum production using fewer external inputs in an eco-friendly manner. Need Developed in response to high capital needs and environmental impacts of HEIA. Combines selected traditional principles with newer technology. The source describes LEISA as integrating bio-dynamic, environmental, natural, organic and regenerative subsystems. Ecological principles Maintain favorable soil conditions and stimulate soil microorganisms. Maintain nutrient balance through fixation, deep nutrient use, recycling and needed supplementation. Control microclimate-related resource losses. Use biological and mechanical erosion control. Prioritize natural biological pest control. Promote biodiversity and plant–plant and plant–animal interactions. Core practices Maintain a living soil. Create biodiversity. Recycle resources. Use natural pest management.

LEISA emphasizes maintaining the biological, physical and chemical characteristics needed for productive soil. Requirements Adequate water, air and nutrients. Favorable soil structure for water, nutrients and root growth. Suitable soil temperature. Absence of poisonous substances. Active soil microorganisms. Soil organisms Microflora: bacteria, fungi and algae. Microfauna: protozoa. Mesofauna: nematodes. Macro animals: weevils, centipedes, termites, rats, worms and snakes. Microorganism functions Decompose organic matter into humus. Mineralize humus and release nutrients. Assist nitrogen fixation. Convert insoluble phosphate to soluble forms. Help plants absorb nutrients. Maintain soil sanitation. Help suppress harmful microorganisms.

Reuse of farm outputs and residues as inputs to maintain nutrient balance and reduce external-input dependence. Nutrient balance Nutrient removal should not exceed nutrient inflow. Natural recycling can maintain nutrient balance when not disturbed. Nitrogen fixation, organic manure, suitable fertilizer combinations and crop rotations support recycling. Farm examples Paddy straw can be recycled as a nutrient source. Maize residues can be returned to the soil. Dairy wastes can become manure. Crop and livestock enterprises can exchange outputs and inputs.

Preventive, biological, mechanical and natural-product methods used to manage pests in sustainable systems. Preventive measures Treat seed and planting material before planting. Use hot-water treatment where suitable. Use wood ash and sun drying where appropriate. Maintain hygiene of farm implements. Remove infested fruits, plants, ratoons and host plants. Crop resistance Select varieties resistant to pests and diseases. Use multiple cropping to promote natural predators. Methods Biological control. Mechanical control. Natural pesticides. Artificial pesticides when included within the listed integrated methods. Natural pesticide examples Garlic. Big onion. Pepper. Tobacco. Neem.

Problems caused by excessive irrigation, poor water quality, high water tables and inadequate drainage. Major problems Soil salinity. Soil alkalinity. High water table. Poor drainage. Main causes Saline irrigation water. Salt deposition from a high water table. Canal seepage. Arid climate. Poor drainage. Backwater flow in coastal areas. Controlling factors Quality of irrigation water. Irrigation frequency. Soil type and permeability. Crop salt tolerance. Climate.

Salt-affected soils distinguished in the source using EC, ESP, pH, salt composition and physical condition. USDA classification Saline: EC >4 mmhos/cm; ESP <15; pH <8.5. Saline-alkali: EC >4; ESP >15; pH >8.5. Alkali: EC <4; ESP >15; pH 8.5–10.0. Saline soil Common in arid and semi-arid areas. Favored by high water table, high salt concentration, high temperature and low rainfall. Main soluble salts include chlorides and sulphates. ESP is below 15%; pH is below 8.5. EC is above 4 mmho/cm. Generally flocculated with relatively normal aeration and permeability. Can be reclaimed mainly through leaching and ponding. Alkali soil Common in Indo-Gangetic plains and poorly drained low-lying areas. Carbonates mainly involve sodium. ESP is above 15%; pH is above 8.5. EC is below 4 mmho/cm. Soil is dispersed and compact with poor aeration and permeability. Amendments such as gypsum or iron pyrite are important. Formulas ESP = exchangeable sodium / total cation exchange capacity × 100. SAR = Na+ / √(Ca2+ + Mg2+) .

Land that is unproductive or underutilized because of neglect, degradation or constraints, though some wastelands can be reclaimed. Definitions Wasteland Survey and Reclamation Committee (1961): lands unavailable for cultivation or left as fallows and cultivable wastes. National Wasteland Development Board: lands currently unutilized due to different constraints. Wastelands include culturable and unculturable categories. They are also termed degraded lands. Classification Culturable wastelands have potential for vegetative cover but face constraints such as erosion, waterlogging and salinization. Many culturable wastelands can be made productive through treatment and reclamation. Unculturable wastelands cannot be developed for vegetative cover, such as barren rocky or snow-covered areas. Source figure About 158 mha of India's 329 mha geographical area is stated as being under different kinds of land degradation.

Site-specific reclamation and vegetation measures for degraded and underutilized lands. Ravine land River erosion and deposition create ravine lands. Known locally as khadar, diara, char, rao and cho in different regions. Use soil-conservation measures. Live hedges help control erosion and sediment deposition. Coastal sandy areas Afforestation is recommended. Wide forest belts can moderate cyclone effects. Casuarina tolerates salinity and moisture stress. High-altitude and steep slopes Excess runoff during monsoon can cause erosion and floods. Dry periods may create moisture deficiency. Indiscriminate grazing is a major erosion cause. Use hedgerow planting and suitable agroforestry trees and shrubs.

A farming system that largely excludes synthetic inputs and relies on ecological processes, organic resources, crop rotations and biological nutrient and pest management. Concept Organic farming has been practiced in India since ancient times. Aims to regenerate natural processes and make the farm ecosystem self-sustainable. Organic components vary with crop, region and time. The common goal is continued production through a self-supporting system. USDA definition in source Avoids or largely excludes synthetic fertilizers, pesticides, hormones and feed additives. Relies on crop rotations, crop residues, animal manures, off-farm organic waste, mineral-grade rock additives and biological nutrient and plant-protection systems. Aims Work within a closed system using local resources. Maintain long-term soil productivity. Avoid agrochemical pollution. Minimize fossil-energy use.

Principles that guide nutrient supply, pest management, biological nitrogen fixation and biomass recycling in organic farming. Core principles Crops should obtain nutrients through soil biological activity under suitable conditions. Pests and diseases should be controlled mainly through natural enemies, predators, biological agents and natural products. Organic sources may be used in digested, semi-digested or undigested forms. Natural resistance of crops to pests and diseases should be utilized. Biological nitrogen fixation should be encouraged. Biomass management should support a self-supporting nutrient system. IFOAM-style principles presented in source Principle of health. Principle of ecology. Principle of fairness. Principle of care.

Major biological and organic inputs used for nutrient supply and soil management. Biofertilizers Contain selected microorganisms. May fix atmospheric nitrogen or make insoluble phosphorus available. Are described as cost-effective, eco-friendly and renewable nutrient sources. Major groups Free-living nitrogen fixers. Symbiotic nitrogen fixers. Associative symbiotic organisms such as Azospirillum. Phosphorus-solubilizing bacteria and fungi. Arbuscular and ectomycorrhiza. Other biological inputs Azolla. Plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR). Mycorrhizal fungi.

Microbial inoculants used for nitrogen fixation, phosphorus mobilization and plant growth support. Nitrogen-fixing groups Azotobacter: free-living nitrogen fixer. Rhizobium: symbiotic association with legumes. Azospirillum: associative symbiotic nitrogen fixer of graminaceous plants. Azolla: free-floating fern capable of fixing atmospheric nitrogen. Phosphorus-related inputs Bacillus spp. and Aspergillus niger can solubilize unavailable phosphorus. Mycorrhiza assists nutrient transfer, especially phosphorus, and may also help zinc and sulphur transfer. PGPR Colonize roots or rhizosphere soil. Benefit crops through growth-promoting effects. Some produce phytohormones and are used as biostimulants.

Organic materials used to supply nutrients and improve soil physical and biological properties. Sources Cattle shed wastes. Human habitation wastes. Poultry litter and sheep/goat droppings. Slaughterhouse wastes. Agro-industry by-products. Crop residues. Water hyacinth, weeds and tank silt. Green manure and green-leaf material. Groups Bulky organic manures. Concentrated organic manures. Benefits of bulky manures Supply plant nutrients including micronutrients. Improve soil structure and water-holding capacity. Increase nutrient availability. Influence soil biological activity during decomposition.

Decomposed mixture of dung and urine of farm animals with associated litter and refuse. Preparation Trenches are described as about 6 m long, 2 m wide and 1 m deep. Dung and urine-soaked material is collected daily. Litter and refuse are mixed with soil to absorb urine. Collected material is placed in the trench in sections. Use Partially rotten FYM should be applied about 3–4 weeks before sowing. Manure left exposed in the field for long periods may lose nutrients. Immediate incorporation after spreading reduces losses. Responsive crops listed include potato, tomato, sweet potato, carrot, radish, onion, sugarcane, rice, Napier grass and several orchard crops.

Controlled decomposition of organic wastes into a stable manure-like material. Aerobic method Organic material is decomposed in the presence of air. Turning is used to facilitate decomposition. The source states decomposition ordinarily completes in about 4–5 months. In heavy rainfall or high-water-table areas, heaps may be prepared above ground. Anaerobic method Uses a pit with compacted layers of farm residues. Fresh cow dung, ash and water are added. The pit is filled and decomposition proceeds without regular aeration.

Compost produced through the feeding and activity of earthworms on organic waste. Process Earthworms feed on waste organic material. Organic matter is converted into vermicompost. The source describes a harvesting and separation process after about four months. The compost is dried in shade and sieved. Earthworms are collected for the next preparation cycle. Handling Water is supplied as required during preparation. Finished compost is packed in suitable polythene or laminated bags.

Ploughing or incorporating green plant material into soil to add organic matter and nutrients. Benefits Recycles nutrients. Adds organic matter. Reduces nutrient leaching. Can improve crop yield. Improves soil fertility. Improves soil structure. Helps prevent soil erosion. Can aid weed control. Green-leaf manuring Uses green leaves and tender twigs from shrubs and trees. Material may be collected from bunds, wastelands and nearby areas. Examples include Glyricidia, Sesbania speciosa and Karanj. In situ practice Green-manure crops are incorporated into the soil at a suitable stage. Legumes and nitrogen-fixing plants are especially useful.

A holistic farm-management approach integrating crops and allied enterprises so that outputs or wastes of one enterprise become inputs for another. Examples Crops. Dairy. Poultry. Fishery. Sericulture. Piggery. Apiary. Tree crops. Integration examples Dairy dung and urine can produce FYM or compost. Crop straw can feed dairy cattle. Mulberry leaves feed silkworms. Maize grain can be used as poultry feed. Objective Optimize production through efficient input use. Maintain environmental quality. Support national goals and farm-household needs.

section: Principles and Scope of Farming System
text: Farming-system planning integrates resource, enterprise, economic and environmental considerations. Overall objectives Identify existing farming systems. Develop models combining main and allied enterprises. Optimize utilization and conservation of resources. Maintain sustainable production without resource damage. Increase farm-household profitability through complementary enterprises. Scope factors Soil and climate. Land, labour and capital availability. Current resource utilization. Economics of the proposed system. Farmer's managerial skill. Enterprise-selection factors Local soil and climate. Farmer resources. Existing resource use. System economics. Managerial skill. Local social customs.

A participatory research approach based on interdependence among farming-system components and the natural environment. Core idea Farmers participate in identifying research problems. Farmers participate in testing possible solutions. Technology should be evaluated beyond technical performance. Research should be grounded in small-farmer conditions.

Features that make farming-system research and development farmer-oriented, location-specific and sustainability-focused. Characteristics Farmer-oriented and holistic. Effective farmer participation. Problem-solving approach. Dynamic system. Gender sensitive. Responsible to society. Environmental sustainability. Location-specific technology. Diversified enterprises to reduce environmental risk. Additional characteristics Bottom-up approach. Focus on small and marginal farmers. Extensive on-farm activities. Collaboration between farmers and scientists. Focus on actual adoption. Recognizes interdependence among multiple clients.

Production, income, employment, resource-use and environmental objectives achieved through integrated enterprises. Objectives Increase productivity per unit area and time. Improve profitability through complementary enterprises. Promote balanced food production. Improve environmental safety. Provide income or cash flow throughout the year. Help meet fodder requirements. Help meet timber and fuel requirements. Generate employment. Create scope for agro-industries. Improve input-use efficiency. Reduce production risk through enterprise diversification.

Physical, biological, resource and human factors that determine the type of farming system. Factors Physical and biological conditions set limits on suitable enterprises. Quantity and quality of land, water and other resources influence choices. Farmer goals and attitudes affect the system. Resource availability and resource-use level shape enterprise combinations.

Principles and practices of cropping and their interaction with farm resources, technology and environmental conditions. Multiple cropping Sequential cropping: two or more crops grown in sequence on the same field in a year. Intercropping: two or more dissimilar crops grown simultaneously. Types of intercropping Mixed intercropping: simultaneous crops without distinct rows. Row intercropping: crops arranged in different rows. Strip intercropping: crops grown in strips wide enough for independent management. Relay intercropping: crops introduced in sequence so growth cycles overlap. Other terms Monoculture: repetitive growing of a sole crop. Diversification and multiple cropping can help distribute production risk.

Integration of dairy livestock with cropping to diversify income, recycle nutrients and reduce production risk. Benefits Livestock diversification helps reduce risk. Forage crops transfer nutrients within the farm. Dung can be used as crop manure. Crop residues provide livestock feed. Cattle groups Draft breeds. Dairy breeds. Dual-purpose breeds. Exotic breeds. Buffaloes. Feed groups Roughages: legumes, non-legume hays, straw and silage. Concentrates: grains and grain/oilseed by-products. Vitamin and mineral mixtures may supplement rations.

A farm enterprise that converts animal dung and organic material into biogas and nutrient-rich slurry. Types Float-dome type, including KVIC models. Fixed-dome type. Technical points from source Dry residual sludge contains approximately N 1.4–1.8%, P2O5 1.1–2.0% and K2O 0.8–1.2%. Fresh dung gas yield is stated as about 0.04–0.1 m³ per kg per day, depending on temperature. Gas production is highest around 30–35°C. Production decreases sharply below 10°C. One m³ of biogas is stated as equivalent to about 0.62 litres of kerosene.

A livestock enterprise suitable for diverse agro-climatic conditions and small-farm resource bases. Advantages High adaptability to different agro-climatic conditions. Disease tolerance is noted in the source. Multiple kids and relatively fast growth support production. Provides employment through the year. Small and marginal farmers can maintain animals with available fodder. Feed Green fodder includes legumes and cereals. Crop residues can be used with suitable treatment or supplementation. Concentrates include grains, bran, oilseed products and other feed materials.

A livestock enterprise integrated into farming systems for eggs, meat, income and nutrient recycling. Management Day-old chicks are commonly used to start a unit. Poultry houses need ventilation, water and power. The site should be well drained and protected from floodwater. Shed width is stated as not exceeding about 25–33 feet. Feed and cost The source states feed may account for 70–75% of poultry-farming expenditure. Maize, rice bran and groundnut cake are examples of feed ingredients in an IFS model.

Fish culture integrated with crops and livestock to use farm water resources and recycle nutrients. Fish species and feeding niches Catla is described as a fast-growing Indian major carp and a surface/vegetation feeder. Rohu is a column feeder. Calbasu is a bottom feeder on detritus. Mrigal is also associated with bottom feeding. Silver carp mainly feeds on phytoplankton near the surface. Grass carp feeds on aquatic plants and cut grass. Integration Fish ponds can receive nutrient-rich wastes from poultry or livestock. Water availability and pond location are important for IFS planning.

Management of honey bees for honey and other products while supporting crop pollination. Bee species Apis cerana is better acclimatized to higher Himalayan areas. Apis mellifera and Apis dorsata are described as more profitable in plains. Management Beekeepers should know local nectar and pollen sources. Nectar sources include tamarind, mango, guava and many fruit crops. Pollen sources include maize, sorghum, millets, sunflower and palm. Timing The source identifies arrival of suitable nectar/pollen sources as important for starting beekeeping.

Integrated production involving mulberry cultivation, silkworm rearing and silk reeling. Core terms Moriculture = cultivation of mulberry. Mulberry is the chief food plant for the mulberry silkworm, Bombyx mori. Sericulture includes mulberry cultivation, silkworm rearing and silk reeling. Source details The source states about 240 thousand ha under mulberry in India. Silk production contributes to rural socio-economic development in some areas. Silk goods are exported to multiple international markets.

Integrated land management combining trees with crops, animals or other agricultural enterprises. Purpose Supports integrated and self-sustained land management. Can supply fuel, fodder, fruit and timber. Can support soil conservation and nutrient cycling. Agri-horticultural system Fruit trees are combined with short-duration arable crops. Also called food-cum-fruit system. Fruit-tree examples: guava, pomegranate, custard apple, sapota and mango. Pulses are important arable crops for this system. Alley cropping Food crops are grown in alleys formed by tree or shrub hedgerows. Tree farming Useful where arable crops are less profitable. Dryland farmers may prefer trees because of labour scarcity and drought-related crop failure.

Additional enterprises that can diversify farming systems. Enterprises listed Rabbit rearing. Duck rearing. Turkey rearing. Piggery. Mushroom cultivation. Mushroom cultivation Mushroom is an edible fungus. It can use agricultural residues and fit into integrated systems.

An integrated rice-based system combining crop, fish, poultry and mushroom enterprises. Model components Rice-based cropping. Fish culture. Poultry. Mushroom production. Example model Cropping area: 0.36 ha. Fish pond: 0.04 ha. Fish pond depth: 1.5 m. Fish stocking: about 7,500 fingerlings/ha. Poultry shed placed near the fish pond. Poultry droppings fall into the fish pond. Oyster mushroom is produced using rice straw. Economic result in source Net profit reported: Rs. 11,755. Conventional cropping comparison: Rs. 6,335. Additional employment: 174 man-days.

section: IFS Model: Tamil Nadu Cauvery Delta Zone
text: A rice–poultry–fish integrated system designed for a canal-irrigated rice-growing zone. System One-hectare model. Fish pond: 0.04 ha. Cropping: rice–rice–cotton on 0.76 ha. Cropping: rice–rice–maize on 0.20 ha. Maize supplies a major poultry-feed component. Poultry and fish Poultry unit uses Babcock and hybrid layer birds in the source model. Feed includes maize, rice bran and groundnut cake. Fish pond is located near the poultry shed. Fish stocking density: about 10,000 fingerlings/ha. Fish harvesting begins after about six and a half months. Economic result Net return reported: Rs. 17,200. Employment generated: 385 man-days.

A one-hectare integrated model combining crops, fodder, dairy, biogas and mushroom production. Cropping components Cotton–green gram–maize + fodder cowpea–Bellary onion: 0.56 ha. Wheat–sunflower–maize + fodder cowpea–summer cotton + green gram: 0.11 ha. Grass Bajra Napier: 0.15 ha. Lucerne: 0.05 ha. Leucaena on bunds: 0.05 ha. Total: 1.00 ha. Farmstead Dairy: 3 Jersey cows + 2 calves. Biogas: 2 m³ capacity. Mushroom production: 1.5–2.0 kg/ha as stated in the source. Results Mean revenue: Rs. 34,600/ha under IFS. Conventional comparison: Rs. 13,950. Employment: about 770 man-days/year. Crop by-products are recycled into dairy feed. Dung is recycled through the biogas unit.

Rice production integrated with fish culture in water-retaining paddy fields. Suitable conditions Paddy fields remain flooded for about 3–8 months. Low-lying fields with good water availability are preferred. Soil should retain water and be fertile. Fish species Cyprinus carpio var. communis: scale carp. Cyprinus carpio var. specularis: mirror carp. Cyprinus carpio var. nudus: leather carp. Field preparation Construct strong bunds to retain water and prevent fish escape. Level the field. Provide irrigation and drainage channels. Use inlets and outlets for water management. Stock fish about 10–15 days after rice transplantation.

section: Management and Production of Paddy-Cum-Fish Culture
text: Water, nutrient, stocking, harvesting and marketing practices for integrated rice-fish production. Water and inputs Water can be diverted from streams through wooden or bamboo barriers. Organic fertilizers include poultry droppings, pig excreta, cow dung and plant wastes. The source specifies no chemical insecticide, pesticide or fertilizer during the described integrated system. Stocking Fish seed rate: about 2,500 fish/ha. Fish rearing period: 3–6 months. Paddy rearing period: 5–7 months. Harvest 3–4 months fish culture: about 200–300 kg/ha reported. 5–6 months fish culture: about 400–500 kg/ha reported. Water is drained through outlets before fish harvesting. Paddy is harvested after fish harvesting. Production and marketing Paddy production is reported as about 3,500–4,500 kg/ha. Fish may be sold live or fresh in local markets. Source reports live fish at Rs.120/kg and fresh fish at Rs.100/kg during the cited period. Prices fluctuate with season.

Management of groundwater extraction and recharge to avoid depletion and support sustainable irrigation. Problems Increasing wells can increase extraction from limited aquifers. Excess extraction lowers the groundwater table. Over-irrigation can accumulate harmful salts. Sustainable approach Maximize groundwater recharge. Minimize surface runoff. Use conjunctive surface- and groundwater management. Use recharge wells, check dams and percolation ponds where suitable.

section: History and milestones of plant breeding
text: Plant breeding developed from deliberate selection and artificial crossing into a science based on genetics. Early milestones Babylonians and Assyrians artificially pollinated date palm as early as 700 BC. Thomas Fairchild produced the first artificial hybrid in 1717. Joseph Kolreuter studied extensive tobacco and Solanum crosses during 1760–1766. Thomas Andrew Knight produced new fruit varieties through artificial hybridization. Le Coutier reported wheat selection results in 1843. Patrick Shireff practiced individual plant selection in wheat and oats. Vilmorin proposed individual plant selection with progeny testing in 1857. Nilsson and associates refined single-plant selection at Svalöf around 1890. Johannsen proposed the pure-line theory in 1903. G.H. Shull's maize work became a foundation for modern hybrid maize breeding. Major achievements Norman Borlaug developed Mexican semi-dwarf wheat varieties in the 1960s. Norin 10 supplied the dwarfing gene used in Mexican semi-dwarf wheat. M.S. Swaminathan introduced Mexican dwarf wheats into India. IRRI used Dee-geo-woo-gen (DGWG) in de

section: Development of plant breeding in India
text: Indian plant breeding developed through agricultural departments, research institutes, coordinated projects and agricultural universities. Institutional milestones Department of Agriculture was created by Government of India in 1871. Imperial Agricultural Research Institute was established at Pusa in 1905. The institute shifted to New Delhi in 1936 after earthquake damage in 1934. Its name changed to Indian Agricultural Research Institute in 1946. Imperial Council of Agricultural Research was established in 1929. It became Indian Council of Agricultural Research in 1946. Indian Central Cotton Committee was established in 1921. PIRRCOM began in 1956 for cotton, oilseeds and millets. All India Coordinated Maize Improvement Project started in 1957. First hybrid maize varieties were released by the project in 1961. First Agricultural University was established at Pantnagar in 1960.

Several classical breeding methods and concepts are associated with named scientists. Named contributions Allard and Bradshaw — G × E interaction. Hull — recurrent selection for SCA. Jenkins — recurrent selection for GCA. Davenport — dominance hypothesis. Flor — gene-for-gene hypothesis. Johannsen — pure-line concept. Harlan and Pope — backcross method. Jones — double-cross scheme. Jones and Davis — cytoplasmic genetic male sterility. Hopkins — ear-to-row method. Lonnquist — modified ear-to-row method. Blakeslee and Nebel — colchicine. Goulden — single-seed descent. Lewis — self-incompatibility classification. Vavilov — centres of diversity and law of homologous series. Vilmorin — progeny testing. Fairchild — first artificial hybrid. Rimpau — triticale. Hugo de Vries — mutation. Shull — heterosis. Yuan Long Ping — father of hybrid rice.

Plant breeding proceeds through creation or discovery of variation followed by selection, evaluation, multiplication and distribution. Sources of variation Naturally existing variability includes domestication, germplasm collection and introduction. New variability can be created by hybridization. Hybridization includes intervarietal, distant and somatic forms. Mutation, polyploidy and somaclonal variation create new variability. Genetic engineering is another source of new variation. Breeding sequence Selection identifies desirable plants or lines. Evaluation tests performance and target traits. Multiplication increases seed or planting material. Distribution makes the improved material available for cultivation.

section: Concept, nature and role of plant breeding
text: Plant breeding is the art, science and technology of improving plant genetic makeup for economic use and human benefit. Core concept Plant breeding is also described as the science of crop improvement. It changes and improves plant heredity. N.W. Simmonds described plant breeding as the current phase of crop evolution in 1979. Role Breeding converts genetic variation into agronomically useful varieties. The programme is directed by the crop, environment and economic objective.

Objectives are crop-specific improvements in yield, quality, resistance, adaptation, maturity and other useful traits. Yield and quality Higher economic yield may mean grain, fodder, fibre, tuber, cane or oil yield. Yield improvement may use high-yielding varieties or hybrids. Quality targets include grain size, colour, milling and baking quality in wheat. Rice breeding may target cooking quality. Barley breeding may target malting quality. Vegetable breeding may target nutritive and keeping quality. Pulse breeding may target protein content. Oilseed breeding may target oil content. Cotton breeding may target fibre length, strength and fineness. Stress and protection Abiotic targets include drought, salinity, heat, cold, frost and wind resistance. Biotic resistance targets diseases and insects. Genetic resistance is described as an economical way to reduce losses. Resistant donor parents can be used from the gene pool. Plant type and maturity Earliness reduces crop management period and may reduce insecticide use. Early varieties can permit new crop rotations. Cotton maturity was red

section: Scope, future prospects and undesirable effects
text: Future breeding combines classical genetics with molecular biology and biotechnology, while maintaining attention to genetic diversity. Future prospects Population growth creates continuing demand for crop improvement. Molecular biology provides sharper tools for breeders. Biotechnology has enabled field testing of genetically modified crops. Genes from diverse organisms may improve biotic and abiotic stress resistance. Plants may be engineered to produce valuable compounds such as pharmaceuticals. The source cites transgenic Brassica napus producing hirudin as an example. Undesirable effects Modern improved varieties may be more uniform than landraces. Reduced diversity can increase vulnerability to new pathogen races. Uniform varieties may have a narrow genetic base and poorer adaptability. Shared pedigree parents can create danger of genetic uniformity. Plant breeding can sometimes create undesirable combinations such as Raphanobrassica and Pomato. Strong selection for major pests and diseases may increase susceptibility to minor pests or diseases. The source cites chickpea grey m

section: Genetics and cytogenetics in plant breeding
text: Genetic and cytogenetic principles provide the basis for planned crop improvement. Important concepts Mitosis and meiosis. Chromosomes and chromosomal structural changes. Numerical chromosome changes. Mendel's laws of inheritance. Gene interaction, linkage and crossing over. Pleiotropy, penetrance and expressivity. Cytoplasmic inheritance. Polygenic and oligogenic characters. Mutations and population genetics. Plant biotechnology. Mode of reproduction Mode of reproduction determines whether crop populations are mainly homozygous or heterozygous. Self-pollinated crops such as wheat are generally homozygous. A homozygous line is therefore a common breeding target in self-pollinators.

Asexual vegetative reproduction produces new plants from vegetative plant parts without gamete fusion. Natural vegetative structures Tuber — potato. Bulb — onion and garlic. Rhizome — ginger and turmeric. Corm — bunda and arvi. Sub-aerial stems include runners, stolons and suckers. Mint and date palm are examples of crops using sub-aerial stems. Artificial vegetative reproduction Stem cuttings are used in sugarcane, grapes and roses. Layering, budding, grafting and gootee are used for fruit trees and ornamentals. Tissue culture permits vegetative multiplication in many plant species. Breeding significance A desirable plant can be used directly as a variety even when heterozygous. Desirable mutant buds, branches or seedlings can be multiplied directly. Vegetative propagation can preserve a selected genotype unchanged.

Apomixis is seed formation in which the embryo develops without fertilization. Types Apomictic progeny is generally genetically identical to the parent. Facultative apomixis occurs when sexual reproduction can also occur. Obligate apomixis occurs when sexual reproduction is absent. Adventive embryony develops embryos directly from nucellus, integument or chalaza. Apospory produces unreduced embryo sacs from ovular somatic cells. Diplospory develops the embryo sac from the megaspore, often with modified meiosis. Parthenogenesis develops the embryo from an embryo-sac cell without pollination. Gonial parthenogenesis uses the egg cell. Somatic parthenogenesis uses another embryo-sac cell. Apogamy develops an embryo from synergids or antipodals. Breeding significance Apomixis is undesirable when sexual progeny, selfs or hybrids are required. It is useful for maintaining a desirable genotype unchanged. Apomictic reproduction can preserve selected varieties without segregation. Asexually reproducing crops are often highly heterozygous and may show severe inbreeding depression. Breeding prog

Sexual reproduction involves fusion of male and female gametes to form a zygote and creates recombination. Flower and sporogenesis Perfect or hermaphrodite flowers contain stamens and pistil. Staminate flowers contain stamens but not pistils. Pistillate flowers contain pistils but not stamens. Monoecious species have male and female flowers on the same plant. Dioecious species have male and female flowers on different plants. Sporogenesis is production of microspores and megaspores. Microsporogenesis occurs in anthers. Each pollen mother cell undergoes meiosis to produce four haploid microspores. Megasporogenesis occurs in ovules. A megaspore mother cell produces four haploid megaspores; usually three degenerate. Gametogenesis Microgametogenesis produces male gametes. The pollen nucleus forms a generative nucleus and vegetative or tube nucleus. The generative nucleus divides to form two sperm cells. The pollen tube enters the ovule through the micropyle. Megagametogenesis forms the embryo sac from the functional megaspore. In most crops, three mitotic divisions produce eight nuclei.

section: Modes of pollination and genetic consequences
text: Pollination is transfer of pollen from anthers to stigmas; its pattern determines genetic structure and breeding strategy. Types Self-pollination or autogamy uses pollen from the same flower. Cross-pollination or allogamy transfers pollen between different plants. Geitonogamy transfers pollen between flowers of the same plant. Genetic consequences of geitonogamy are similar to autogamy. Self-pollination mechanisms Cleistogamy prevents flower opening and promotes complete self-pollination. Some cereals open only after pollination. In tomato and brinjal, anthers closely surround the stigma. In legumes, floral organs enclose anthers and stigma within the keel. These mechanisms make self-pollination efficient. Genetic consequence Self-pollination rapidly increases homozygosity. Self-pollinated populations are highly homozygous. The source states that self-pollinated species generally do not show inbreeding depression. Breeding usually aims at developing homozygous varieties. Cross-pollination mechanisms Dicliny produces separate staminate and pistillate flowers. Monoecy has male and fema

Self-incompatibility is failure of pollen from a flower or plant to fertilize compatible female tissue on the same plant. Classification More than 300 species in about 20 angiosperm families show self-incompatibility in the source. Heteromorphic and homomorphic systems are recognized. Homomorphic systems include gametophytic and sporophytic control. Heteromorphic system Flower morphology differs between incompatibility groups. Primula has pin and thrum forms; this is distyly. Lythrum shows tristyly. In distyly, compatible mating occurs between pin and thrum flowers. The source gives Ss for thrum and ss for pin. Pin × thrum produces Ss and ss progeny in equal frequencies. Gametophytic system Pollen incompatibility is determined by its own genotype. A single S locus with multiple alleles commonly controls the system. Pollen carrying an S allele is rejected by stylar tissue carrying the same allele. Examples include Trifolium, Nicotiana, Lycopersicon, Solanum and Petunia. S1S2 × S1S2 is fully incompatible. S1S2 × S3S4 is fully compatible. S1S2 × S2S3 is partially compatible; about 50% p

Male sterility is production of nonfunctional pollen while female fertility remains functional. Types Genetic male sterility is usually controlled by a recessive ms gene. Dominant male-sterility genes are also known, including in safflower. Cytoplasmic male sterility is controlled by cytoplasm. Cytoplasmic-genetic male sterility combines sterile cytoplasm with nuclear fertility-restorer genes. Genetic male sterility ms ms × Ms ms gives about 1:1 male-sterile and male-fertile progeny. Male-sterile and maintainer lines can be isogenic except at the ms locus. Male-fertile plants must be identified and removed from the female line before pollen shedding. This rouging requirement increases hybrid-seed production cost. The source notes commercial use in castor in the USA and arhar in India. Cytoplasmic male sterility Cytoplasm is inherited mainly through the egg, so progeny of a male-sterile female remain male sterile. A recurrent pollinator can maintain the male-sterile A line. The fertile maintainer is called the B line. The source associates CMS genes particularly with mitochondria in m

Domestication is the evolutionary and human-directed transformation of wild plants into cultivated forms. Key features Domestication begins with selection and cultivation of useful plants. Selection under cultivation changes plant form, reproduction and adaptation. Domestication is a major source of cultivated crop diversity. Breeding relevance Domesticated material provides variation for selection. Traits associated with cultivation can differ markedly from wild relatives. Domestication history helps breeders understand available variation.

Plant introduction is bringing crop germplasm from one geographical region into another for cultivation, breeding or evaluation. Types and purpose Introductions may be primary or secondary. Primary introduction can be directly cultivated after testing and selection. Secondary introduction is used as breeding material and may produce improved varieties after crossing or selection. The source cites popularization of grape cultivation in Haryana and introduction of wheat as examples. History and institutions Crop plants have been moved into new regions throughout agricultural history. The source describes an organized Indian plant-introduction programme supported by ICAR from 1956. NBPGR is identified with national management of agricultural and horticultural germplasm. The Botanical Survey of India is associated with botanical and medicinal plant resources.

section: Procedure and purposes of plant introduction
text: Introduction requires procurement, quarantine, evaluation and multiplication before safe use. Procedure Procurement of planting material is the first step. Imported material is subjected to quarantine. Introductions are evaluated for adaptation and useful traits. Selected material is multiplied after successful evaluation. Promising introductions can be released as varieties after required trials. Purpose Introduce useful variation into breeding programmes. Obtain traits not available in local material. Provide material for direct cultivation after adaptation. Support diversification of crops and growing regions.

Germplasm collection assembles genetic resources needed for present and future crop improvement. Collection Germplasm may be collected from cultivated and wild material. Collections preserve genetic diversity for breeding. Characterization and evaluation identify useful accessions. Breeding value Germplasm supplies donors for disease, insect, quality and stress traits. Exotic and indigenous material can broaden the genetic base. Conserved accessions support future breeding when new traits are required.

Centres of origin and diversity identify regions where crops or their diversity are concentrated. Vavilov concept Vavilov developed the concept of centres of diversity. Centres of diversity are important sources of genetic variability. The law of homologous series is also associated with Vavilov. Breeding significance Regions rich in diversity can provide germplasm for crop improvement. Wild and cultivated forms in diversity centres can supply useful alleles. Knowledge of origin helps guide exploration and germplasm collection.

Observed phenotypic variation is partitioned into genetic and environmental components for selection decisions. Variance components Phenotypic variation contains genetic and environmental components. Genetic variation includes additive and non-additive effects. Environmental variation can mask genetic differences. Genotype × environment interaction contributes to observed performance across environments. Breeding significance Selection is effective when useful variation is heritable. Partitioning variation helps predict response to selection. Heritability and genetic advance are used together as selection parameters.

Heritability measures the proportion of phenotypic variance attributable to genetic variance in a specified population and environment. Broad-sense heritability Broad-sense heritability is the proportion of total phenotypic variance due to total genetic variance. H² = Vg / Vp. The source also expresses estimation using variance components from generations such as VF2 and VF1. Narrow-sense heritability Narrow-sense heritability focuses on additive genetic variance. It is especially relevant to response from selection because additive effects are transmitted predictably. Interpretation Heritability is population- and environment-dependent. High heritability does not by itself guarantee large genetic gain. Genetic advance should be considered with heritability.

Genetic advance is the expected improvement in mean genotypic value from selection. Measures Genetic advance is the difference between mean genotypic value of selected lines and the original population. Genetic advance as percent of mean = Genetic advance / population mean × 100. The source classifies GA% mean as low below 10%, moderate at 10–20% and high above 20%. Joint interpretation High heritability + high genetic advance suggests additive gene effects and effective selection. High heritability + low genetic advance suggests greater non-additive effects and less rewarding direct selection. Low heritability + high genetic advance can occur when additive effects exist but environmental effects are large. Low heritability + low genetic advance suggests strong environmental influence and ineffective selection.

A pure line is the progeny of a single self-fertilized homozygous plant. Johannsen's findings Johannsen studied Phaseolus vulgaris, variety Princess. A market seed lot contained mixtures of larger and smaller seeds. Selection produced genetically distinct pure lines. Variation within a pure line was attributed to environment. Selection within a pure line was ineffective because individuals were genetically homozygous. Requirements and value Successful selection requires variation. The variation must be heritable. Progeny testing helps distinguish genetic from environmental performance. Pure-line selection is particularly useful in self-pollinated crops.

section: Pure-line selection method: merits and limitations
text: Pure-line selection identifies superior individual plants from a variable self-pollinated population and evaluates their progenies. Method Select superior individual plants from a heterogeneous population. Grow progenies separately. Compare progenies for uniformity and target traits. Discard inferior lines. Test promising pure lines in yield and adaptation trials. Multiply and release the superior line after confirmation. Merits Produces highly uniform varieties. Useful for self-pollinated crops. Uses existing variability without requiring a planned cross. Limitations Selection cannot create new genetic variation within an already pure line. The method depends on available variability. Narrow genetic base can result if the source population is limited.

Hybridization combines desirable genes from different parents to create new segregating variation. Objectives Combine complementary characters from parents. Transfer specific resistance or quality traits. Create transgressive segregants. Generate variation not present in a single parent. Types Intervarietal hybridization crosses varieties of the same species. Distant hybridization uses more remote parents. Somatic hybridization can combine cells or genomes through tissue-culture approaches. Basic procedure Select suitable parents. Synchronize flowering. Emasculate the female parent where needed. Bag and protect the female flower. Apply pollen from the selected male parent. Tag and record the cross. Harvest and store F1 seed separately. Grow F1 plants to confirm hybridity.

Emasculation removes or disables anthers of the female parent before pollen shedding to prevent unwanted selfing. Methods Hand emasculation removes anthers manually. Hot-water treatment can kill pollen without removing floral parts. Alcohol treatment can sterilize or kill pollen in suitable crops. Suction methods can remove pollen from some flowers. Male-sterility systems can replace manual emasculation. Crossing steps Emasculate at the appropriate floral stage. Bag the emasculated flower. Collect mature pollen from the male parent. Pollinate the receptive stigma. Rebag to prevent contamination. Label the cross with parent identities and date. Harvest crossed heads or pods after seed maturation. Store F1 seed with original tags.

F2 and later generations after selfing an F1 segregate for parental genes; some individuals may exceed both parents. Concept F2 and onward generations are called segregating generations. Transgressive segregation produces individuals exceeding either parent for one or more characters. Transgressive breeding exploits these superior segregants. Main methods Pedigree breeding. Bulk breeding. Single-seed descent. Backcross breeding. Multiple-cross breeding.

Pedigree breeding selects individual plants and records their ancestry generation by generation until desirable lines become sufficiently homozygous. Procedure F1 plants are space planted to obtain F2 seed. About 2,000–10,000 F2 plants may be grown in the source procedure. About 200–500 desirable F2 plants are selected. Selected plants are grown as separate progenies in F3. About 3–5 best plants may be selected from each superior row. The process continues through F4 and F5; about 20–50 families may be retained at F5. By F6 many lines become homozygous and uniform. F7 preliminary yield trials are conducted. F8–F10 confirm superior lines across trials. F10–F11 seed is multiplied and distributed. Merits and limitations Provides information on inheritance. Allows breeder judgement during selection. Can recover useful transgressive segregants. Accurate pedigree records require substantial time. Large selected material becomes difficult to handle. Success depends on breeder skill. Modified form Mass pedigree method combines bulk handling when selection conditions are unfavorable with pedi

Bulk breeding advances segregating generations in bulk and postpones intensive individual-plant selection until later generations. Procedure F1 plants are grown and F2 seed is harvested in bulk. F2 to about F5 generations are grown as bulk populations with little or no deliberate selection. F6 is space planted for single-plant selection. Selected plants are grown as separate progenies in F7. Preliminary yield testing begins around F8–F9. Multi-location trials are conducted in later generations. The source gives F9–F12 as a typical testing and multiplication period. Merits Simple and convenient. Inexpensive and less labour-intensive. No detailed pedigree records are required. Natural selection operates during early generations. Useful for studying survival of genes and genotypes. Limitations May take longer to develop a variety. Breeder has less opportunity for early selection. Inheritance information is limited. Natural selection may favor survival rather than highest economic yield.

Single-seed descent rapidly advances segregating generations by taking one seed from each plant for the next generation. Core method The method was suggested by Goulden in 1939. One seed from each plant is carried forward generation after generation. Rapid generation advance increases homozygosity without early intensive selection. Individual plants or lines are evaluated after sufficient homozygosity. Use Useful when large segregating populations must be advanced quickly. Reduces space and record requirements during early generations. Selection is concentrated after advanced generations are obtained.

Backcross breeding repeatedly crosses a hybrid to one recurrent parent to transfer a specific desirable trait. Concept The recurrent parent supplies most of the final genetic background. The donor parent supplies the target gene or trait. Repeated backcrossing recovers the recurrent-parent genotype. Selection is made for the desired donor trait during the process. Use Useful for transferring disease or insect resistance. Useful for transferring a specific quality or stress trait. Particularly effective when the donor character is readily identifiable.

A multiline variety is a mixture of genetically similar lines that differ mainly in resistance genes or another specific feature. Concept Lines in a multiline have a common or similar genetic background. They differ for specific resistance genes. A multiline reduces uniform vulnerability to a pathogen population. The approach was associated in the source with Jenson. Procedure Develop or identify lines differing for the desired resistance genes. Select lines that are similar for agronomic background. Combine the component lines in an appropriate proportion. Evaluate the mixture for agronomic performance and disease response. Applications Main application is management of diseases with variable pathogen populations. Useful where uniform single-gene resistance is vulnerable to pathogen change.

Under specified assumptions, allele and genotype frequencies remain constant across generations in a random-mating population. Law For two alleles A and a, p + q = 1. Expected genotype frequencies are p² AA, 2pq Aa and q² aa. Equilibrium means genotype frequencies remain stable from generation to generation. The law was independently developed by Hardy in 1908 and Weinberg in 1909. Assumptions Random mating. No selection. No mutation. No migration. No random genetic drift. A sufficiently large Mendelian population is implied by the equilibrium model.

Evolutionary forces alter allele frequencies and therefore disturb Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. Forces Selection changes reproductive contribution of genotypes. Mutation introduces new alleles or changes existing alleles. Migration moves genes between populations. Genetic drift changes frequencies through random sampling. Non-random mating changes genotype frequencies. These forces are treated as evolutionary forces because they change population genetic structure.

Population improvement increases the frequency of desirable alleles in cross-pollinated populations while retaining useful heterozygosity. Basis Cross-pollinated crops are highly heterozygous and heterogeneous. Inbreeding should be avoided or minimized because of inbreeding depression. Individual genotypes are less important than allele frequencies in population improvement. Selection can be with or without progeny testing. Classes Selection without progeny testing includes mass selection. Selection with progeny testing includes progeny selection, line breeding and recurrent selection.

Mass selection chooses many superior plants phenotypically and mixes their seed to form the next generation. Procedure Select plants based on phenotype. Allow selected plants to intermate or open-pollinate according to the scheme. Harvest seed from selected plants as required by the method. Use the selected bulk as the next breeding population. Repeat cycles when further improvement is required. Use Simple method for increasing frequency of favorable phenotypes. Useful when target traits have adequate heritability. Does not require detailed progeny testing.

Recurrent selection repeatedly selects superior plants or progenies, intermates selected material and recombines favorable alleles. Purpose Increase frequency of favorable alleles. Maintain sufficient genetic variability for continued selection. Improve a population over repeated cycles. Forms Recurrent selection for general combining ability targets performance with a tester or reference population. Recurrent selection for specific combining ability targets performance in a particular cross combination. The source associates GCA recurrent selection with Jenkins and SCA recurrent selection with Hull. Cycle Select superior plants or families. Evaluate progenies as specified by the scheme. Select the best materials. Intermate selected plants or families. Advance the recombined population into another selection cycle.

Heterosis is superiority of an F1 hybrid over a defined parental or standard reference for a target trait. Types The term heterosis was first used by Shull in 1914. Average or mid-parent heterosis compares F1 with the average of two parents. Heterobeltiosis compares F1 with the superior parent. Economic, standard or useful heterosis compares F1 with the best commercial or standard variety. The source describes economic heterosis as the commercially useful estimate. Formula Mid-parent heterosis (%) = (F1 − MP) / MP × 100. Superior-parent heterosis (%) = (F1 − BP) / BP × 100. Standard heterosis (%) = (F1 − standard check) / standard check × 100.

Inbreeding depression is reduction in vigor, fertility, yield or related performance caused by increased homozygosity in cross-pollinated populations. Concept Inbreeding increases homozygosity. Recessive deleterious alleles become more frequently expressed. Cross-pollinated crops can show mild to severe inbreeding depression. Self-pollinated crops generally show much less inbreeding depression. Relation to heterosis Inbred lines often lose vigor during inbreeding. Crossing suitable inbred lines can restore vigor in the hybrid. The magnitude depends on crop, population and genetic constitution.

section: Genetic bases of heterosis and inbreeding depression
text: The source discusses dominance, overdominance and epistatic explanations for heterosis and inbreeding depression. Hypotheses Dominance hypothesis explains heterosis through masking deleterious recessive alleles. Overdominance attributes superior performance to heterozygous advantage at loci. Epistatic explanations involve interactions among genes at different loci. No single mechanism necessarily explains all cases of heterosis. Breeding implication Understanding genetic basis helps guide parent choice and hybrid development. Genetic divergence and combining ability influence hybrid performance.

Heterosis can be expressed through physiological differences in growth, metabolism and resource use. Manifestations Hybrid vigor may increase growth rate, size and yield. Differences can occur in photosynthesis, respiration and assimilate production. Improved physiological efficiency can contribute to superior hybrid performance. Practical view Physiological expression is a result of underlying genetic differences. The breeder evaluates the final phenotype and economic performance of hybrids.

Commercial hybrid breeding exploits heterosis by producing seed from selected parental lines. Requirements Parents must be sufficiently uniform and stable. Crossing must be reliable and economical. Hybrid seed production requires effective control of self-pollination. The hybrid must outperform relevant commercial standards for the target trait. Systems Male sterility can facilitate hybrid seed production. Self-incompatibility can also be used in some crops. Manual emasculation is possible where economical.

section: Development and evaluation of inbred lines
text: Inbred lines are highly homozygous lines developed through repeated selfing or related inbreeding and used as hybrid parents. Development Select suitable source populations. Self-pollinate selected plants repeatedly. Select uniform and fertile lines during inbreeding. Evaluate lines for agronomic performance and combining ability. Maintain superior lines through controlled selfing or appropriate seed-production procedures. Evaluation Evaluate general combining ability where relevant. Test specific combining ability through crosses. Assess yield, quality, resistance, maturity and other target traits. Discard weak or unstable lines.

Composite and synthetic varieties are population varieties formed from selected parents or lines while retaining genetic diversity. Definitions A synthetic variety is produced by intercrossing selected lines with good combining ability. A composite variety is formed by combining selected genotypes or varieties and allowing them to intermate. Both maintain more genetic diversity than a single pure line. Synthetic production Evaluate candidate lines for combining ability. Select lines with desirable performance and compatibility. Intermate selected lines in a controlled scheme. Bulk and maintain the resulting population. Evaluate performance across environments. Merits and limitations Synthetics can maintain useful heterozygosity and broad adaptation. They may be easier to maintain than commercial single-cross hybrids in some crops. Performance can decline across generations due to recombination and segregation. The number and combining ability of component lines influence performance.

Clonal breeding improves crops propagated through vegetative organs and preserves selected genotypes as clones. Characteristics A clone is a group of plants produced from one plant by asexual reproduction. Asexually propagated crops may lack seed, have short seed viability or produce seed rarely. Many are perennials; annual examples include potato, cassava and sweet potato. Many show reduced flowering or seed set. They are commonly cross-pollinated, highly heterozygous and may show severe inbreeding depression. Many are polyploids, such as sugarcane and potato. Some are interspecific hybrids, including banana and sugarcane. Clone properties Members of a clone are genetically identical in principle. Within-clone phenotypic variation is mainly environmental. Phenotype reflects genotype, environment and G × E interaction. Clones can be maintained for generations. Clones may deteriorate through pathogens and mutation.

Clonal selection identifies superior plants and multiplies them vegetatively without fixing the genotype through sexual reproduction. Selection Select superior individual plants from a variable clonal population. Multiply selected plants vegetatively. Test clonal progenies in replicated and multi-environment trials. Discard unstable or inferior clones. Maintain elite clones through disease-free propagation. Advantages Heterozygous genotypes can be preserved. A desirable plant can be released without homozygosity. Genetic combinations can be maintained generation after generation. Problems Disease accumulation is a major concern in vegetatively propagated crops. Sexual recombination may be difficult because flowering or seed set is poor. Severe inbreeding depression can limit selfing. Polyploidy and sterility complicate genetic analysis. Long generation time is a problem in perennial crops.

Accurate records allow breeders to identify, compare, trace and evaluate large numbers of breeding materials. Need for records Variety development requires evaluation across environments and locations. Breeders may handle thousands of strains each year. Complete and accurate records support identification and decision-making. Major records Accession records. Project book. Sowing or planting plan. Planting list. Record book of crosses. Field book. Maintenance registers Accession register. Germplasm bank records. Descriptive blank register. Crossing programme records. Single-plant selection register. Row test and replicated-row test records. Preliminary and initial evaluation trial records. Comparative yield and yield evaluation trial records. Multi-location trial records. Quality observation notebook. Segregating-generation notebook.

An accession register tracks the identity, source, receipt and evaluation history of germplasm or planting material. Contents Record receipt date. Record source and accession number. Assign the number at the receiving unit. Maintain a short description of planting material. Record destination for evaluation. Record evaluation feedback. Numbering The source describes accession numbers as serial number plus year of entry. EC denotes exotic collection. IC denotes indigenous collection.

Designation systems provide unique identifiers for crosses, selections and introductions. Purpose Identify breeding material through generations. Connect a selected line to its original cross or introduction. Prevent loss of ancestry information during large breeding programmes. Source convention The source describes codes containing programme or material identifiers and year information. Selection, cross and introduction series numbers are used to trace material. Correct designation is essential for pedigree and trial records.

Wide hybridization crosses individuals from different species or genera to transfer useful variation across reproductive boundaries. Definitions and history Interspecific hybridization crosses different species within the same genus. Example: Oryza sativa × O. perennis. Intergeneric hybridization crosses species belonging to different genera. Example: wheat × rye. Wide or distant hybridization includes interspecific and intergeneric crosses. Thomas Fairchild produced the first cited distant hybrid in 1717: carnation × sweet william. Raphanobrassica was an amphidiploid radish × cabbage hybrid. Triticale is cited as an intergeneric hybrid with major potential. Objectives Transfer disease-resistance genes from wild relatives. Transfer insect resistance. Transfer drought resistance and cold tolerance. Improve quality, such as cotton fibre or tobacco leaf traits. Improve yield in oats, tobacco, maize and sugarcane. Transfer CMS, earliness, dwarfness or useful morphological characters.

section: Barriers to wide hybridization and their overcoming
text: Wide crosses are limited by pre-fertilization, post-fertilization and chromosome-related barriers. Barriers Poor pollen germination or pollen-stigma incompatibility can prevent fertilization. Pollen-tube growth may be inhibited in the style. Embryo development may fail after fertilization. Hybrid sterility can result from chromosome imbalance or poor chromosome pairing. Genetic incompatibility may prevent normal hybrid development. Breeding approaches Use appropriate parents and reciprocal crosses. Manipulate pollination timing. Use embryo rescue when hybrid embryos abort. Double chromosome number where fertility requires chromosome pairing. Backcross useful hybrids to a cultivated parent to recover agronomic background. Repeated selection can stabilize useful introgressed characters.

Wide hybridization broadens the genetic base by moving useful genes from related species or genera into crops. Applications Disease and insect resistance from wild relatives. Abiotic stress tolerance such as drought and cold tolerance. Quality improvement in fibre and leaf products. Yield improvement. Transfer of male sterility, earliness and dwarfness. Creation of new amphidiploids or crop types.

Mutation breeding uses induced heritable variation to obtain useful changes not readily available through existing variation. Concept and history Hugo de Vries coined the term mutation in 1900. Mutation means a sudden heritable change other than ordinary Mendelian segregation and recombination. 1927 marked discovery of X-ray mutagenesis by Muller in Drosophila. Stadler demonstrated X-ray mutagenesis in barley in 1929. Auerbach and Robson demonstrated chemical mutagenesis using nitrogen mustard. After 1953, molecular understanding of DNA expanded mutation studies. Types by genetic basis Gene mutations alter DNA base sequence. Changes may involve base substitution, deletion or addition. Chromosomal mutations alter chromosome structure or number. Structural changes include deletion, duplication, inversion and translocation. Numerical changes include polyploidy and aneuploidy. Cytoplasmic or plasmagene mutations affect genetic material in cytoplasmic organelles.

Mutagens are physical or chemical agents used to increase mutation frequency. Physical mutagens X-rays. Gamma rays. Other ionizing radiation may be used according to the material and objective. Chemical mutagens Nitrogen mustard is cited as an early chemical mutagen. Chemical mutagens alter DNA or chromosome behavior and can create heritable variation. Treatment material Seeds, buds, pollen, cuttings and other plant materials can be treated. Treatment dose must balance mutation frequency with survival and fertility. The source describes irradiation procedures followed by generation-wise selection.

Mutation breeding requires screening and selection across generations because most induced changes are not immediately fixed or useful. Generation handling Treated material is advanced to produce segregating mutant generations. M1 plants are generally treated material and mutation expression is evaluated in later generations. M2 is important for detecting recessive mutations. Subsequent generations are used to confirm stability and performance. Promising mutants are evaluated in replicated trials. Selection Select for the desired phenotype. Confirm that the character is heritable and stable. Compare mutant lines with the parent variety. Test yield, quality, resistance and adaptation before release.

Polyploid breeding changes chromosome number to create new variation, restore fertility or modify plant size and other traits. Autopolyploidy Autopolyploidy increases chromosome sets from the same species. Colchicine is used to induce chromosome doubling. Polyploids may show larger cells and organs. Limitations include reduced fertility, meiotic irregularity and difficulty in fixation of desirable types. Allopolyploidy Allopolyploidy combines chromosome sets from different species. Chromosome doubling can restore pairing and fertility in a sterile interspecific hybrid. It can stabilize wide-hybrid combinations. Limitations include complex inheritance and fertility problems.

Abiotic-stress breeding develops crop varieties that tolerate environmental stresses such as temperature, water and salinity. Temperature stress Cold tolerance is important in rice-growing areas such as Gudalur and Cumbum valley. Artificial low-temperature and freeze tests are available, but single-plant selection is difficult. Field testing of segregating lines is considered suitable but can be time-consuming. High temperature can reduce seed set. High temperature may break male sterility in male-sterile lines. Leaf-disc heat tests and desiccation tolerance tests are used. Water stress About 75% of cultivated area is described as rainfed in the source. Drought escape means completing the life cycle before severe water deficit. Drought tolerance can occur with high tissue water potential. Drought tolerance can also occur with low tissue water potential. Physiological traits include stomatal aperture, photosynthetic rate and root characteristics. Proline accumulation in leaves can be used as a drought-screening indicator. Excess-water tolerance is important in tail-end Cauvery delta a

Genetic markers are heritable biological features associated with loci that can track individuals, chromosomes or genes. Concept Markers can act as genetic tags near genes controlling traits. Markers occupy defined genomic positions called loci. Marker quality is commonly assessed by heterozygosity in the population of interest. Important properties include abundance, polymorphism, locus specificity and reproducibility. No single marker is best for every application. Classes Classical markers include morphological, cytological and biochemical markers. DNA markers include RFLP, AFLP, RAPD, SSR and SNP systems. Markers support genetic mapping, germplasm characterization, marker-assisted introgression and variety protection. History Alfred Sturtevant produced an early genetic map in Drosophila using morphological factors. Genetic markers progressed from morphological markers to isozyme markers and then DNA markers.

Classical markers use visible traits or chromosome features to identify inherited variation. Morphological markers Examples include leaf shape, flower colour, pubescence, pod colour, seed shape and fruit shape. They are easy to observe and inexpensive. They can be used as indirect selection criteria when linked to target traits. They are limited in number. They may be strongly influenced by environment. Some appear only late in plant development. The source cites semi-dwarfism selection in rice and wheat as an example. Cytological markers Cytological markers identify chromosome structure and banding patterns. Q bands use quinacrine hydrochloride. G bands use Giemsa stain. R bands are reversed G bands. They help classify chromosomes and identify chromosome changes. They support physical mapping and linkage-group identification.

section: DNA markers and ideal marker characteristics
text: DNA markers detect heritable DNA-sequence differences and provide genotype-level information largely independent of phenotype. Characteristics of an ideal marker High polymorphism. High reproducibility. Clear inheritance. Genome-wide or suitable genomic distribution. High locus specificity. Easy and reliable assay. Low cost and high throughput where possible.
