Applications Genetic diversity analysis. Linkage mapping. Gene tagging. Germplasm characterization. Marker-assisted introgression. Marker-assisted selection. Variety identification and protection. Selection of favorable recurrent-parent genome in breeding programmes.

DNA marker systems differ in how polymorphism is detected and in dominance, reproducibility, cost and throughput. RFLP RFLP detects DNA polymorphism using restriction-fragment differences. It is based on restriction digestion and hybridization. It is generally reproducible and codominant but technically demanding. RAPD RAPD uses short random primers for PCR amplification. The source states that about 5–50 ng template DNA may be sufficient. Advantages include speed, simplicity and no requirement for prior sequence information. Main limitations are low reproducibility and dominant inheritance. RAPD cannot reliably distinguish homozygous from heterozygous bands. AFLP AFLP combines restriction digestion with selective PCR amplification. Main steps are restriction, adapter ligation, preselective amplification, selective amplification and gel analysis. The source gives typical AFLP fragments of about 80–500 bp. Advantages include high genomic abundance and many polymorphic bands per reaction. Limitations include dominant scoring and technical demands. SSR and SNP SSR markers are based on v

MAS integrates DNA-marker detection with conventional breeding to select plants carrying desired alleles. Procedure Select parents in which at least one parent carries the marker allele for the desired trait. Grow F1 and use markers to confirm hybrids or remove false hybrids. Screen F2 individuals and retain plants carrying desired marker alleles. Screen F2:3 rows and select plants with required marker alleles plus desirable phenotypes. Continue marker screening in F4 and F5. Bulk best lines around F4:5 or F5:6 using marker and phenotypic information. Conduct yield, quality, resistance and other performance trials. Important considerations Phenotypic selection remains useful when the trait can be evaluated reliably. A marker does not guarantee expression of the target trait. Marker–QTL association may vary across environments. Genetic background can affect QTL expression. QTL × environment, QTL × QTL and QTL × genetic-background interactions should be considered. When MAS is especially useful Target traits expressed late in plant development. Recessive target genes. Traits requiring

section: Intellectual property and major forms of protection
text: Intellectual property protects creations of the mind and can provide recognition or economic rights under law. Forms IP is intangible and must be expressed in a discernible form to be protectable. Examples include patents, trademarks, copyrights, trade secrets, geographical indications and plant varieties. Copyright protects literary and artistic works and related rights. Industrial property includes distinctive signs and technology-related rights. Distinctive signs Trademarks distinguish goods or services of one enterprise from another. Geographical indications identify goods associated with a specific geographical origin and its characteristics. Technology-related protection Patents protect inventions. Industrial designs protect ornamental or aesthetic aspects of articles. Trade secrets protect confidential information with commercial value.

section: Patent criteria and plant-variety registration criteria
text: A patent gives an exclusive right for an invention for a limited period when statutory criteria are satisfied. Patent criteria Novelty means the invention is not known in prior art. Non-obviousness means the invention involves an inventive step. Usefulness means it has industrial application. Plant variety criteria For PPV&FR registration, varieties must satisfy distinctiveness, uniformity and stability (DUS) criteria. Distinctiveness means the variety differs from previously known varieties. Uniformity means essential traits are sufficiently consistent among plants. Stability means essential characteristics remain after reproduction. Purpose Patent protection is intended to stimulate innovation and research investment. Publication of patent information provides technical information while granting limited exclusive rights.

India adopted a sui generis plant-variety protection system through the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001. Legal framework TRIPS requires WTO members to protect plant varieties through patents or an effective sui generis system under Article 27.3(b). India adopted a sui generis approach. The Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act came into force in 2001. The source states that the Act covers almost all plants except microorganisms. Breeders and researchers Registered breeders receive exclusive rights to produce, sell, market, distribute, import or export the variety under Section 28(1). The breeder's rights can pass to a successor, agent or licensee. Researchers may use protected varieties for research under Section 30. A protected variety can serve as an initial source for developing other varieties. Authorization is required when repeated use as a parental line is necessary for commercial production of the new variety. Protection duration Trees and vines: 18 years from registration in the source table. Other crops: 15 years from registration

The source describes farmer-oriented rights intended to recognize conservation, use and contribution of agricultural genetic resources. Rights listed in the source Farmers may save, use, reuse, exchange and sell farm produce including seed of registered varieties, subject to the Act's provisions. Farmers can claim compensation if a registered variety fails to perform as represented at registration. Farmers are exempted from certain registration and proceeding fees described in the source. A farmer group or community can register a variety evolved, cultivated and conserved by them. Farmers may seek benefit sharing when their genetic material contributes to a new registered variety. Compulsory licensing may be sought when a registered variety is unavailable to farmers at a reasonable price. The source describes protection from innocent infringement where lack of awareness is established. Farmers and communities may receive recognition or rewards when conserved material contributes genes to registered varieties.

Participatory plant breeding is breeding carried out collaboratively by breeders, farmers and other stakeholders. Definition and goals PPB involves collaboration among breeders, farmers, marketers, processors, consumers and policy makers. The approach is especially emphasized for developing-world farming systems with complex and risk-prone conditions. Goals include increasing production and profitability. PPB can target the needs of specific user groups or broader user groups. It builds farmer skills in selection and seed production. Participation Breeders can direct research toward the needs of specific farmer groups. Farmers can help breeders assess trade-offs among traits. On-farm research evaluates varieties under real farming conditions. Research can be managed by researchers, farmers or both. Participatory approaches can improve adoption of innovations. Activities Identify breeding objectives. Generate genetic variability and provide plants for breeding. Select within variable populations. Evaluate experimental varieties through participatory variety selection. Support variety

Applied meteorology dealing with crop and animal responses to the physical environment. Meaning Studies physical atmospheric processes producing weather in relation to agricultural production. Includes meteorological, climatological and hydrological conditions significant to agriculture. Focuses on interactions between environmental conditions and agricultural production. Scope Study climatic resources for effective production. Quantify favourable weather normals for farm operations. Develop crop/animal-weather relationships for productivity estimation. Study weather–crop–pest and disease relationships. Modify microclimate to increase agricultural productivity. Delineate agro-ecological zones for efficient resource use and technology transfer. Prepare crop-weather diagrams and crop-weather calendars. Develop crop/animal growth simulation models. Determine and monitor drought for drought management. Provide value-added weather-based agro-advisories in real time.

Weather is the short-term state of the atmosphere; climate describes longer-term average atmospheric conditions. Weather State of the atmosphere at a specific place and time. Includes temperature, moisture, wind velocity and barometric pressure. Usually concerns day-to-day changes over minutes to weeks. Climate Weather averaged over a long period and large area. The source uses a 30-year period for climate normals. Climate system components: atmosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, land surface and biosphere. Comparison Weather is studied in meteorology. Climate is studied in climatology. Weather uses real-time atmospheric measurements. Climate uses aggregated weather statistics over long periods.

The major weather elements used to describe weather and climate are temperature, pressure, wind, humidity and rain. Major elements Temperature indicates how hot or cold the atmosphere is. Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the atmosphere. Precipitation results from condensation processes and includes rain, snow, hail, sleet, drizzle, fog and mist. Atmospheric pressure is the weight of air resting on the Earth's surface. Wind is movement of air masses, especially near the Earth's surface. Agricultural relevance These elements provide the basis for weather forecasting. Long-term analysis of the same elements supports climatology.

The atmosphere is a thick gaseous envelope surrounding Earth and held by gravitational force. Gas composition Nitrogen: 78.08% by volume. Oxygen: 20.95%. Argon: 0.93%. Water vapour: 0–4% in the table. Carbon dioxide: 0.0360% in the table. Other trace gases include neon, helium, methane, hydrogen, nitrous oxide and ozone. Nitrogen and oxygen together form about 99% of dry atmospheric volume. Water vapour Atmospheric vapour may range from zero to about 5% by volume in the text. More than 90% of total atmospheric vapour occurs up to 5 km. Water vapour absorbs terrestrial radiation and contributes to atmospheric heating. Particulate matter Includes dust, salt particles, pollen, smoke and volcanic ash. Particles remain suspended in the atmosphere. Selective scattering contributes to blue sky appearance. Salt particles can act as hygroscopic nuclei for cloud and precipitation formation. Ozone Ozone is concentrated mainly around 15–55 km in the source discussion. It absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation. The source attributes severe ozone thinning primarily to chlorofluorocarbon emissions.

The atmosphere is divided into layers with characteristic temperature and physical properties. Troposphere Lowest atmospheric layer. Average height about 12 km in one source description; 9 km at poles and 17 km at equator. Contains roughly 75–80% of atmospheric mass. Nearly all water vapour and dust occur here. Most weather phenomena occur here. Temperature normally decreases upward at about 6.5°C per km. Upper boundary is the tropopause. Stratosphere Extends from roughly 12 km to 50–55 km. Contains the ozone layer. Temperature increases with altitude because ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation. Atmosphere is stable with little weather-producing turbulence. Upper boundary is the stratopause. Mesosphere Extends approximately from 50 km to 80–85 km. Temperature decreases upward. Most meteors burn up in this layer. Mesopause is near 80–85 km and is the coldest atmospheric region in the source discussion. Thermosphere and exosphere Thermosphere begins near 80 km and temperature increases strongly with height. Lower thermosphere contains the ionosphere. Auroral phenomena occur in the ther

Applications of atmospheric information for crop planning, productivity prediction and risk management. Applications Crop-weather calendars support timely farm operations. Weather-crop relationships support productivity estimation. Weather information helps manage drought. Agro-ecological zoning supports resource-efficient production. Growth simulation models can predict productivity and potential yield. Weather-based advisories can reduce input costs and improve productivity.

Pressure exerted by the weight of air in the atmosphere. Definition and variation Low-pressure areas have less atmospheric mass above them. High-pressure areas have more atmospheric mass above them. Atmospheric pressure decreases with increasing elevation. A one-square-centimetre column of air from sea level to the top of the atmosphere has a mass of about 1.03 kg. Mean sea-level pressure is about 101.325 kPa = 1013.25 hPa = 1013.25 mbar. Equivalent mean sea-level pressure is about 29.92 inHg or 760 mmHg. Pressure and altitude Increasing elevation reduces the mass of overlying air. Mean sea-level pressure is the adjusted pressure commonly reported in weather reports.

Wind is air in motion caused primarily by spatial differences in atmospheric pressure. Forces Pressure-gradient force controls wind speed. Pressure gradient is the rate of pressure change over space. Coriolis force deflects medium- and large-scale air movement due to Earth's rotation. Coriolis force depends on latitude and wind speed. Centripetal force acts when wind follows curved paths around pressure centres. Friction affects wind near the Earth's surface.

Winds are classified according to their scale, persistence and periodic behaviour. Planetary winds Blow throughout the year between latitude belts in response to pressure differences. Major prevailing winds include trade winds and westerlies. Trade winds Blow from subtropical high-pressure belts near 30° toward the equatorial low-pressure belt. Deflected right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern Hemisphere. Known as tropical easterlies. Generally steady in direction and force. Westerlies Blow from subtropical high-pressure belts toward subpolar low-pressure belts. Southern Hemisphere westerlies are described as stronger and more constant. 40°–65°S latitudes are associated with Roaring Forties, Furious Fifties and Shrieking Sixties. Periodic winds Direction changes periodically with seasons or daily heating differences. Examples: monsoons, land/sea breezes, mountain/valley breezes. Local winds Produced by local temperature and pressure differences. Types listed: hot, cold, convectional and slope winds.

Local coastal winds produced by differential heating and cooling of land and water. Land breeze Occurs mainly at night. Land cools faster than the sea. Air flows from relatively higher-pressure land toward lower-pressure water. Usually weaker than the daytime sea breeze. Dies as land warms the next morning. Sea breeze Develops after sunrise as land heats faster than water. Warm air over land expands and lowers surface pressure. Air moves from relatively higher-pressure sea toward lower-pressure land. Strength increases with the land–sea temperature difference. A strong offshore wind above about 15 km/h can prevent development.

Diurnal mountain winds caused by differential heating and cooling of mountain slopes and valleys. Valley breeze Occurs during the day. Heated mountain slopes cause air to move upward from valleys. Mountain breeze Occurs after sunset. Cold dense air moves downslope from mountains toward valleys.

Cyclones are low-pressure systems with inward rising flow; anticyclones are high-pressure systems with outward surface flow and subsidence. Cyclone Large-scale air mass rotating around a strong low-pressure centre. Northern Hemisphere rotation is counter-clockwise. Southern Hemisphere rotation is clockwise. Surface air converges inward and rises near the centre. Rising air expands and cools, increasing humidity and cloudiness. Cyclones are generally associated with rain, clouds and unsettled weather. Tropical cyclone Warm-core system driven by significant convective activity and latent heat release. Six source-listed requirements: warm sea surface, atmospheric instability, lower/middle tropospheric humidity, sufficient Coriolis force, pre-existing low-level disturbance, and low vertical wind shear. Called hurricane in the Atlantic/northeastern Pacific. Called cyclone in the Indian and South Pacific oceans. Called typhoon in the northwestern Pacific. Extratropical cyclone Also called mid-latitude or wave cyclone. Large-scale low-pressure system generally occurring in middle latitudes.

Radiant energy emitted by the Sun and the prime external energy source for Earth's biosphere. Sun and energy Solar radiation is the flux of radiant energy from the Sun. Sun diameter: about 1.39 × 10^6 km. Mean Sun–Earth distance: about 1.5 × 10^8 km. Source gives solar surface temperature around 5462 K in one description. Energy is produced by fusion in which hydrogen is transformed to helium. The source states about 99% of biosphere energy comes from the Sun. Insolation Electromagnetic energy radiated into space by the Sun. Factors affecting insolation: solar constant, atmospheric transparency, duration of daily sunlight and noon solar angle.

Heat moves by conduction, convection and radiation. Conduction Heat transfer through matter without bulk movement of the substance. Heat flows from warmer to cooler parts. Example: heating along an iron rod. Convection Heat transfer through actual movement of molecules or fluid masses. Predominant in many atmospheric weather processes. Example: boiling water. Radiation Energy transfer by electromagnetic waves without a material medium. Solar energy reaches Earth by radiation. Radiation produces heat when absorbed by a surface.

Solar radiation spans a broad electromagnetic spectrum with different wavelengths and biological effects. Major bands Ultraviolet: about 0.20–0.39 μm. Visible radiation: about 0.39–0.76 μm. Infrared: greater than 0.76 μm in the source table. Visible colours progress from violet through indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red. Plant significance Visible light is essential for photosynthesis. Infrared provides thermal energy. Shorter-than-visible radiation is chemically active and potentially damaging. Ultraviolet radiation is strongly absorbed by atmospheric ozone. Wavelength units 1 μm = 10^-6 m = 10^-4 cm. 1 millimicron = 10^-9 m = 10^-7 cm. 1 Å = 10^-10 m = 10^-8 cm.

Crop production depends on the intensity, quality and duration of solar radiation. Spectral effects Radiation below visible wavelengths can be detrimental at high exposure. Infrared has a thermal effect and supplies thermal energy to the plant environment. Visible light is indispensable to photosynthesis. Light affects tillering, culm stability, culm length, yield, plant biomass, leaf size and root development. Critical stages Maize: radiation intensity during the third month is highlighted. Rice: about 25 days before flowering. Barley: flowering period. Specific spectral bands 700–900 nm far-red region influences photoperiodism, germination, flowering and fruit coloration. 720–510 nm is strongly absorbed by chlorophyll and has strong photosynthetic activity. 510–400 nm includes strong chlorophyll/yellow pigment absorption and strong blue-violet photosynthetic effects. 400–315 nm can produce formative and dwarfing effects. Below 280 nm has lethal/germicidal effects in the source.

section: Radiation Balance, Albedo and Earth Energy Budget
text: Radiation balance is the difference between incoming and outgoing radiation; albedo is the percentage of incident radiation reflected by a surface. Radiation properties Absorptivity = absorbed radiant energy / incident radiant energy. Reflectivity = reflected radiant energy / incident radiant energy. Albedo is reflectivity expressed as a percentage. Transmittivity = transmitted radiation / incident radiation. Emissivity = radiation emitted by a surface / radiation emitted by a blackbody under comparable conditions. A blackbody completely absorbs incident radiation and has absorptivity and emissivity of unity. Earth energy budget The atmosphere filters, absorbs, scatters and reflects solar radiation. Source example: 324 W m^-2 reaching Earth in the upper-atmosphere budget discussion. 236 W m^-2 are re-emitted to space as infrared radiation in the cited budget. 86 W m^-2 are reflected by clouds. 20 W m^-2 are reflected by the ground as short-wave radiation. Atmospheric absorption and re-radiation contribute to the greenhouse effect. Albedo values Pure water: 5–20%. Vegetation: 10–40%.

Long-wave radiation emitted by the heated Earth and modified by atmospheric absorbers. Characteristics Average Earth surface temperature is given as about 285 K in the source. About 99% of emitted terrestrial radiation is in the infrared range of 4–120 μm. About 90% of outgoing radiation is absorbed by the atmosphere in the source discussion. Water vapour absorbs in approximately 5.3–7.7 μm and beyond 20 μm. Ozone absorbs around 9.4–9.8 μm. CO2 absorbs around 13.1–16.9 μm. Clouds absorb across broad wavelengths. Atmospheric window Long-wave radiation escapes relatively freely between about 8.5 and 11 μm. This region is called the atmospheric window. The source notes its use in microwave remote sensing and its role in limiting excessive night cooling through counter-radiation.

Physical relationships connecting wavelength, frequency, energy, emission and temperature. Wave relation λ = c/ν. λ = wavelength. c = velocity of light ≈ 3 × 10^10 cm s^-1. ν = frequency. Planck's law E = hν. h = Planck's constant ≈ 6.62 × 10^-34 J s. Higher frequency means higher quantum energy. Shorter wavelength corresponds to higher frequency and energy. Kirchhoff's law a(λ) = e(λ). A good absorber is a good emitter under similar conditions. Stefan–Boltzmann law E = σT^4. T is absolute temperature in kelvin. σ ≈ 5.673 × 10^-8 W m^-2 K^-4 for the blackbody constant given. Wien's displacement law λmax = 2897/T μm. Higher temperature shifts maximum emission toward shorter wavelengths. For Sun temperature around 5793 K, λmax is about 0.5 μm. For Earth surface near 287 K, λmax is about 10 μm.

Air temperature describes the molecular kinetic state of air and strongly controls atmospheric and crop processes. Definition and heat transfer Temperature is described as a measure of molecular motion. Heat is energy associated with molecular motion and transfer due to temperature differences. Conduction, convection and radiation transfer heat. Factors affecting air temperature Latitude. Altitude. Distribution of land and water. Ocean currents. Prevailing winds. Cloudiness. Mountain barriers. Nature of surface and relief. Convection and turbulence. Examples Northern India source example: January is the coldest month and June the warmest. Southern India source example: December is the coldest month and May the warmest. Land shows larger temperature variations than water. Ocean currents redistribute heat and create temperature contrasts.

Air temperature changes systematically within a day and across seasons. Diurnal variation Minimum air temperature generally occurs near sunrise. Temperature rises after sunrise and reaches a maximum around 13:00–14:00 h. Temperature then declines toward sunrise. Difference between daily maximum and minimum is the diurnal range. Clear days have larger diurnal ranges. Cloudy conditions reduce daily temperature amplitude. Daily mean temperature = (daily maximum + daily minimum) / 2. Seasonal variation Northern Hemisphere winter minimum is stated as January. Northern Hemisphere summer maximum is stated as July. Horizontal distribution Isotherms join places with equal temperature. Temperature generally decreases from equator toward poles. Land-water distribution modifies latitudinal temperature patterns. Mountain barriers and local topography alter horizontal temperature distribution.

Atmospheric layers can be distinguished by how temperature changes with altitude. Troposphere Average height about 14 km in this chapter; about 16 km at equator and 7–8 km at poles. Seat of weather phenomena. Temperature decreases upward at about 6.5°C/km. Contains most atmospheric moisture and aerosols. Stratosphere Extends roughly from 20 km to 50–55 km in the source chapter. Called a seat of photochemical reactions. Temperature increases with height. Ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation and warms the upper stratosphere. Upper boundary is the stratopause. Mesosphere and ozonosphere Ozone concentration is highlighted between about 30 and 60 km. Ozone absorbs UV radiation. Mesosphere lies approximately 50–80 km. Mesospheric temperature decreases with height. Mesopause temperature may reach nearly −95°C in the source. Thermosphere and exosphere Thermosphere/ionosphere extends from about 80 km to 400 km in the chapter. Temperature rises again and may reach about 1000°C. Ionosphere reflects radio waves and supports long-distance radio communication. Exosphere is the outermost layer, roug

Lapse rate is temperature change with height; adiabatic temperature change occurs without external heat exchange. Lapse rates Average atmospheric lapse rate is about 6.5°C/km. Dry adiabatic lapse rate is about 10°C/km. Moist adiabatic lapse rate is usually below 6°C/km. Moist air cools more slowly because condensation releases latent heat. Mountain process Moist air forced upward over mountains expands and cools. Cooling may cause condensation and precipitation. Descending air becomes warmer and drier after losing moisture. Descending air warms at the dry adiabatic rate in the source explanation. Adiabatic change No outside heat is involved. Rising air expands and cools. Sinking air compresses and warms.

A temperature inversion occurs when temperature increases with altitude over a layer instead of decreasing normally. Causes Ground air can cool faster than overlying air during clear cooling nights. A warm layer may pass over a lower cold layer. Cold air can drain downslope and be replaced by warmer air. Significance Influences cloud formation and precipitation. Can cause fog near the ground. Reduces visibility and can affect air navigation. Affects diurnal temperature behaviour and conversion of incoming solar radiation to heat.

section: Heat Units and Growing Degree Days
text: Heat units quantify accumulated warmth above a crop-specific threshold during growth. GDD concept Heat unit represents departure of mean daily temperature above a minimum threshold. Base temperatures in the source commonly range from 4.5–12.5°C. 6.0°C is stated as a commonly used value. Formula GDD = Σ[(Tmax + Tmin)/2 − Tb]. Tmax = daily maximum air temperature. Tmin = daily minimum air temperature. Tb = crop base or threshold temperature. Uses Guide agricultural operations and planting land use. Forecast crop harvest dates, yield and quality. Estimate labour requirements. Support introduction of crops and varieties into new areas. Predict likelihood of successful crop growth.

section: Heat and Cold Injuries in Crops
text: Extreme temperatures cause physiological and physical injuries to crop plants. Heat injury Thermal death point is given as about 50–60°C, varying with species. Aquatic and shade-loving plants may be killed at around 40°C. High temperature causes desiccation. It disrupts photosynthesis and respiration. High temperature increases respiration and rapidly depletes stored food. Cold injury Chilling injury affects warm-climate plants exposed to low temperatures. Sugarcane, sorghum and maize may show chlorotic bands when night temperature falls below 20°C in the source example. Freezing injury forms ice crystals in plant tissues and dehydrates cells. Examples include frost damage in potato and tea. Suffocation can occur under thick ice/snow due to restricted oxygen entry. Heaving occurs when ice crystals expand soil and mechanically lift plants. Specific injury Stem griddle is bark/stem injury associated with high daytime and low nighttime temperatures. Young cotton seedlings in sandy soil may be affected when soil temperature exceeds 60°C.

section: Role of Temperature in Crop Production
text: Temperature controls crop distribution, development, physiological processes and productivity. Crop effects Influences crop and vegetation distribution. Affects leaf production, expansion and flowering. Changes gas and liquid diffusion rates. Affects solubility of substances. Biochemical reaction rates increase strongly with temperature; the source states reactions may double or more per 10°C rise. Affects enzyme stability and system equilibrium. Most higher plants grow between about 0–60°C; crop plants are more restricted, around 10–40°C. Maximum dry matter production is stated around 20–30°C. High temperature plus high humidity favours some pests and diseases. High night temperature increases respiration and metabolism. Cardinal temperatures Crops have minimum, optimum and maximum temperatures. Wheat and barley: minimum 0–5°C; optimum 25–31°C; maximum 31–37°C. Sorghum: minimum 15–18°C; optimum 31–36°C; maximum 40–42°C. Thermoperiodism Response of living organisms to regular temperature changes between day and night or seasons.

Soil temperature influences seed, root and microbial processes and is controlled by meteorological and soil factors. Importance Governs uptake of water and nutrients. Controls soil microbial activity; source optimum range is 18–30°C. Influences seed germination and root development. Influences mineralization of organic nitrogen. Low soil temperature favours greater persistence of organic matter. Affects mineral weathering and soil reactions. Influences soil structure and exchangeable ions. Meteorological factors Solar radiation directly affects soil temperature. Wind/convection transfers heat to the soil. Evaporation cools soil. Condensation and freezing can release heat. Precipitation may warm or cool soil depending on its temperature. Soil factors Slope/aspect affect received insolation. Sandy soils warm faster than clay soils. Light soils generally show larger temperature ranges. Tillage and soil mulch modify heat flow and moisture. Organic matter lowers heat capacity and thermal conductivity while increasing water-holding capacity. Dark soils absorb more radiation than light soil

Humidity is the amount of water vapour present in air. Meaning and sources Humidity is a highly variable climatic factor. Source gives atmospheric water vapour as roughly 0–4% by volume, averaging around 2%. Measured with a hygrometer. Water vapour enters the atmosphere through evaporation, plant transpiration and animal respiration. Importance Supports precipitation formation. Absorbs incoming and terrestrial radiation and influences Earth's heat budget. Stores latent energy important in storms and cyclones. Influences sensible temperature and human cooling.

Weight of actual water vapour present per unit volume of air. Definition Usually expressed as grams of water vapour per cubic metre of air. Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air. At 10°C, one cubic metre of air can hold about 11.4 g water vapour in the source example. At 21°C, the same volume can hold about 22.2 g. Limitation Not a fully reliable index because temperature and pressure change air volume and therefore absolute humidity.

Relative humidity is the ratio of actual water vapour content to the moisture-holding capacity of air at a given temperature, expressed as a percentage. Relative humidity Adding moisture by evaporation increases relative humidity. Cooling air decreases its moisture-holding capacity and increases relative humidity. Saturated air has relative humidity of 100%. Air containing half of its moisture-holding capacity has relative humidity of 50%. Relative humidity strongly influences evaporation. Dew point Temperature at which a given air sample becomes saturated without changing its moisture content. Further cooling below the dew point promotes condensation.

Specific humidity relates water-vapour mass to total moist-air mass; mixing ratio relates water-vapour mass to dry-air mass. Specific humidity Weight of water vapour per unit weight of air. Usually expressed in grams per kilogram. Less affected by changes in pressure or temperature than absolute humidity. Mixing ratio Mass of water vapour divided by mass of dry air. Expressed as grams of water vapour per kilogram of dry air.

Saturation occurs when evaporation and condensation reach dynamic equilibrium at a given temperature. Saturation Saturation does not mean evaporation stops. In a closed water system, evaporation initially exceeds condensation. At equilibrium, evaporation rate equals condensation rate and the air is saturated. Higher temperature permits more water to remain in the vapour phase. Vapour pressure Saturation vapour pressure increases with air temperature. Below 0°C, saturation curves differ over liquid water and ice. Supercooled liquid water can persist below 0°C in clouds. Vapour pressure deficit VPD = saturated vapour pressure (SVP) − actual vapour pressure (AVP). VPD is useful in crop-growth and atmospheric-moisture studies.

Condensation is the change of water vapour into liquid or solid form when atmospheric conditions exceed moisture-holding capacity. Requirements Cooling moist air can reduce moisture-holding capacity below actual vapour content. Condensation generally begins when air temperature reaches or falls below the dew point. Relative humidity near 100% means the air is near saturation. Dust, smoke, pollen and ocean salt can act as hygroscopic condensation nuclei. Ways condensation can occur Air temperature can fall to the dew point at approximately constant volume. Air volume can increase without addition of heat. Combined temperature and volume changes can reduce moisture-holding capacity. Evaporation can add moisture to the air. Products Condensation may produce dew, frost, fog, mist and clouds. Direct vapour-to-solid deposition is described as sublimation in the source.

Cooling processes that produce condensation are classified into adiabatic and non-adiabatic changes. Adiabatic cooling Rising air expands and cools without external heat loss. Vertical air displacement is a major cause of adiabatic temperature change. Katabatic flow is cold, dense air moving downslope. Non-adiabatic cooling Includes cooling by radiation, conduction or mixing with colder air. Radiational cooling can produce fog or clouds when nuclei are present. Contact cooling can produce dew, frost or fog. Effects are mainly confined to a thin atmospheric layer. Source states non-adiabatic cooling generally produces dew, fog or frost rather than substantial precipitation.

section: Dew, Frost, Fog, Mist, Haze and Smog
text: These are near-surface atmospheric moisture or particulate phenomena formed under different temperature, humidity and condensation conditions. Dew Water droplets deposited on cool solid surfaces such as leaves, grass and stones. Ideal conditions: clear sky, calm air, high relative humidity, cold and long nights. Dew point must be above freezing. White frost Forms on cold surfaces when condensation occurs at or below 0°C. Moisture deposits as minute ice crystals rather than liquid droplets. Formation conditions resemble dew except temperature is at or below freezing. Fog Cloud with base at or very near the ground. Visibility is less than 1 km in the source. Radiation fog forms from radiational cooling and is common in winter. Advection fog forms when warm air moves over a cold surface; it is thick and persistent. Frontal or precipitation fog forms near converging warm and cold air masses. Mist Contains more moisture per nucleus than fog in the source description. Droplets are less coalesced, so mist is less dense and dissipates faster. Visibility is more than 1 km but less than 2 km.

section: Importance and Variation of Humidity for Crops
text: Atmospheric humidity interacts with temperature, rainfall and wind to influence crop water relations, pests, diseases and yield. Crop effects Helps determine which crops can be grown in a region. Affects internal plant water potential. Influences transpiration and potential evapotranspiration. Determines crop water requirement. High humidity can reduce irrigation requirement by reducing evapotranspiration losses. High humidity can prolong crop survival under moisture stress. Very high or very low relative humidity is generally unfavorable for high yields in the source. High humidity favours some fungi, bacteria and pests. Examples include potato blight and thrips/jassid damage. High humidity during grain filling can reduce yield. Very high relative humidity is described as beneficial to maize, sorghum and sugarcane but harmful to sunflower and tobacco. Moderate relative humidity above 40% is described as generally safe for most crops. Variation Absolute humidity is highest near the equator and lowest near the poles. Absolute humidity is minimum around sunrise and maximum around 14:00

A climatic normal is the average value of a weather element over 30 years. Meaning and use The period may be represented by weekly, monthly or annual averages. Crop distribution, production and productivity depend on climatic normals. Crop selection based on optimum climatic requirements can improve production potential.

Prediction of weather from the next few hours to seasonal periods. Importance for agriculture Weather has major social and economic impacts. The source states weather aberrations alone can explain up to 50% variation in crop production. Rainfall is especially important for crop production and regional economy. Forecasts support moisture conservation during weak monsoon conditions. Forecasts support flood-relief planning during strong monsoon conditions. Timely pest and disease warnings can reduce recurring crop losses. Forecasts help plan water use. Reliable forecasts can support sustainability and reduce damage from adverse weather. Forecast types Nowcast: next few hours. Short-range: about 24 hours, with outlook for another 24 hours. Medium-range: about 3–7/10 days. Long-range: beyond 7 days up to a season. Seasonal climate forecast supports farm decisions, especially rainfall-related decisions.

Forecast services differ in lead time, predicted elements, methods and agricultural users. Service table Nowcasting: IMD; thunderstorms, dust storms, cold/heat waves; lead time 1–2 hours; source accuracy 90–98%. Short range: IMD; cloud spread, rainfall, temperature and cyclone warnings; lead time about 1 day; source accuracy 80–90%. Medium range: IMD; rainfall, temperature, relative humidity, wind speed/direction and cloud cover; 3–10 days; source accuracy 70–75%. Long range: IMD; seasonal rainfall; 30–40 days in the source table; source accuracy about 60%. Methods Synoptic method uses surface and upper-air observations from multiple locations and prepares charts of atmospheric status. Statistical methods include multiple regression and ARIMA. Numerical weather prediction integrates equations representing Coriolis, frictional, pressure-gradient and gravitational forces. NWP model results depend strongly on accurate initial conditions. Farmer use Forecasters should understand crops grown in each agroclimatic zone. Forecast warnings should match crop growth stages. Farmers need to unde

Climate change is a significant long-term change in expected regional or global weather patterns; accelerated change is linked in the source to anthropogenic activities and greenhouse gases. Climate change Can occur over decades, centuries or much longer periods. The source emphasizes faster recent change associated with industrialization, urbanization, deforestation, agriculture and land-use change. Scenarios include higher temperature, changed precipitation and higher atmospheric CO2. The greenhouse effect is described as a natural process that helps maintain a warm Earth surface. Agricultural pathways Higher CO2 can directly affect crop and weed growth. CO2-driven climate changes can alter temperature, rainfall and sunshine. Sea-level rise can inundate farmland and increase salinity of coastal groundwater. Crop production is weather-dependent, so climate changes can affect productivity. Elevated CO2 and temperature affect respiration, photosynthesis, growth, reproduction and water use. GWP values Source gives Global Warming Potential values of CO2 = 1, CH4 = 25 and N2O = 310 for t

Climate variability refers to temporal changes in weather phenomena associated with atmospheric circulation and natural or human-related drivers. Meaning and impacts Occurs from year to year and across regions. Recurring drought and desertification threaten land-dependent livelihoods. Weather-related disasters include droughts, floods, ice storms, dust storms, landslides, lightning-associated storms and forest fires. External causes Solar output changes. Earth orbital eccentricity varies from nearly circular to more elliptical. Precession causes wobble of Earth's axis. Earth's axial tilt is given as varying between 21.8° and 24.4°. Internal and anthropogenic causes Changes in atmospheric greenhouse-gas composition. Land-surface changes including afforestation and deforestation. Southern Oscillation/El Niño–La Niña dynamics involving western tropical Pacific sea-surface temperature. Anthropogenic greenhouse gases and aerosols.

section: El Niño, La Niña and Climate Variability
text: El Niño and La Niña are natural short-term climate fluctuations associated with tropical Pacific Ocean conditions and the Southern Oscillation. ENSO effects El Niño is associated with tropical Pacific warming. La Niña is associated with tropical Pacific cooling. Strong events can produce year-to-year changes in temperature and rainfall in many regions. The source links strong events with extreme weather such as flooding and drought. These short-term fluctuations are described as smaller than the long-term 20th-century warming trend. Related drivers Southern Oscillation Index is described through normalized pressure differences between Tahiti and Darwin. Natural variability can also arise from volcanic aerosols and changes in Earth's orbit.

section: Effects of Climate Change on Agriculture
text: Climate change affects crop production through changes in temperature, rainfall, atmospheric CO2 and related biological processes. Major effects Higher greenhouse-gas concentrations are expected to increase Earth's temperature. Changes in weather can alter crop production and productivity. Elevated CO2 and temperature affect photosynthesis, respiration, growth, reproduction and water use. CO2 effects can differ with latitude and environmental context. Evidence in model simulations The source describes simulations using only natural factors as showing negligible warming or slight cooling over the 20th century. Including greenhouse-gas emissions and other human activities produced temperature changes closer to observations in the source discussion.

section: Climate Change Mitigation and Adaptation in Agriculture
text: Agricultural adaptation combines weather services, resilient crops, improved water and nutrient management, and risk-reduction practices. Adaptation measures Provide value-added weather services to help farmers manage current climate risks. Shift planting dates when appropriate. Choose varieties with different growth durations. Modify crop rotations. Establish early-warning systems for pest and disease outbreaks. Use integrated pest management under changing climatic conditions. Use participatory and formal breeding for heat-, drought- and salinity-tolerant varieties. Develop short-duration varieties that mature before peak heat. Select genotypes with higher per-day yield potential to offset heat-related shortening of growth periods. Drought prevention Use on-farm reservoirs in medium lands. Grow pulses and oilseeds instead of rice in uplands where suitable. Use ridge-and-furrow systems in cotton. Use intercrops instead of pure crops in uplands. Use land grading and leveling. Stabilize bunds with stone and grasses. Use graded line bunds and contour trenches for runoff collection. Use

Agriculture is the systematic practice and science of growing crops, raising animals, and managing natural resources to produce food, fiber, fuel, medicines, and other useful products for humans. Agriculture is much broader than simply farming. It includes: • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • Crop production Horticulture Livestock production Dairy farming Poultry Fisheries and aquaculture Forestry and agroforestry Soil management Irrigation and water management Seed production Plant protection Agricultural engineering Harvesting and post-harvest management Food processing Agricultural economics and marketing Modern technologies such as precision agriculture, remote sensing, GIS, IoT, AI, robotics and biotechnology In simple terms: Agriculture is the management of biological and natural resources to produce useful products while maintaining productivity, profitability, and environmental sustainability. 2. Definition of Agriculture General definition Agriculture is the science, art, business, and technology of cultivating plants and raising animals for human use. Scientific definition Agri

Agronomy deals primarily with the principles and practices of producing and managing field crops and soils. It includes: • • • • • • Crop production Soil management Nutrient management Weed management Water management Cropping systems

Horticulture deals with intensively cultivated crops such as: • • • • • • Fruits Vegetables Flowers Ornamentals Spices Plantation crops Major branches include: • • • • • Pomology — fruit science Olericulture — vegetable science Floriculture — flower cultivation Landscape horticulture Plantation crop science 5.3 Soil Science Soil science studies: - Soil formation - Soil properties - Soil classification • • • • • Soil fertility Soil chemistry Soil physics Soil biology Soil-water relationships 5.4 Agricultural Entomology Agricultural entomology deals with insects associated with agriculture. It covers: • • • • • • Insect identification Beneficial insects Harmful insects Pest biology Pest damage Pest management 5.5 Plant Pathology Plant pathology is the study of plant diseases. It deals with: • • • • • • Disease-causing organisms Disease symptoms Disease cycles Disease diagnosis Disease prevention Disease management Important pathogens include: • • • • • • Fungi Bacteria Viruses Viroids Phytoplasmas Nematodes 5.6 Agricultural Engineering Agricultural engineering applies engineering princ

Includes: • • • • • Temperature Rainfall Humidity Solar radiation Wind 5. Crop/animal genetics The genetic characteristics of a variety or breed strongly influence: - Yield • • • • Quality Disease resistance Stress tolerance Maturity

Plants require essential nutrients for growth and reproduction. 7. Biological organisms Agricultural ecosystems contain: • • • • • • • • Plants Animals Microorganisms Insects Earthworms Beneficial organisms Pathogens Pests 8. Human resources Farmers, workers, scientists, extension personnel and other professionals contribute to agricultural production.

Modern agriculture uses: • • • • • • • • • Machinery Irrigation technology Sensors Drones Satellites GIS AI Robotics Biotechnology 10. Capital and markets Farm production requires investment and access to markets. 8. Agricultural Production System Agriculture can be represented as a system: Natural resources + Inputs + Management + Biological processes → Agricultural products For crop production: Seed + Soil + Water + Nutrients + Light + Suitable temperature + Management → Crop growth → Yield The final yield depends on the interaction of genetics × environment × management. A useful conceptual model is: Yield = f(Genotype, Environment, Management) where: - Genotype = genetic characteristics of the crop - Environment = soil, climate, water, etc. - Management = farmer's production practices 9. Types of Agriculture Agriculture can be classified in many ways. Based on water availability Rainfed agriculture Production depends primarily on rainfall. Irrigated agriculture Water is supplied artificially through irrigation systems. Based on production objective Subsistence agriculture Primari

Definition Monoculture is the repeated cultivation of the same crop on a field or production area. Example: Wheat → Wheat → Wheat Advantages • • • • Simplifies farm operations Specialized machinery can be used Crop management becomes more standardized May be economically efficient in suitable situations Disadvantages Repeated monoculture can increase: • • • • • Pest pressure Disease pressure Weed problems Nutrient depletion/imbalance Soil health problems The severity depends on the crop and management system. 12. Multiple Cropping Multiple cropping means growing more than one crop on the same piece of land within a defined period, usually a year. Examples: Rice → Wheat - r Maize → Vegetable crop 13. Multiple Cropping Systems Major forms include: Double cropping Two crops are grown successively on the same land during a year or production period. Triple cropping Three crops are grown successively. Multi-cropping More than one crop is produced within the same land-use period. 14. Mixed Cropping Definition Mixed cropping is growing two or more crops simultaneously on the same land witho

Definition Intercropping is growing two or more crops simultaneously in a planned spatial arrangement. Example: Maize + Soybean Common forms - Row intercropping - Strip intercropping - Relay intercropping Potential benefits • • • • • Better resource utilization Crop diversification Risk reduction Weed suppression in some systems Complementary nutrient/resource use 16. Mixed Cropping vs Intercropping Feature Mixed Cropping Intercropping Crops Two or more Two or more Simultaneous cultivation Yes Yes Spatial arrangement Generally not strongly defined Planned arrangement Row pattern Not necessarily Often defined Management Less spatially structured More spatially structured 17. Plantation Agriculture Definition Plantation agriculture is a large-scale, commercially oriented system typically involving perennial or long-duration crops cultivated systematically for markets. Examples • • • • • • Tea Coffee Rubber Coconut Oil palm Cocoa Characteristics • • • • • • Commercial orientation Specialized production Often large-scale Processing may occur near production Significant investment may be

Definition Agroforestry is the deliberate integration of trees with crops and/or livestock within an agricultural production system. Examples: Trees + Crops Trees + Livestock Trees + Crops + Livestock Potential benefits - Diversification • • • • • Soil protection Carbon storage Biodiversity Additional products Microclimate modification 31. Shifting Cultivation Shifting cultivation is a land-use system in which a plot is cultivated for a period and then left fallow while cultivation shifts to another area. It is historically practiced in several regions. Traditional cycle Forest/vegetation → Clearing → Cultivation → Fallow → Regrowth → Cultivation elsewhere Its sustainability depends heavily on: • • • • Fallow length Population pressure Land availability Management practices Shortened fallow periods can cause degradation. 32. Nomadic Pastoralism Nomadic pastoralism is a livestock production system in which pastoral communities move animals between grazing areas according to seasonal resource availability. Animals can include: • • • • • Sheep Goats Cattle Camels Yaks The system is part

GIS Sensors Drones Satellite imagery Variable-rate application Yield monitors IoT Data analytics AI Example Instead of applying exactly the same fertilizer rate everywhere: Soil data → field map → nutrient recommendation → variable-rate application This can improve resource-use efficiency when appropriately designed and implemented. 37. Smart Agriculture Smart agriculture uses digital technologies, sensors, connectivity, automation and data analytics to improve agricultural decision-making and management. Examples: • • • • • • Smart irrigation Soil-moisture sensors Automated greenhouse systems Weather stations AI disease detection Farm-management software 38. Urban Agriculture Urban agriculture is agricultural production within or around urban areas. Examples: • • • • • Rooftop farming Terrace gardens Community gardens Vertical farms Hydroponic systems 39. Vertical Farming Vertical farming produces crops in vertically stacked growing systems. It may use: • • • • • Controlled environments Artificial lighting Hydroponics Aeroponics Automated climate control Advantages - High production

Permaculture is a design approach inspired by ecological systems that seeks to create productive, resilient and relatively self-sustaining human-managed ecosystems. It may emphasize: • • • • • • Diversity Resource cycling Perennial plants Water conservation Soil protection Integration of plants and animals Permaculture is broader than a specific crop-production technique. 43. Conservation Agriculture Conservation agriculture generally rests on three widely recognized principles: 1. Minimum soil disturbance 2. Permanent soil cover 3. Definition A plant is an individual living organism belonging to the plant kingdom. In agriculture, a plant is the individual biological organism growing in a field, garden, orchard, greenhouse, forest, or other environment. Definition A crop is a plant or group of plants that is cultivated and managed by humans for a particular useful purpose, usually food, feed, fiber, oil, medicine, fuel, or industrial raw material. The key difference is: Plant = biological organism Crop = plant cultivated for a purpose Examples - Rice crop - Wheat crop - Cotton crop - Soybean crop - Tomato crop - Sugarcane crop A crop usually refers to the cultivated production system, rather than one individual plant. Example Suppose a farmer plants 50,000 rice plants in a field. - One individual = rice plant - The cultivated population in the field = rice crop - The crop belongs to a particular species and variety/cultivar. 3. For example, "cereal crops" includes several species: - Wheat - Rice - Maize - Barley - Oats - Sorghum Similarly, "oilseed crops" include: - Soybean - Groundnut - Mustard - Sunflower - Sesame Therefore, crop is a functional/agricultural classification, not a botanical classification.

General meaning A variety is a group of plants within a species that has distinguishable characteristics. In agriculture, the word is commonly used for a cultivated type that differs from other types in characteristics such as: - Yield - Plant height - Maturity duration - Grain/fruit characteristics - Disease resistance - Pest resistance - Drought tolerance - Temperature tolerance - Quality - Color - Shape Example Rice may have many varieties/types with different: - Grain lengths - Maturity periods - Yield potential - Disease resistance - Water requirements - Cooking qualities 5. Definition Domestication is the long-term process through which humans changed wild plant populations by repeatedly cultivating and selecting plants with desirable characteristics. Farmers historically selected plants that had useful traits. For example: - larger seeds - larger fruits - better taste - reduced seed shattering - uniform maturity - easier harvesting - higher yield - better storage - reduced bitterness - improved nutritional quality Over many generations, these traits became increasingly common. 7. How Domestication Occurred Early humans probably did not begin with modern scientific breeding. Instead, domestication was largely a gradual process involving: Gathering Humans collected useful wild plants. Cultivation Useful plants were deliberately grown. Selection Plants with desirable characteristics were preferentially retained. Replanting Seeds or propagules from selected plants were planted again. Repeated selection The process continued over many generations. This resulted in genetic changes in crop populations. 8. The Domestication Syndrome Many domesticated crops dev

The crop life cycle is the complete sequence of biological and developmental events through which a crop plant passes, beginning with a seed or other propagating unit and ending with reproduction, maturity, and completion of its life cycle. In a typical seed-propagated crop: growth development formation For an annual crop, the plant generally completes this cycle and dies within one growing season or year. For biennial crops, reproduction generally occurs during the second growing season. For perennial crops, the plant survives and can repeat reproductive cycles for several years.

The root system is the underground or soil-associated part of a plant consisting of the primary root, lateral roots, adventitious roots, root hairs, and their branches. Its major roles are anchorage, absorption of water and mineral nutrients, transport, storage, interaction with soil organisms, and sometimes vegetative propagation. In crop science, the root system is extremely important because much of a plant's ability to obtain water and nutrients, withstand drought, remain anchored, and produce yield depends on root architecture. A simplified relationship is: Root system→Anchorage + Absorption + Transport + Storage + Interaction 2. Root vs Root System These terms are related but not identical. Root An individual root structure. Root system The entire network of roots belonging to a plant. For example, a mature maize plant may have: - Primary root remnants - Lateral roots - Adventitious roots - Brace/stilt roots - Fine roots - Root hairs Together, these constitute its root system. 3. Roots hold the plant firmly in the soil. This prevents plants from being easily uprooted by: - Wind - Rain - Irrigation - Soil movement Strong anchorage is particularly important in tall crops. 18.2 Water Absorption Roots absorb water from the soil. Water then enters the plant and eventually moves through the vascular system. Simplified pathway: Soil→Root hairs→Root tissues→Xylem→Shoot 19. Roots are connected to the vascular system. Xylem Primarily transports: Water + mineral nutrients from roots toward shoots. A flower is the specialized reproductive structure of flowering plants (angiosperms). Its main biological role is to enable sexual reproduction, leading to pollination, fertilization, seed formation, and often fruit formation. In agriculture, flowers are extremely important because successful flowering directly affects: - Pollination - Fertilization - Seed production - Grain formation - Fruit formation - Yield - Hybrid seed production - Crop breeding The overall reproductive sequence can be represented as: Flower initiation→Flower development→Flowering→Pollination→Fertilization→Seed formation→Fr uit development 2. What Is a Flower? A flower is a modified reproductive shoot whose organs are specialized for sexual reproduction. A typical flower contains four major floral whorls: 1. Calyx — sepals 2. Corolla — petals 3. Androecium — stamens 4. Gynoecium — carpels/pistil The first two are generally considered accessory/non-reproductive floral parts, while the last two are the principal reproductive whorls. Flower=Calyx+Corolla+Androecium+Gynoecium = + + + Not every flower possesses all f

The pedicel is the stalk that supports an individual flower. A flower with a pedicel is called pedicellate. A flower without a distinct pedicel is called sessile. The pedicel connects the flower to the plant's shoot system.

The receptacle is the expanded portion of the floral axis where floral organs are attached. It may support: - Sepals - Petals - Stamens - Carpels Its shape and development can influence fruit formation in some plants.

The calyx is the outermost floral whorl, usually consisting of sepals. Individual units are called: Sepal Functions - Protect the developing flower bud - Sometimes contribute to photosynthesis - May persist after flowering - Can sometimes contribute to fruit appearance

The corolla is generally the floral whorl consisting of petals. Individual units are called: Petal Petals may be: - Colorful - Scented - Nectar-associated - Modified in shape Main function In many flowers, petals help attract pollinators. They may provide visual and chemical signals such as: - Color - Scent - Nectar guides

When sepals and petals are not clearly differentiated, the floral covering is called the perianth. Its individual parts are commonly called tepals. This is common in several monocots. Thus: Sepals + petals distinct→Calyx + corolla while: Not clearly differentiated→Perianth/tepals

The anther is the pollen-producing portion of the stamen. Its primary function is to produce and release pollen grains. Pollen contains the male gametophytic generation and ultimately gives rise to male gametes.

The filament is the stalk supporting the anther. Its main function is to position the anther so that pollen can be effectively dispersed and transferred. The height and position of stamens can influence pollination.

Pollen grains carry the male reproductive cells/gametophytic structures of flowering plants. After compatible pollen reaches the stigma: Pollen→Germination→Pollen tube→Ovule→Fertilization Pollen characteristics can vary in: - Size - Shape - Surface - Viability - Longevity
Carpel=Stigma+Style+Ovary = + + The term pistil is commonly used for the female reproductive structure. Depending on floral structure, a pistil may consist of one carpel or multiple fused carpels.

The stigma is the receptive surface at the top of the pistil. Its functions include: - Receiving pollen - Recognizing compatible pollen - Supporting pollen germination The stigma may be: - Sticky - Hairy - Branched - Feather-like These characteristics can facilitate pollen capture.

The style is the structure connecting the stigma with the ovary. After compatible pollen germinates on the stigma, the pollen tube grows through the style toward the - vary. Simplified: Stigma→Style→Ovary

The ovary is the basal portion of the gynoecium containing one or more ovules. After fertilization: Ovary→Fruit in typical angiosperm fruit development. The ovules develop into seeds. Thus: Ovule→Seed and: Ovary→Fruit These are fundamental relationships in plant reproduction.

The ovule is the structure within the ovary that contains the female gametophyte. After successful fertilization: Ovule→Seed The ovule contains the embryo sac, which includes the egg cell and other cells involved in double fertilization. 19. Floral Whorls A typical flower can therefore be organized as: Whorl Main structure Major role Calyx Sepals Protection Corolla Petals Attraction/protection Androecium Stamens Pollen production Gynoecium Carpels/pistil Ovules, pollen reception, fertilization The reproductive whorls are: Androecium + Gynoecium 20. Complete and Incomplete Flowers Complete flower A flower possessing all four major whorls: - Calyx - Corolla - Androecium - Gynoecium is called a complete flower. Incomplete flower A flower lacking one or more of these whorls is called an incomplete flower. This classification is structural. 21. Bisexual and Unisexual Flowers Bisexual flower A flower containing both: - Stamens - Gynoecium is called bisexual. Examples include many flowers of: - Tomato - Pea - Mustard - Wheat Unisexual flower A flower possessing only one functional reproduct

An inflorescence is the arrangement of multiple flowers on a common floral axis or system. Instead of occurring as isolated flowers, many crop plants produce flowers in organized groups. Examples: - Spike - Raceme - Panicle - Umbel - Capitulum/head - Spadix - Cyme Inflorescence architecture strongly influences: - Flower visibility - Pollination - Fruit/seed arrangement - Harvesting 24. Flowering is the stage when reproductive structures become developed and flowers become visible/open or otherwise reproductively active. Flowering involves a transition: Vegetative phase→Reproductive phase This transition is controlled by: - Genetics - Temperature - Photoperiod - Plant age - Nutrition - Water status - Hormonal signals 26. Flower Initiation vs Flowering These are not identical. Flower initiation The developmental transition in which the shoot meristem begins forming reproductive structures. Flowering The subsequent visible development/opening of flowers. Therefore: Flower initiation→Flower development→Flowering This distinction is important in crop growth studies.

Photoperiodism is the response of plants to the relative duration of light and darkness. Plants may be broadly classified as: Short-day plants Flower when day length is below a critical value, or more precisely when the uninterrupted night period meets their requirement. Long-day plants Flower when day length exceeds a critical requirement. Day-neutral plants Flowering is relatively less dependent on photoperiod. Examples and exact classifications can depend on genotype and environmental conditions.

Vernalization is the induction or acceleration of flowering by exposure to a suitable period of low temperature. It is important in some crops and biennial plants. For example, temperature exposure can influence flowering behavior in: - Wheat - Barley - Some biennial crops Vernalization interacts with genotype and developmental stage.

Anthesis refers broadly to the period when a flower opens and becomes reproductively functional. It is associated with: - Anther dehiscence - Pollen release - Stigma receptivity - Pollination The exact timing of anthesis is important in crop production. 30. Anther Dehiscence Anther dehiscence is the opening of the mature anther to release pollen. Conceptually: Anther maturation→Dehiscence→Pollen release Environmental conditions such as: - Temperature - Humidity - Wind can affect pollen release. 31. Stigma Receptivity The stigma is receptive when it can successfully receive and support compatible pollen. Pollination success depends on synchronization between: Pollen availability+Stigma receptivity + If pollen is released when the stigma is not receptive, successful fertilization may be reduced.

Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther to a receptive stigma. It can occur through: - Wind - Insects - Birds - Other animals - Water - Human intervention Two major categories are: Self-pollination and Cross-pollination Pollination is not the same as fertilization.

Self-pollination occurs when pollen reaches the stigma of: - The same flower, or - Another flower of the same plant Self-pollinating crops often have mechanisms that favor reproductive assurance. Examples include: - Wheat - Rice - Pea However, the degree of selfing can vary among cultivars and environmental conditions.

Cross-pollination occurs when pollen is transferred between flowers of genetically different plants, generally within the same species. It increases opportunities for: - Genetic recombination - Genetic diversity - Heterozygosity Common cross-pollination agents include: - Wind - Bees - Other insects Examples of predominantly cross-pollinated crops include: - Maize - Pearl millet - Many cucurbits 35. Pollination Agents Wind pollination Called anemophily. Common features can include: - Abundant pollen - Exposed anthers - Large/feathery stigmas - Reduced dependence on attractive petals Examples: - Maize - Wheat - Rice Insect pollination Called entomophily. Flowers may possess: - Bright colors - Fragrance - Nectar - Pollen rewards Examples: - Mustard - Sunflower - Many fruit crops 36. Floral Biology Floral biology is the study of: - Flower structure - Flower development - Anthesis - Pollen production - Pollen viability - Stigma receptivity - Pollination - Fertilization - Flowering behavior It is particularly important in: - Seed production - Hybridization - Crop breeding - Fruit productio

Flower Types Based on Position of Ovary Flowers can be classified according to the relationship between ovary and other floral parts. Superior ovary The ovary lies above the attachment of other floral parts. Inferior ovary The ovary is positioned below the attachment of other floral parts. Intermediate/semi-inferior conditions Intermediate arrangements occur in some plants. This classification becomes important when studying fruit development. 43. Floral Symmetry Flowers can differ in symmetry. Actinomorphic Radially symmetrical. The flower can be divided into similar halves through multiple planes. Zygomorphic Bilaterally symmetrical. It can generally be divided into similar halves through one main plane. Floral symmetry can be useful in botanical identification and pollination biology. 44. Floral Sex and Breeding System A crop's floral biology determines how it reproduces. Important terms include: Term Bisexual Staminate Pistillate Monoecious Dioecious Self-pollinated

Emasculation is the removal of anthers or male reproductive structures from a bisexual flower before pollen release. Purpose: Prevent unwanted self-pollination It is an important technique in controlled hybridization. 49. Artificial Pollination In plant breeding, pollen can be deliberately transferred from a selected male parent to a selected female parent. General sequence: Select parents→Emasculate if required→Collect pollen→Apply pollen→Protect flower→Harvest hybr id seed 50. Flowering and Environmental Factors Flowering is influenced by: Temperature Extreme heat or cold can interfere with: - Pollen development - Pollen viability - Stigma receptivity - Fertilization Water Drought can reduce: - Flower initiation - Flower retention - Pollen viability - Fruit set Nutrition Nutrient imbalance can alter reproductive growth. Light Photoperiod and light intensity influence flowering in many crops. Humidity Can influence: - Pollen release - Pollen dispersal - Disease - Stigma conditions 51. Pollination vs fertilization - Pollination = pollen reaches stigma. - Fertilization = male and female gametes fuse. A fruit is the mature reproductive structure of a flowering plant that develops primarily from the ovary after fertilization. Its major biological functions are to protect seeds and help in their dispersal. In agriculture, fruits are important in two different senses: 1. Botanical fruit — a structure developing from the ovary and associated tissues. 2. Fruit crop — a crop cultivated primarily for edible fruits, such as mango, apple, banana, citrus and grapes. These two ideas should not be confused. Botanically, tomato, cucumber, pumpkin and brinjal are fruits, even though they are commonly treated as vegetables in agriculture and cooking. The basic developmental relationship is: Flower→Fertilization→Fruit development→Mature fruit and: Ovule→Seed Ovary→Fruit 2. What Is a Fruit? A fruit is generally the mature ovary of a flowering plant, often together with other floral tissues that become incorporated during development. After successful fertilization:

│ ├── Ovary │ │ │ ↓ │ Fruit │ └── Ovule │ ↓ Seed However, fruit development is more diverse than simply "ovary becomes fruit." In some fruits, tissues - utside the ovary also contribute substantially to the edible structure. 3. Functions of Fruits Fruits perform several important functions. 3.1 Seed protection The fruit surrounds and protects developing seeds against: - Mechanical damage - Desiccation - Some pathogens - Herbivory 3.2 Seed dispersal Fruits help move seeds away from the parent plant. Dispersal can occur through: - Wind - Water - Animals - Gravity - Explosive mechanisms - Human activity 3.3 Attraction of animals Many fleshy fruits become: - Sweet - Colorful - Fragrant - Nutrient-rich This can attract animals that consume the fruit and subsequently disperse seeds. 3.4 Agricultural food production Fruits provide: - Carbohydrates - Dietary fiber - Vitamins - Minerals - Organic acids - Pigments - Antioxidant compounds - Water Their nutritional composition varies considerably among species and cultivars. 4. Basic Fruit Structure A typical fleshy fruit can contain:

The exocarp is the outermost layer of the fruit. It is often called the skin or peel in common language. Functions include: - Protection - Reduction of water loss - Defense against pathogens and pests - Contribution to fruit color and appearance Example: The outer skin of a mango or peach represents the exocarp.

The mesocarp is the middle layer of the pericarp. Depending on the fruit, it may be: - Fleshy - Juicy - Fibrous - Dry In many fruits, the mesocarp constitutes much of the edible portion. Examples: - Mango - Peach - Papaya

The endocarp is the innermost layer of the pericarp. It may be: - Soft - Papery - Fibrous - Hard and stony In a drupe, the hard inner layer is commonly called the stone or pit. Example: In mango, the hard fibrous structure surrounding the seed is associated with the endocarp.
The pericarp is the fruit wall derived primarily from the ovary wall. It is divided into: Exocarp→Mesocarp→Endocarp The appearance of these layers differs greatly between fruit types.

The seed develops from an ovule following fertilization. A typical seed contains: - Seed coat - Embryo - Cotyledon(s) - Sometimes endosperm or other storage tissue Thus: Ovule→Seed The seed is the next generation of the plant. 10. Fruit Development Fruit development generally follows successful reproductive events. A simplified sequence is: Flower→Pollination→Fertilization→Fruit set→Fruit growth→Maturation→Ripening However, not every fruit requires normal fertilization. Some fruits can develop through parthenocarpy. 11. Fruit Set Fruit set is the developmental transition in which a flower or ovary begins developing into a fruit. Factors affecting fruit set include: - Pollination - Fertilization - Temperature - Water availability - Nutritional status - Hormonal balance - Pollinator activity - Genetic characteristics - Pest and disease pressure Therefore: Flowering does not automatically mean fruit set 12. Fruit Growth After fruit set, the fruit undergoes growth. Growth can involve: - Cell division - Cell expansion - Accumulation of carbohydrates - Water accumulation - Organic acid cha

A berry is a fleshy fruit in which the pericarp is generally fleshy throughout, with seeds embedded in the pulp. Examples include: - Tomato - Brinjal - Grape - Guava - Banana Botanical classification can differ from culinary usage. For example: A tomato is botanically a berry, although it is commonly called a vegetable.

A drupe is a fleshy fruit typically characterized by: - Fleshy outer/middle tissues - A hard or stony endocarp - Usually one seed enclosed by the stone Examples: - Mango - Peach - Plum - Cherry - Coconut Mango is a particularly important agricultural example. Structure: Skin→Fleshy mesocarp→Hard endocarp→Seed ## 22. Pome A pome is an accessory fruit in which a substantial part of the edible fruit develops from tissues associated with the floral cup/receptacle in addition to the ovary. Examples: - Apple - Pear The true ovary-derived core is surrounded by the fleshy accessory tissue. Therefore: Pome=Ovary-derived tissue + substantial accessory tissue =

A pepo is a specialized berry characteristic of the cucumber family (Cucurbitaceae). Examples: - Watermelon - Cucumber - Pumpkin - Muskmelon - Bottle gourd - Bitter gourd Typical characteristics include: - Fleshy fruit - Tough outer rind - Usually many seeds - Inferior ovary

A hesperidium is a specialized citrus fruit. Examples: - Orange - Lemon - Lime - Mandarin It generally has: - Leathery rind - Oil glands - Segmented interior - Juice-filled sacs The edible portion is largely derived from specialized internal tissues. 25. Dry Fruits Dry fruits have relatively dry pericarp at maturity. They may be: Dehiscent Open at maturity to release seeds. Indehiscent Do not normally split open at maturity. Schizocarpic Split into separate units, each usually containing one seed. 26. Dehiscent Fruits Dehiscent fruits open naturally at maturity. Examples include: - Legume/pod - Capsule - Follicle Legume Common in many members of Fabaceae. Examples: - Pea - Bean - Groundnut pod The fruit opens along one or more seams depending on the crop.

A capsule is a dry fruit formed from multiple carpels that opens in various ways to release seeds. Examples occur in many plant families. Cotton produces a capsule. At maturity, the cotton boll opens and exposes the fibers associated with the seeds. 28. Indehiscent Fruits Indehiscent fruits generally remain closed at maturity. Examples include: - Achene - Caryopsis - Nut

A caryopsis is the characteristic fruit of grasses. Examples: - Wheat - Rice - Maize - Barley - Sorghum It is commonly called a grain. A major characteristic is that the fruit wall is closely fused with the seed coat. Therefore: Cereal grain=Botanically a caryopsis = This is a very important agricultural concept. 30. Wheat Grain The wheat grain is a caryopsis. Its major components include: - Bran - Endosperm - Germ/embryo The outer layers include the fruit wall and seed coverings. The endosperm contains much of the starch reserve. 31. Rice Grain A rice grain is also a caryopsis. The harvested rice grain with its husk is a spikelet-derived structure, while the dehulled grain is the caryopsis. This distinction becomes important in crop morphology and post-harvest science. 32. Maize Grain Maize grain is also a caryopsis. The kernel contains: - Pericarp/seed coat region - Endosperm - Embryo/germ The endosperm is a major starch-storage tissue. 33. Parthenocarpy is fruit development without normal fertilization. Such fruits are often: - Seedless - Nearly seedless Examples can include certain cultivars of: - Banana - Citrus - Grapes Parthenocarpy is agriculturally valuable because seedless fruits can have desirable eating quality. 43. Seedless Fruits Seedlessness can arise through different biological mechanisms, including: - Parthenocarpy - Stenospermocarpy - Sterility - Genetic mutations - Breeding Therefore: Seedless fruit≠Always the same biological mechanism 44. Fruit Ripening Fruit ripening involves coordinated biochemical changes. Color Chlorophyll may decline while other pigments become visible or accumulate. Texture Cell-wall components are modified, leading to softening in many fruits. Flavor Sugars, acids and volatile compounds change. Aroma Volatile compounds are produced or altered. Nutritional composition Some vitamins and phytochemicals change during development and ripening. 45. Fruit Color Important pigments include: Chlorophyll Green color. Carotenoids Yellow, orange and some red colors. Anthocyanins Red, purple

A seed is a mature ovule that develops after fertilization in a flowering plant. It contains a young plant embryo, usually a food reserve, and a protective covering. The seed is one of the most important structures in agriculture because it serves as: - The starting point of a new plant - A means of crop propagation - A genetic carrier - A storage structure - A unit of planting - A major agricultural input The fundamental relationship is: Ovule→fertilization + developmentSeed and: Seed→Germination→Seedling→Mature plant 2. What Is a Seed? A seed is a mature ovule containing an embryo and enclosed by a seed coat, usually with stored food reserves. A generalized seed contains: 1. Seed coat
