Why Seeds Are Important in Agriculture Seeds are important because they determine: - Crop establishment - Plant population - Genetic identity - Early plant vigor - Uniformity - Yield potential - Disease-free planting material - Storage and transport - Breeding and genetic conservation A poor-quality seed lot can result in: Poor germination→Poor plant population→Uneven crop→Potential yield reduction Therefore, seed quality is a major determinant of successful crop establishment. 4. Seed Formation Seed formation occurs after sexual reproduction. The simplified sequence is: Flower→Pollination→Pollen germination→Fertilization→Embryo development→Seed maturation xed In angiosperms, double fertilization produces: - A zygote, which develops into the embryo - A primary endosperm nucleus, which develops into endosperm Meanwhile: Ovule→Seed and the integuments of the ovule generally develop into the seed coat.

Scar showing the point where the seed was attached to the parent structure. Not all seeds display these structures equally clearly. 6. Seed Coat The seed coat is the protective covering of the seed. It develops primarily from the integuments of the ovule. Its functions include: - Protection from mechanical damage - Protection against pathogens - Regulation of water entry - Regulation of gas exchange - Protection from environmental stress - Contribution to dormancy In many seeds, the outer coat is called the testa, while an inner layer may be called the tegmen.

The embryo is the young developing plant contained within the seed. It contains the basic structures needed to produce the future plant. Major embryo parts include: - Radicle - Plumule - Cotyledon(s) - Hypocotyl - Epicotyl The embryo can therefore be considered the future plant in an embryonic state.

The radicle is the embryonic root. During germination: Radicle→Primary root It is usually the first major embryonic structure to emerge. Its early functions include: - Anchorage - Water absorption - Mineral absorption
The plumule is the embryonic shoot. It eventually develops into: - Stem - Leaves - Branches Simplified: Plumule→Shoot system

Cotyledons are embryonic leaves. Their functions vary among species. They may: - Store food - Absorb nutrients from endosperm - Supply nutrients to the embryo - Become photosynthetic after emergence The number of cotyledons is important in broad botanical classification. 11. Monocot and Eudicot Seeds Monocot seeds Generally have: 1 cotyledon Example: - Maize - Rice - Wheat The single cotyledon in grasses is called the scutellum. Eudicot seeds Generally have: 2 cotyledons Examples: - Bean - Groundnut - Chickpea - Pea - Soybean 12. Monocot vs Eudicot Seed Feature Monocot Eudicot Cotyledons Usually 1 Usually 2 Example Maize Bean Common storage Endosperm often Often reduced/absorbed during seed development in tissue retained many species Embryo Relatively specialized Usually two cotyledons clearly visible Germination Varies Varies This is a general botanical pattern, not a rule without exceptions.

The endosperm is a nutritive tissue formed following the second fertilization event in angiosperms. Its main function is to nourish the developing embryo. It can store: - Starch - Proteins - Lipids Depending on the species. Examples In cereal grains, the endosperm is a major storage tissue. Examples: - Wheat - Rice - Maize 14. Albuminous and Exalbuminous Seeds Albuminous/endospermic seeds Retain substantial endosperm at maturity. Examples include: - Wheat - Rice - Maize - Castor Exalbuminous/non-endospermic seeds Much of the endosperm is consumed during embryo development, and food reserves are primarily stored in the cotyledons. Examples include: - Bean - Pea - Groundnut Again, the terminology describes the mature seed condition.

The hilum is a scar marking the point where the seed was attached to the parent plant or fruit structure. It is especially visible in many legume seeds. For example, the black or white "eye" on a bean seed is associated with the hilum region.

The micropyle is a small opening in the seed coat derived from the opening in the ovule. It can be involved in: - Water entry - Gas exchange - Germination processes Its visibility varies among seeds. 17. Seed Types Based on Food Storage Seeds store food in different locations. Endosperm-storing Food mainly remains in the endosperm. Examples: - Rice - Wheat - Maize Cotyledon-storing Food is mainly stored in cotyledons. Examples: - Pea - Bean - Groundnut - Soybean Other storage tissues Some plants have specialized storage structures or tissues. Therefore: Seed storage location varies among crops 18. Seed Food Reserves Seeds may store: Carbohydrates Especially starch. Common in cereals. Proteins Important in pulses and oilseeds. Lipids Important in oilseed crops. For example: - Wheat → starch-rich - Rice → starch-rich - Soybean → protein- and oil-rich - Groundnut → oil- and protein-rich - Mustard → oil-rich 19. Respiration is the metabolic process through which plant cells break down organic compounds, mainly carbohydrates, and release energy that can be captured in usable forms such as ATP. A simplified equation for aerobic respiration is: C6H12O6+6O2→6CO2+6H2O+Energy O 6+6O 2 6CO 2+6H 2O+ The released energy is not simply "lost as heat." A significant portion is captured in ATP, which powers cellular activities. In agriculture, respiration is extremely important because plants must continuously respire to: - Grow - Absorb nutrients - Maintain cells - Transport substances - Develop roots, stems, leaves, flowers and seeds - Produce fruits and storage organs - Germinate seeds - Respond to stress - Maintain living tissues after harvest

Respiration is the series of biochemical reactions by which cells oxidize organic substrates and capture released energy in forms such as ATP for cellular work. The most important substrates include: - Carbohydrates - Organic acids - Lipids - Proteins under certain conditions The main respiratory substrate in the simplified equation is glucose. 3. Respiration Is Not the Same as Breathing This distinction is very important. Breathing / gas exchange Refers mainly to movement of gases: O2↔CO2O 2 CO 2 Cellular respiration Refers to biochemical reactions that extract energy from organic molecules. Therefore: Breathing≠Cellular respiration A plant does not have lungs. Gases move through structures such as: - Stomata - Lenticels - Root surfaces - Intercellular spaces 4. Why Do Plants Respire? Plants need energy continuously. ATP generated through respiration supports: - Active transport - Ion uptake - Mineral absorption - Biosynthesis - Cell division - Cell expansion - Protein synthesis - DNA/RNA synthesis - Membrane maintenance - Phloem loading - Root growth - Seed germination - Reproducti

The mitochondrion is the major organelle associated with aerobic respiration. Important structures include: - Outer membrane - Intermembrane space - Inner membrane - Cristae - Matrix Cristae Folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane. They increase membrane surface area for respiratory electron transport and ATP synthesis. Matrix Contains enzymes involved in: - Pyruvate oxidation - Krebs cycle 9. Three Major Stages of Aerobic Respiration For simplified plant respiration, the major stages are: Glycolysis→Pyruvate oxidation + Krebs cycle→Electron transport + oxidative phosphorylation These stages are connected but chemically distinct. 10. Stage 1 — Glycolysis Glycolysis literally means: Glyco=sugar = lysis=splitting = It occurs in the cytosol. One six-carbon glucose molecule is converted into two three-carbon pyruvate molecules. Simplified: Glucose→2Pyruvate 11. Energy Investment in Glycolysis The pathway initially uses ATP. Therefore, ATP is invested to activate glucose and its intermediates. Later reactions produce ATP. This gives a net gain of ATP. For one glucose molecule, classical

ATP │ │ └──────┬─────┘ ↓ Electron transport chain CO₂ is released during - xidative reactions The actual cycle contains multiple intermediates and enzyme-catalyzed reactions. 16. What Is the Purpose of the Krebs Cycle? The Krebs cycle does not simply exist to "make ATP." A major function is to generate reduced electron carriers: NADH and FADH2 These carry high-energy electrons to the electron transport chain. Therefore: Krebs cycle→NADH+FADH2→ETC NADH+FADH 2 17. Electron Transport Chain The electron transport chain (ETC) is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane. NADH and FADH₂ donate electrons. Electrons pass through several protein complexes and electron carriers. Their energy is used to pump protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane. This establishes a proton gradient. 18. Proton Gradient The electron transport chain creates a difference in proton concentration across the inner mitochondrial membrane. This is: Proton motive force The stored electrochemical energy drives ATP synthesis. 19. ATP Synthase Protons flow back across the membrane through ATP synthase. This driv

Fermentation allows glycolysis to continue by regenerating NAD⁺ from NADH. The key idea is: NADH→NAD+ This permits glycolysis to continue temporarily. But fermentation produces much less ATP. Primarily: 2ATP/glucose from glycolysis. 28. Waterlogging and Respiration This is extremely important in agriculture. When soil becomes waterlogged: Waterlogging→Soil pore spaces filled with water→O2 diffusion decreases O 2 Roots can experience hypoxia or anoxia. Then: Root aerobic respiration↓ and plants may increase fermentative metabolism. 29. Hypoxia vs Anoxia Hypoxia Oxygen concentration is lower than normal. Anoxia Very little or essentially no oxygen is available. Therefore: Hypoxia=low O₂ = Anoxia=extremely low/absent O₂ = 30. Respiration in Seeds Respiration is particularly important during germination. A dry seed has relatively low metabolic activity. After imbibition: Water uptake→Metabolic activation→Respiration increases Respiration provides ATP required for: - Enzyme synthesis - Cell division - Cell expansion - Mobilization of food reserves - Root emergence - Shoot development 31.

Respiration in the Complete Crop Life Cycle Respiration is involved throughout the crop life cycle: Seed→Germination→Seedling→Vegetative growth→Flowering→Fruit/seed formation→Maturity→S enescence At every stage: Respiration→ATP→Metabolic activity ATP 79. The Most Important Agricultural Concept Crop productivity depends on the balance between carbon acquisition and carbon expenditure. A simplified model is: Photosynthetic carbon gain−Respiratory carbon loss=Net carbon available - = Then: Net carbon available→Growth + Storage + Reproduction This is why respiration is neither "bad" nor something plants should eliminate. Plants need respiration to live. The agricultural objective is not zero respiration; it is maintaining efficient metabolism and avoiding unnecessarily high respiratory losses caused by unfavorable conditions such as excessive heat, injury or poor storage. 80. Transpiration is the process by which plants lose water in the form of water vapor, mainly from their aerial parts, especially through tiny pores called stomata in leaves. A simple representation is: Soil water→Roots→Xylem→Leaves→Atmosphere At the leaf: H2Oliquid→H2Ovapor→Atmosphere H 2O Transpiration is not simply "water loss." It is an important component of the plant's water relations, mineral transport, cooling, stomatal regulation, and photosynthesis.

Transpiration is the loss of water from a living plant, primarily in the form of water vapor, from aerial plant surfaces. The majority of transpiration in many crops occurs through stomata. Other routes are: 1. Stomatal transpiration 2. Cuticular transpiration 3. Lenticular transpiration 3. Why Is Transpiration Important? Transpiration contributes to: - Movement of water through the plant - Transport of dissolved minerals - Cooling of leaves - Maintenance of plant water relations - Generation of transpiration pull - Xylem flow - Regulation of stomata - Coordination between water uptake and CO₂ uptake - Photosynthetic activity - Nutrient acquisition The overall relationship is: Root water uptake→Xylem transport→Leaf water loss 4. Transpiration Is Different from Evaporation These terms are related but not identical. Evaporation Water changes from liquid to vapor from a surface. Transpiration Water vapor is lost from plant tissues, primarily through stomata. Thus: Transpiration = biological water loss while evaporation can occur from: - Soil - Water surfaces - Wet leaves - Irrigation wa

Stomata are microscopic pores in the epidermis of plant organs, especially leaves. Each stoma is associated with guard cells. Simplified structure: Leaf surface ───────────────────── Guard cell ╭───╮ │ │ ╰─┬─╯ │ Pore │ ╭─┴─╮ Guard cell Leaf internal air space The stomatal pore allows: - CO₂ entry - O₂ movement - Water vapor exit 9. Guard Cells Guard cells regulate stomatal opening. When stomata open: CO2 entry↑CO 2 but: H2O loss↑H 2O When stomata close: H2O loss↓H 2O but: CO2 entry↓CO 2 Therefore stomata create a fundamental physiological trade-off: Carbon gain↔Water conservation 10. Where Does the Water Come From? The water lost through transpiration ultimately comes mainly from the soil. The pathway is: Soil→Root hairs→Root→Xylem→Stem→Leaf→Atmosphere 11. Root Water Absorption Roots absorb water from the soil. Water can move through root tissues by pathways involving: - Apoplast - Symplast - Transmembrane routes Eventually water reaches the xylem. 12. Role of Root Hairs Root hairs are microscopic extensions of epidermal cells. They: - Increase root-soil contact - Increase effective

The xylem is the major water-conducting tissue. It transports: - Water - Dissolved mineral nutrients from roots toward shoots. The major conducting elements include: - Tracheids - Vessel elements 14. The Cohesion–Tension Theory The major explanation for long-distance upward water movement in plants is the cohesion–tension mechanism. The sequence is: Transpiration→Water evaporation from leaves→Negative pressure/tension→Xylem water pulled upwa rd This is one of the most important concepts in plant physiology.
Water molecules attract one another through hydrogen bonding. This property is called: Cohesion It helps maintain a continuous water column in the xylem.

Water also interacts with the walls of xylem conduits. This is called: Adhesion Together: Cohesion + Adhesion→Support for continuous water transport 17. Transpiration Pull When water evaporates from leaf surfaces, it reduces the water potential of leaf tissues. This creates tension that is transmitted through the continuous water column in the xylem. Conceptually: Leaf evaporation→Tension→Xylem water movement This is called transpiration pull. 18. Water Potential Water movement is fundamentally related to differences in water potential. Water generally moves from: Higher water potential→Lower water potential A simplified pathway is: Soil→Root→Xylem→Leaf→Atmosphere The atmosphere often has much lower water potential than hydrated leaf tissues, providing a strong driving force for water vapor loss. 19. Complete Water Movement Pathway The entire process can be represented as:

↑ Leaf air spaces ↑ Xylem ↑ Stem ↑ Root ↑ Root hairs ↑ Soil Therefore: Soil→Root→Xylem→Leaf→Atmosphere 20. How Does Water Actually Leave the Leaf? Inside the leaf, mesophyll cell walls are covered by thin films of water. Solar energy warms the leaf. Water molecules gain enough energy to move into the vapor phase. The vapor accumulates in internal air spaces and then diffuses outward through stomata. Thus: Liquid water→Mesophyll cell walls→Water vapor→Intercellular spaces→Stomata→Atmosphere d 21. Major Driving Force: Vapor Pressure Difference Transpiration is strongly influenced by the difference in water vapor concentration or vapor pressure between the moist leaf interior and the surrounding atmosphere. Generally: Leaf vapor pressure>Atmospheric vapor pressure > creates a gradient favoring water-vapor diffusion outward. 22. Relative Humidity Relative humidity (RH) describes how much water vapor is present in air relative to the maximum amount the air could hold at that temperature. When relative humidity is low: Vapor pressure deficit↑→Transpiration tendency↑ When relative humidity

Effect of Light Light generally causes stomata to open in many plants. Therefore: Light↑→Stomatal opening↑→Transpiration↑ But the response depends on plant species and environmental conditions. 26. Effect of Temperature Increasing temperature can increase the capacity of air to hold water vapor and can increase evaporation. Within a suitable range: Temperature↑→Transpiration tendency↑ But very high temperature can cause stomatal closure due to water stress. Therefore: Extreme heat→Stomatal closure→Transpiration may decline 27. Effect of Humidity High humidity: Humidity↑→VPD↓→Transpiration↓ Low humidity: Humidity↓→VPD↑→Transpiration↑ 28. Effect of Wind Wind removes the humid layer of air surrounding the leaf. This boundary layer normally slows water-vapor movement. Moderate wind can therefore increase transpiration. But under severe wind: - Stomata may close - Leaves may roll - Physical damage may occur - Water stress may de

Plants adapted to dry environments are called xerophytes. Common adaptations include: - Thick cuticle - Reduced leaf area - Stomatal adaptations - Deep or extensive roots - Water storage - Leaf hairs - Leaf rolling - CAM metabolism in some species The objective is generally: Maintain carbon gain while reducing excessive water loss

Hydrophytes are plants adapted to aquatic or very wet environments. They may have: - Reduced structural support - Large air spaces - Specialized stomatal distribution - Thin or reduced cuticles in submerged tissues Their water relations differ substantially from terrestrial crops. 46. Transpiration Efficiency and Water-Use Efficiency A useful agricultural concept is water-use efficiency (WUE). At a physiological scale, one form can be expressed conceptually as: WUE=Carbon assimilationWater loss At crop scale, definitions vary and may use: WUE=Crop biomass or yieldWater used The exact numerator and denominator must therefore be specified. 47. Transpiration vs Water-Use Efficiency High transpiration does not automatically mean poor water-use efficiency. Likewise, low transpiration does not automatically mean high efficiency. The important question is: How much useful carbon gain occurs per unit water lost? 48. Transpiration and Drought During drought: Soil water↓ ↓ Plant water status↓ ↓ ABA signaling↑ABA ↓ Stomatal closure ↓ Transpiration↓ But: CO2 uptake↓CO 2 so: Water conservation↔Ca

Evapotranspiration (ET) is the combined loss of water from: 1. Soil/water surfaces through evaporation 2. Plants through transpiration Therefore: Evapotranspiration=Evaporation+Transpiration = + This is one of the most important concepts in irrigation management. 56. Crop Evapotranspiration Crop water requirements are commonly related to crop evapotranspiration. A widely used conceptual relationship is: ETc=Kc×ET0 where: - ETcET c = crop evapotranspiration - KcK c = crop coefficient - ET0ET 0 = reference evapotranspiration The crop coefficient changes with crop development stage. 57. Crop Growth Stage and Transpiration Transpiration generally changes as crop canopy develops. Early stage Small canopy: Transpiration relatively low Vegetative development Leaf area increases: Transpiration increases Full canopy Potential water use can become high. Maturity/senescence Leaf area and physiological activity decline: Transpiration decreases This is one reason crop water requirements vary throughout the season. 58. Transpiration and Critical Growth Stages Water stress during sensitive stages c

Wilting occurs when plant tissues lose sufficient water and turgor pressure declines. A simplified sequence is: Water deficit→Cell turgor↓→Leaves lose rigidity→Wilting Wilting can be temporary or severe depending on stress. 71. Permanent Wilting Point The permanent wilting point refers to a soil-water condition at which a plant cannot recover its turgor under the specified conditions without additional water. A commonly used soil-physics reference is around: −1.5 MPa-1.5\ MPa - f soil water potential, but this is a generalized convention rather than a universal plant-specific threshold. 72. Field Capacity After saturated soil drains freely under gravity, the remaining water content is often described as field capacity. It represents a useful soil-water reference point. Between field capacity and the permanent wilting point lies much of the water that plants can potentially access, although plant-available water is crop- and soil-dependent. Conceptually: Field capacity→Available soil water→Permanent wilting region 73. Plant-Available Water A simplified soil-water relationship is: PAW≈

This shows why plant physiology is interconnected rather than a collection of isolated processes. 80. Reproductive biology is the study of how plants produce new individuals through sexual and asexual reproduction, including the development of reproductive organs, formation of gametes, pollination, fertilization, embryo and seed development, fruit formation, and mechanisms controlling self- and cross-reproduction. In crop science, reproductive biology is extremely important because successful reproduction ultimately determines: Flowering→Pollination→Fertilization→Seed/Fruit formation→Yield It is also the foundation of: - Crop breeding - Hybrid seed production - Variety development - Seed production - Fruit production - Understanding flowering behavior - Pollination management - Conservation of genetic diversity 2. What Is Plant Reproduction? Reproduction is the biological process through which plants produce new individuals or reproductive propagules. There are two major forms: Plant reproduction=Sexual reproduction+Asexual reproduction = + Sexual reproduction Involves: - Male gametes - Female gametes - Fusion of gametes - Formation of a zygote - Genetic recombination Asexual reprodu

The two major reproductive whorls are: Androecium=Male reproductive structure = Gynoecium=Female reproductive structure = 6. Male Reproductive System The male reproductive organ is the stamen. A stamen consists of: Stamen=Filament+Anther = + Filament Supports the anther. Anther Produces pollen grains.
A typical young anther commonly has four pollen sacs or microsporangia. These contain cells that ultimately produce pollen. General sequence: Microspore mother cell→Meiosis→Microspores→Pollen grains

Microsporogenesis is the formation of haploid microspores from diploid pollen/microspore mother cells through meiosis. Simplified: 2n→Meiosis→n+n+n+n2n n+n+n+n The four products form a tetrad of microspores. Each microspore can develop into a pollen grain.

Microgametogenesis is the development of a microspore into the mature male gametophyte, generally the pollen grain. A typical angiosperm pollen grain contains: - Vegetative/ tube cell - Generative cell The generative cell eventually produces two sperm cells. Thus: Microspore→Pollen grain→Generative cell→2 sperm cells 2 10. Pollen Grain A pollen grain is the male gametophytic structure. Important parts include: - Exine - Intine - Germ pore - Vegetative cell - Generative cell Exine Outer protective layer, largely composed of sporopollenin. Intine Inner wall layer. Germ pore Region through which the pollen tube can emerge. 11. Female Reproductive System The female reproductive structure is the carpel/pistil. It consists of: Pistil=Stigma+Style+Ovary = + + Stigma Receives pollen. Style Provides the pathway for pollen tube growth. Ovary Contains ovules.

The ovule is the structure that develops into the seed after successful fertilization. A typical ovule contains: - Integuments - Nucellus - Embryo sac - Micropyle - Funicle - Chalaza The embryo sac contains the female gametophyte.

Megasporogenesis is the formation of megaspores from a diploid megaspore mother cell through meiosis. Simplified: 2n→Meiosis→4 haploid megaspores 4 Usually only one megaspore remains functional in the common Polygonum-type developmental pattern.

The functional megaspore undergoes mitotic divisions to form the female gametophyte or embryo sac. A common angiosperm embryo sac is: 7 cells and 8 nuclei 8 It contains: Micropylar end - 1 egg cell - 2 synergids Central region - Central cell containing two polar nuclei or their equivalent nuclear contributions Chalazal end - 3 antipodal cells 15. Male and Female Gametophytes Male side Female side Anther Ovule Microspore Megaspore Pollen grain Embryo sac Male gametes/sperm Egg Pollen tube Female reproductive pathway The important point is: Pollen carries male gametes while: Embryo sac contains female gametophyte and egg

Before reproduction can occur, the plant must transition from vegetative development to reproductive development. This involves: Vegetative meristem→Reproductive transition→Floral meristem The timing is influenced by: - Genetics - Temperature - Photoperiod - Plant age - Nutrition - Water availability - Hormones 17. Flower Initiation vs Flowering These terms are not identical. Flower initiation Beginning of the developmental transition toward reproductive structures. Flowering Visible reproductive development and opening/anthesis of flowers. Thus: Flower initiation→Flower development→Flowering/anthesis

Photoperiodism is the response of plants to the relative duration of light and darkness. Plants can broadly be classified as: Short-day plants Flowering is promoted by sufficiently long uninterrupted dark periods. Long-day plants Flowering is promoted by sufficiently long day conditions or short nights. Day-neutral plants Flowering is less dependent on photoperiod. The exact response depends on genotype and environmental conditions.

Vernalization is the promotion of flowering by exposure to an appropriate period of low temperature. It is particularly important in some winter cereals and biennial plants. Simplified: Suitable low temperature→Reproductive competence→Flowering

Anthesis refers to the period when a flower opens and becomes reproductively functional. During this period: - Anthers may release pollen - Stigma may become receptive - Pollination can occur The timing of anthesis is very important for seed production and hybridization. 21. Pollen Viability Pollen viability refers to whether pollen is alive and capable of functioning reproductively. Pollen viability can be affected by: - Temperature - Humidity - Age - Storage conditions - Genetic factors - Nutritional status High temperature during flowering can reduce pollen viability in sensitive crops. 22. Stigma Receptivity The stigma must be physiologically capable of receiving and supporting pollen germination. This period is called the stigma receptive period. Successful reproduction requires overlap between: Pollen viability↔Stigma receptivity

Pollination is: The transfer of pollen from the anther to a receptive stigma. It occurs before fertilization. Pollination≠Fertilization Sequence: Pollen release→Pollen transfer→Stigma 24. Types of Pollination Self-pollination Pollen reaches the stigma of the same flower or genetically compatible flower on the same plant. Cross-pollination Pollen is transferred between flowers of genetically different plants of the same species. 25. Self-Pollinated Crops Examples include: - Rice - Wheat - Pea - Chickpea - Lentil - Soybean Self-pollination generally maintains greater genetic uniformity than cross-pollination, although natural - utcrossing can still occur at varying frequencies. 26. Cross-Pollinated Crops Examples include: - Maize - Pearl millet - Many cucurbits - Onion - Many fruit crops Cross-pollination increases opportunities for: - Genetic recombination - Genetic diversity - Heterozygosity 27. Pollination Agents Pollination may occur through: Wind Anemophily Example: - Maize - Wheat and other grasses have wind-mediated pollen transfer, though reproductive structures differ among gr

Male and female reproductive functions mature at different times. Two major forms: Protandry Anthers mature/release pollen before stigma becomes receptive. Male first Protogyny Stigma becomes receptive before pollen release from the same flower. Female first

Herkogamy is spatial separation or physical arrangement of anthers and stigma that reduces selfpollination. For example: Anther position≠stigma position This encourages pollen transfer from another flower.

Self-incompatibility (SI) is a genetically controlled system in which pollen from the same plant or genetically related plant is prevented from successfully fertilizing the ovule. Possible mechanisms include: - Pollen germination inhibition - Pollen tube growth inhibition - Recognition-based rejection This promotes outcrossing without necessarily requiring separate male and female plants. 33. Male Sterility A male-sterile plant produces nonfunctional or insufficiently functional pollen but may have functional female reproductive organs. This is extremely important in: Hybrid seed production Major categories include: - Genetic male sterility - Cytoplasmic male sterility - Cytoplasmic-genetic male sterility 34. Monoecious Plants A monoecious plant has separate male and female flowers on the same plant. Example: Maize Maize has: - Male inflorescence = tassel - Female inflorescence = ear/cob 35. Dioecious Plants Male and female flowers occur on different plants. Therefore individual plants are functionally male or female. This strongly promotes cross-pollination.

Fertilization occurs after successful pollination. The pollen grain germinates and produces a pollen tube. Sequence: Pollen→Pollen germination→Pollen tube→Ovule→Sperm release 37. Pollen Tube Growth The pollen tube grows through: Stigma→Style→Ovary→Ovule It transports the two sperm cells toward the embryo sac. 38. Double Fertilization Double fertilization is a characteristic feature of angiosperms. Two fusion events occur. Syngamy Sperm+Egg→Zygote + n+n=2nn+n=2n Triple fusion The second sperm combines with the two polar-nuclear contributions in the central cell. Typically: n+n+n=3n forming the primary endosperm nucleus. Therefore: Double fertilization=Syngamy+Triple fusion = + 39. What Happens After Fertilization? After successful fertilization: Zygote→Embryo Primary endosperm nucleus→Endosperm Ovule→Seed Ovary→Fruit This is one of the most important transformations in crop reproductive biology. 40. Embryo Development The zygote divides and develops into the embryo. In many eudicots, generalized developmental stages include: Zygote→Proembryo→Globular→Heart→Torpedo→Mature embryo The ma

The endosperm provides nutrients for the developing embryo in many seeds. It can contain: - Starch - Proteins - Oils - Other storage compounds In cereals, the endosperm is a major component of the harvested grain. For example, much of the carbohydrate-rich portion of rice, wheat and maize grain is endosperm. 43. Seed Formation Seed development can be summarized as: Fertilized ovule→Embryo+Endosperm+Seed coat→Mature seed + + The seed provides a protected structure through which the next generation begins. 44. Fruit Formation Generally: Ovary→Fruit while: Ovule→Seed Fruit development protects seeds and can aid dispersal. 45. Fruit Set Fruit set is the successful transition from a flower to a developing fruit. It depends on: - Successful pollination - Pollen viability - Stigma receptivity - Fertilization - Hormonal signaling - Water - Temperature - Nutritional status - Crop load - Pest and disease status Therefore: Flower number≠Fruit number Many flowers may fail to develop into mature fruits.

Parthenocarpy is fruit development without normal fertilization. It can result in seedless or nearly seedless fruits. Examples can include certain: - Banana - Citrus - Grape - Cucumber - Tomato depending on cultivar and production system. Important: Fruit formation does not always require normal fertilization 47. Sexual Reproduction and Genetic Variation Sexual reproduction creates genetic variation through: - Meiosis - Independent assortment - Recombination - Crossing over - Fusion of genetically different gametes Therefore: Sexual reproduction→Genetic recombination→Variation This variation is fundamental to crop evolution and breeding.

Meiosis reduces chromosome number from diploid to haploid. 2n→n It occurs during the formation of: - Microspores - Megaspores Meiosis contributes to genetic variation through: - Crossing over - Independent assortment 49. Mitosis vs Meiosis Feature Mitosis Main role Growth/development Chromosome number Usually maintained Divisions One Meiosis Gametophyte/spore formation Reduced Two successive divisions Feature Genetic variation Crop importance Mitosis Meiosis Usually limited High contribution Growth and tissue development Sexual reproduction 50. Asexual Reproduction Asexual reproduction does not require normal fusion of gametes. New plants arise from vegetative structures. Examples: Structure Crop/example Tuber Potato Rhizome Ginger Bulb Onion Corm Colocasia Runner Strawberry Stem cutting Sugarcane and many horticultural crops Sucker Banana Grafting Mango and many fruit crops Layering Some fruit crops Tissue culture Banana, potato and many crops 51. Vegetative Propagation Vegetative propagation uses plant parts such as: - Stem - Root - Leaf - Bud - Specialized organs Because gamete fu

Apomixis is seed formation without the normal sexual process leading to fertilization. It can allow maternal genetic characteristics to be transmitted through seed with little or no meiotic recombination, depending on the mechanism. It is important because it has potential applications in: - Hybrid fixation - Maintaining desirable genotypes - Seed propagation of genetically uniform plants 54. Selfing, Outcrossing and Mating Systems Crop reproductive biology can be understood through mating systems. Predominantly self-pollinating Examples: - Rice - Wheat - Chickpea - Pea Predominantly cross-pollinating Examples: - Maize - Pearl millet - Many cucurbits Often intermediate or variable Some crops have both selfing and outcrossing depending on: - Variety - Environment - Pollinator availability - Flower structure - Crop density Therefore, "self-pollinated" and "cross-pollinated" often describe predominant reproductive behavior rather than absolute rules. 55. Genetic Consequences of Self-Pollination Repeated self-pollination generally increases homozygosity. Conceptually: Selfing→Homozygosit

When genetically distinct parents are crossed, the resulting hybrid may show superior performance for certain traits relative to the parents. This phenomenon is called: Heterosis It can occur in: - Yield - Vigor - Growth rate - Stress tolerance - Uniformity Heterosis is especially important in hybrid crop breeding. 58. Hybrid Seed Production A simplified hybrid seed-production system is: Parent A×Parent B→F1 hybrid F 1 The challenge is preventing unwanted self-pollination of the female parent. Methods include: - Manual emasculation - Male sterility - Chemical hybridization agents in some systems - Controlled pollination - Genetic incompatibility systems

Emasculation means removal of anthers from a bisexual flower before pollen release. Purpose: Prevent self-pollination The emasculated flower is then pollinated with pollen from the desired male parent. 60. Artificial Pollination A simplified breeding process is: Select female parent→Emasculation→Collect pollen→Apply pollen→Protect flower→Harvest hybrid seed This is a fundamental technique in controlled hybridization. 61. Environmental Factors Affecting Reproduction Reproductive development is highly sensitive to environmental conditions. Major factors include: Temperature Affects: - Flower initiation - Pollen viability - Pollen tube growth - Fertilization - Fruit set - Seed development Water Water stress can cause: - Flower abortion - Reduced pollen viability - Poor stigma function - Poor fruit set - Reduced seed filling Light Affects: - Photoperiodic flowering - Photosynthesis - Carbohydrate supply Humidity Can influence: - Pollen release - Pollen viability - Disease - Stigma receptivity Nutrients Nutrient imbalance can affect: - Flower formation - Pollen development - Ovule develop

Sowing time is the period or date at which seed is placed in the soil so that germination, establishment, growth and subsequent reproductive development occur under favorable environmental conditions. It is one of the most important decisions in crop production because the sowing date determines the environmental conditions experienced by the crop during almost every subsequent growth stage. The central concept is: Sowing Time→Environmental Conditions at Each Growth Stage→Crop Development→Yield and Qua lity A crop can have excellent seed, fertile soil and good irrigation, yet an inappropriate sowing time can expose it to: - excessive heat, - cold, - drought, - excessive rainfall, - frost, - unsuitable photoperiod, - pest and disease pressure, - unfavorable conditions during flowering or maturity.

Sowing time is the appropriate period or date for sowing a crop, selected according to the crop's biological requirements, prevailing and expected environmental conditions, soil conditions, available water and the desired production system. In simple words: Sowing Time = When to put the seed in the soil But scientifically, it means: Choosing the date that gives the crop the most suitable environment throughout its life cycle 3. Why Is Sowing Time Important? The sowing date determines the environmental conditions encountered by: 1. germination, 2. seedling establishment, 3. vegetative growth, 4. flowering, 5. pollination, 6. fruit/grain/pod formation, 7. grain or seed filling, 8. maturity, 9. harvest. For example: Sowing Date→Flowering Date→Temperature at Flowering If flowering coincides with extreme heat: Heat Stress→Poor Pollination/Fertilization→Poor Fruit/Grain Set→Yield Loss Therefore sowing time is essentially a crop-calendar management decision. 4. Sowing Time Is Not the Same for Every Crop Different crops have different environmental requirements. For example: - wheat generall

Temperature is one of the most important determinants of sowing time. Every crop has temperature requirements for: - germination, - emergence, - vegetative growth, - flowering, - reproductive development, - maturity. The basic concept is: Tmin<Topt<Tmax <T opt <T max where: - TminT min = approximate lower threshold for a particular process, - ToptT opt = favorable range, - TmaxT max = upper threshold. These values are process-, stage- and genotype-specific. 7. Sowing Too Early Early sowing can expose a crop to environmental conditions that are unsuitable for its initial or later stages. Possible problems: - low-temperature germination, - slow emergence, - seedling injury, - excessive vegetative growth, - premature flowering in some crops, - pest/disease exposure, - waterlogging if early-season rainfall is excessive. Therefore: Earlier≠Always Better 8. Sowing Too Late Late sowing can shorten the effective growing period or shift sensitive stages into unfavorable weather. Possible consequences: - reduced vegetative growth, - delayed or altered flowering, - heat exposure during flowerin

Photoperiod is the duration of light and darkness in a 24-hour cycle. Some crops respond to day length during development. Photoperiod→Developmental Signals→Flower Initiation/Phenology Therefore changing sowing time can alter the photoperiod experienced at important developmental stages. 17. Sowing Time and Photoperiod-Sensitive Crops For photoperiod-sensitive varieties: Sowing Date→Developmental Environment→Flowering Time This can influence: - flowering, - crop duration, - reproductive synchronization, - maturity. Genotype matters greatly. 18. Growing Degree Days Sowing time affects the thermal environment accumulated by the crop. Seed rate is one of the most important decisions in crop establishment. It determines how much seed should be used to obtain the desired plant population over a given area. The basic relationship is: Seed Rate→Plant Population→Canopy Development→Resource Competition→Yield Using too little seed can result in: - gaps in the field, - poor canopy development, - greater weed competition, - lower plant population. Using too much seed can result in: - excessive competition, - weak plants, - lodging, - higher disease pressure, - unnecessary seed cost. Therefore, higher seed rate does not automatically mean higher yield.

Seed rate is the quantity of seed required to be sown per unit area of land to establish the desired plant population under specified crop, variety, seed-quality and field conditions. It is commonly expressed as: - kg/ha, - g/m², - seeds/ha, - seeds/m². In simple terms: Seed Rate = How much seed to use for a given area 3. Direct sowing is a crop-establishment method in which seeds are sown directly in the field where the crop is intended to grow, rather than first raising seedlings in a nursery and then transplanting them. In simple terms: Seed→Directly into Field→Germination→Crop It is one of the simplest and most widely used methods of crop establishment, particularly for crops that can tolerate field germination and early growth.

Direct sowing is the method of establishing a crop by placing seeds directly into the final field at the appropriate time, depth, spacing and soil conditions, without raising and transplanting nursery seedlings. The essential characteristic is: The seed germinates and establishes at its final growing location. 3. Dibbling is a sowing method in which seeds are placed individually or in a predetermined number in small holes made in the soil at specified depth and spacing, followed by covering with soil. Broadcasting is a sowing method in which seed is uniformly or approximately uniformly distributed over the surface of a prepared field, followed by suitable covering or incorporation where required, to establish the crop. The key idea is: Area-based seed distribution rather than point-based placement 3. Basic Principle The fundamental principle is to distribute an appropriate quantity of seed over the target area so that sufficient plants emerge and establish. Seed Rate+Distribution+Seed-Soil Contact+Suitable Moisture→Crop Establishment + + + Unlike dibbling, the farmer does not normally create a separate planting hole for every seed. 4. Drilling is a method of sowing in which seeds are metered and placed in continuous or nearly continuous rows at a predetermined depth and spacing, followed by covering the seed with soil. The key characteristics are: Defined Rows+Controlled Seed Rate+Controlled Depth + + 3. Basic Principle The objective is to distribute the required quantity of seed uniformly along rows while maintaining an appropriate depth and seed-soil contact. Correct Seed Rate+Correct Row Spacing+Correct Depth+Good Seed-Soil Contact→Uniform Crop Est ablishment + + + 4. Precision planting is a highly controlled planting method in which individual seeds are metered and placed at predetermined positions, depths, and within-row spacing, with the objective of achieving a uniform and desired plant population. It is more precise than ordinary drilling because the goal is not merely to put seed into rows, but to control the position of individual seeds. Seed Metering→Singulation→Controlled Spacing→Controlled Depth→Seed Covering→Uniform Em ergence Simple meaning Precision Planting = One seed, one planned position, at a controlled depth and spacing

Precision planting is a planting system in which individual seeds are accurately metered and placed at predetermined horizontal spacing, row spacing, and depth to achieve a uniform and desired plant population. The major idea is: Precise Seed Rate+Precise Spacing+Precise Depth→Uniform Crop Stand + + 3. Precision Planting vs Precision Agriculture These terms should not be confused. - sensors, - satellite imagery, - drones, - variable-rate application, - yield maps, - soil maps, - data analytics, - automation. Instead of: ∙∙∙∙∙ where seeds may fall very close together, precision planting aims for: ∙∙∙∙ with a predetermined spacing. Thus: Seed→Meter→Separate→Place Precisely 5. Gap filling is the agricultural practice of replacing missing, dead, or poorly established plants in a crop stand after sowing or planting, so that the field approaches the desired plant population and has a more uniform crop stand. In simple terms: Gap Filling = Replacing missing plants in the crop stand A field may develop gaps because some seeds: - fail to germinate, - fail to emerge, - die soon after emergence, - are damaged by pests or diseases, - are washed away, - are buried too deeply, - are affected by drought or waterlogging, - are damaged during mechanical operations.

Gap filling is the practice of re-establishing missing plants at vacant positions in a crop field by sowing additional seed or planting suitable seedlings or propagules, with the objective of maintaining an adequate and uniform plant population. Plant water requirement is the amount of water a crop needs over a particular period to maintain physiological processes, growth, development, and the desired yield under specific environmental and management conditions. In simple terms: Plant Water Requirement = Water needed by the crop for healthy growth and production It is one of the most important concepts in irrigation management because irrigation should supply the crop's actual water deficit, rather than simply applying as much water as possible. The basic concept is: Water Requirement→Crop Water Use+Other Necessary Water Uses + For field irrigation planning, the most important component is evapotranspiration (ET).

Plant water requirement is the quantity of water needed by a crop during a specified period to compensate for water losses through transpiration and evaporation and to support growth, development and production under given soil, climatic, crop and management conditions. The crop continuously loses water through: Transpiration+Evaporation + Therefore: Evapotranspiration (ET) = Evaporation + Transpiration 3. Evapotranspiration (ET) is the combined loss of water to the atmosphere through evaporation from soil, water and plant surfaces and transpiration from plants. In the simplest form: ET = Evaporation + Transpiration It is one of the most important concepts in agriculture because it tells us how rapidly water is being transferred from the soil–plant system to the atmosphere. ET is therefore central to: - crop water requirement, - irrigation scheduling, - drought monitoring, - water budgeting, - irrigation-system design, - crop productivity, - water-use efficiency.

Evapotranspiration is the combined process by which water is transferred from the soil, water and plant surfaces to the atmosphere through evaporation and plant transpiration. Thus: ET=E+T where: - ETET = evapotranspiration, - EE = evaporation, - TT = transpiration. 3. Why Is ET Important? Plants continuously exchange water with the atmosphere. The basic pathway is: Soil Water→Roots→Plant→Leaves→Atmosphere At the same time: Soil/Water Surface→Evaporation→Atmosphere Together: E+T=ET Therefore ET provides a practical estimate of crop water use.

Evaporation is the conversion of liquid water into water vapor from non-living surfaces. Agricultural evaporation can occur from: - exposed soil, - irrigation water, - ponds, - puddles, - wet crop surfaces, - wet residue. E=Water loss from non-plant surfaces

Transpiration is the loss of water vapor from living plant tissues, mainly through stomata. Water moves: Soil→Roots→Xylem→Leaves→Stomata→Atmosphere Therefore: T=Plant water loss to the atmosphere 6. Soil moisture is the amount of water present in the soil pores at a particular time. It is one of the most important components of agricultural water management because soil acts as a water reservoir for plant roots. The basic pathway is: Rainfall/Irrigation→Soil→Water Storage→Roots→Plant→Atmosphere Soil moisture determines whether water is: - available to roots, - too strongly held for roots to extract, - moving through the soil, - draining away, - evaporating, - causing waterlogging.

Soil moisture is the water contained within the pore spaces of soil, including water available to plants and water held too strongly or weakly for effective plant uptake. In agriculture, we are particularly interested in: How much soil water is available to the crop root system? 3. Why Soil Moisture Is Important Soil moisture affects: 1. seed germination, 2. seedling establishment, 3. root growth, 4. nutrient availability, 5. nutrient transport, 6. photosynthesis, 7. transpiration, 8. plant water status, 9. microbial activity, 10.fertilizer efficiency, 11.crop growth, 12.flowering, 13.fruit/grain/pod development, 14.yield, 15.irrigation scheduling. Permanent Wilting Point (PWP) is a fundamental soil-water concept that represents the lower reference limit of plant-available water. As a soil dries, plants initially have plenty of water available. As water is continuously removed through evapotranspiration, the remaining water is held increasingly tightly by soil particles. Eventually, the plant can no longer extract enough water to maintain its water status and remains wilted even when placed under the standard recovery conditions used to define PWP. Critical moisture stages are the specific stages of crop growth during which adequate soil moisture is particularly important for maintaining normal growth, development, reproductive success, and yield. A crop does not have the same sensitivity to water shortage throughout its entire life cycle. For example, a short period of drought during early vegetative growth may sometimes be partly compensated for later, whereas water stress during flowering, pollination, fruit set, or grain filling can cause much larger and sometimes irreversible yield losses. The basic concept is: Crop Stage+Water Stress→Stage-specific Effect on Yield +

Critical moisture stages are crop-growth stages at which adequate soil moisture is especially important because water stress during those stages can cause disproportionately large effects on reproductive development, yield formation, quality, - r crop establishment. They are also commonly called: - critical growth stages, - critical irrigation stages, - critical water-requiring stages, - moisture-sensitive stages. The exact stages differ among: - crops, - varieties, - climates, - soils, - production systems. Therefore: Critical Stage≠Universal Stage for Every Crop 3. Why Are They Important? Water stress can occur at any time, but its consequences differ by growth stage. A simplified relationship is: Yield Loss=f(Stress Intensity,Duration,Timing,Crop,Genotype) , , , , ) Two identical droughts can therefore produce different yield losses if they occur at different stages. 4. Irrigation scheduling is the process of deciding when to irrigate and how much water to apply to a crop so that sufficient moisture is maintained in the root zone without unnecessary water application. In simple terms: Irrigation Scheduling=When to irrigate+How much to irrigate = + It connects: Crop Water Requirement→Soil Moisture→Weather/ET→Irrigation Timing→Irrigation Amount The objective is not to keep soil continuously wet. The objective is to maintain adequate root-zone moisture while avoiding harmful water stress, waterlogging, and unnecessary water use.

Irrigation scheduling is the planning and determination of the timing, frequency, and amount of irrigation water to be applied to a crop based on crop water requirements, soil-water availability, weather conditions, growth stage, root-zone characteristics, and irrigation-system efficiency. It answers two fundamental questions: Question 1 — When? When should irrigation be applied? Question 2 — How much? How much water should be applied? 3. Main Objectives Irrigation scheduling aims to: 1. maintain adequate soil moisture, 2. prevent severe water stress, 3. protect critical moisture stages, 4. maximize water-use efficiency, 5. maintain yield and quality, 6. avoid over-irrigation, 7. reduce waterlogging, 8. reduce nutrient leaching, 9. reduce pumping/energy costs, 10.improve irrigation efficiency, 11.conserve limited water resources, 12.coordinate irrigation with rainfall, 13.optimize crop production under available water. The overall objective is: Right Amount of Water + Right Time + Right Root Zone 4. Why Irrigation Scheduling Is Necessary Crop water demand is not constant. It changes

Flood irrigation is a traditional surface-irrigation method in which water is released onto a field and allowed to spread over a large portion or the entire field surface, mainly under gravity. The basic principle is: Water Source→Field Surface→Spreading→Infiltration→Root Zone It is one of the simplest forms of irrigation because it generally requires relatively simple field infrastructure and uses gravity rather than pressurized pipes to distribute water.

Flood irrigation is a surface-irrigation method in which irrigation water is released - nto the field and allowed to flow and spread over the soil surface, often covering a substantial portion of the field, before infiltrating into the root zone. One-line definition Flood Irrigation = Allowing irrigation water to spread over the field surface by gravity. 3. Basic Principle Flood irrigation depends primarily on: - gravity, - field slope, - field elevation, - soil infiltration, - water flow rate, - field surface condition. The basic principle is: Water Source→Furrow→Surface Flow→Infiltration→Root Zone In contrast to flood irrigation, where water may spread broadly over the field surface, furrow irrigation concentrates water into specific channels.

Furrow irrigation is a surface-irrigation method in which water is applied through small, elongated channels or furrows between crop rows and allowed to move along the field by gravity while infiltrating into the soil and supplying water to the crop root zone. Basin irrigation is a type of surface irrigation in which the field is divided into relatively level, enclosed areas called basins using bunds or small embankments. Water is released into a basin and allowed to spread over the enclosed surface by gravity before infiltrating into the soil. The basic principle is: Water Source→Basin Inlet→Water Spreads in Basin→Infiltration→Root Zone Unlike furrow irrigation, water does not primarily travel through narrow channels between crop rows. Instead, it is temporarily contained within a basin.

Basin irrigation is a surface-irrigation method in which a field is divided into relatively level, enclosed areas by bunds, and water is applied to each basin and allowed to spread over the soil surface under gravity before infiltrating into the root zone. One-line definition Basin Irrigation = Irrigating an enclosed, level field area by temporarily ponding water within it. 3. Water conservation in agriculture means the planned and efficient management of available water so that water losses are minimized, soil moisture is retained, crop water requirements are met efficiently, and water resources remain available for future use. The objective is not simply to use less water. The real objective is: Produce More or Adequate Crop Yield with Less Unnecessary Water Loss A complete agricultural water-conservation approach combines: - rainwater harvesting, - soil-moisture conservation, - efficient irrigation, - proper irrigation scheduling, - reduction of runoff, - reduction of evaporation, - reduction of deep percolation, - groundwater recharge, - watershed management, - suitable crops and varieties, - improved soil health, - mulching and residue management, - water-quality management. Water conservation is the planned management and efficient use of water resources to reduce unnecessary losses, improve water availability and productivity, conserve soil moisture, and maintain water resources for sustainable agricultural production. 3. Why Water Conservation Is Important in Agriculture Agriculture requires water for: - seed germination, - plant establishment, - photosynthesis, - nutrient transport, - cell expansion, - flowering, - pollination, - fruit/pod/grain formation, - grain and seed filling, - cooling through transpiration. The basic pathway is: Water→Root Uptake→Plant Processes→Growth→Yield But not all water supplied to a field becomes useful crop water. Water can be lost through: ET+Runoff+Deep Percolation+Evaporation+Leakage Therefore water conservation attempts to reduce avoidable losses. 4. Drainage in agriculture is the planned removal of excess water from the soil, crop root zone, or agricultural field so that soil moisture, aeration, salinity and root-zone conditions remain suitable for crop growth. The fundamental idea is: Drain Excess Water, But Retain Useful Soil Moisture This is important because crops need water, but they also need oxygen in the soil pores. A good agricultural drainage system therefore maintains a balance: Water+Air+Root Zone + +

Agricultural drainage is the controlled removal and disposal or management of excess surface water and/or subsurface water from agricultural land to maintain suitable soil moisture, aeration, salinity conditions and root-zone environments for crop production. One-line memory Drainage = Removing excess water from the crop root zone safely and effectively. 3. Why Is Drainage Necessary? Plants need water for: - germination, - nutrient transport, - photosynthesis, - cell expansion, - flowering, - fruit/grain development. But roots also require oxygen for respiration. When soil becomes saturated: Water Content↑→Air-Filled Pores↓→O2↓→Root Respiration↓ Filled\ Pores O 2 Root\ Respiration Therefore: Too Little Water→Drought Stress Too Much Water→Waterlogging Stress The objective of drainage is to keep the root zone between these extremes. 4. Water quality refers to the physical, chemical and biological characteristics of water that determine whether it is suitable for a particular agricultural use. Saline irrigation water is irrigation water containing a sufficiently high concentration of dissolved salts that, depending on the crop, soil, climate, drainage and irrigation management, it can create salinity stress in plants or cause salts to accumulate in the root zone. The key point is that saline water is not simply “water with salt.” The agricultural problem develops when salt enters the soil faster than it can be removed, or when the salt concentration becomes high enough to restrict plant water uptake. Saline irrigation water is water containing elevated concentrations of dissolved salts that may adversely affect crop growth, soil properties or irrigation-system performance when used for irrigation, depending on crop tolerance and management conditions. Dissolved salts commonly include ions such as: Cations - Na+Na + — sodium - Ca2+Ca 2+ — calcium - Mg2+Mg 2+ — magnesium - K+K + — potassium Anions - Cl−Cl - — chloride - SO42−SO 4 2- — sulfate - HCO3−HCO 3 - — bicarbonate - CO32−CO 3 2- — carbonate The total concentration of dissolved ions contributes to water salinity. 4. Main Indicator — Electrical Conductivity Electrical conductivity (EC) is one of the most widely used indicators of salinity. Common unit: dS/m Higher EC generally means greater dissolved-ion concentration: EC↑→Salinity Risk↑ However, EC alone does not describe every water-quality hazard. 5. Conceptually: Fresh/Suitable Water→Root Zone→Salt Dissolution→Downward Movement→Drainage The objective is: Root-Zone Salt↓ Zone\ Salt 32. Leaching Requirement Where saline irrigation water is used, additional water may sometimes be required to control salt accumulation. The exact calculation depends on: - irrigation-water salinity, - desired root-zone salinity, - crop tolerance, - evapotranspiration, - soil, - drainage. Nitrogen (N) is one of the most important essential mineral nutrients required by plants. It is a primary macronutrient, along with phosphorus (P) and potassium (K), and is required in relatively large quantities. Nitrogen is fundamental because it forms part of: - amino acids, - proteins, - enzymes, - chlorophyll, - nucleic acids (DNA and RNA), - ATP and other energy-transfer compounds, - many coenzymes and metabolites. A simplified relationship is: N→Amino Acids→Proteins/Enzymes→Photosynthesis+Growth+Metabolism Nitrogen therefore strongly influences: - vegetative growth, - leaf area, - chlorophyll concentration, - photosynthesis, - tillering and branching, - biomass production, - yield formation, - protein content. But more nitrogen does not automatically mean more yield. Excess N can cause excessive vegetative growth, lodging, delayed maturity, pest/disease problems and environmental losses. 2. Definition of Nitrogen Nitrogen is an essential primary macronutrient required by plants for the synthesis of amino acids, proteins, nucleic acids, chlorophyll, enzymes and numerous other b

Nitrogenase catalyzes the reduction of atmospheric nitrogen. Simplified representation: N2→NH3 Nitrogenase is highly sensitive to oxygen, so nodules have specialized mechanisms for maintaining an appropriate oxygen environment.

In legume nodules, leghemoglobin helps regulate oxygen availability around nitrogen-fixing bacteria. It contributes to maintaining conditions suitable for nitrogenase activity while supporting respiration. This is why healthy active nodules often have a pinkish/red interior.
Mineralization is the conversion of organic nitrogen into inorganic forms that plants can potentially use. Simplified: Organic N→NH4+ Microorganisms carry out much of this process.
Ammonification is commonly used for the microbial conversion of organic nitrogen into ammonium. Organic N→NH4+ It is an important part of nitrogen mineralization.

Nitrification is the biological oxidation of ammonium. Simplified: NH4+→NO2−→NO3− Different microbial groups perform the successive steps. Nitrification generally requires oxygen. 30. Nitrifying Microorganisms The first step is associated with organisms such as: - Nitrosomonas and related ammonia-oxidizing organisms. The second step is associated with organisms such as: - Nitrobacter and related nitrite-oxidizing organisms. Modern microbiology recognizes broader groups, including archaea and other bacteria, so these classical examples should not be interpreted as the only organisms involved.

Under low-oxygen or anaerobic conditions, microorganisms can reduce nitrate. A simplified pathway is: NO3−→NO2−→NO→N2O→N2 This can result in nitrogen loss to the atmosphere. Denitrification is favored by conditions such as: - waterlogging, - low oxygen, - available carbon, - suitable microbial activity. 32. Nitrogen Leaching Nitrate is highly mobile. When water moves downward through soil: NO3−+Downward Water Movement→Leaching Consequences include: - fertilizer-N loss, - lower nitrogen-use efficiency, - groundwater contamination risk. Leaching risk is especially important in: - sandy soils, - excessive irrigation, - heavy rainfall, - shallow-rooted crops. 33. Ammonia Volatilization Nitrogen can also be lost as ammonia gas: NH4+⇌NH3(g)+H+ Volatilization risk is particularly important for surface-applied: - urea, - ammonium-containing fertilizers, - manures. Risk increases under conditions such as: - high pH, - warm temperatures, - moist but drying surfaces, - surface application without incorporation, - high carbonate/bicarbonate conditions. 34. Potassium (K) is an essential primary macronutrient required for normal plant growth, water relations, stomatal regulation, enzyme activation, photosynthesis, carbohydrate transport, protein metabolism, stress tolerance, and crop quality. The three primary macronutrients are: N−P−K A useful way to remember them is: - Nitrogen (N) → growth, proteins, chlorophyll - Phosphorus (P) → energy, DNA/RNA, roots, reproduction - Potassium (K) → water regulation, enzymes, transport, strength and stress tolerance The central concept of potassium is: K→Osmotic Regulation+Enzyme Activation+Stomatal Control+Transport+Stress Tolerance Unlike nitrogen and phosphorus, potassium is not incorporated into major organic structural molecules in the same way. Micronutrients Plants require micronutrients in much smaller quantities than macronutrients, but small requirement does not mean small importance. Micronutrients are essential because they participate in enzyme activity, electron transport, hormone metabolism, photosynthesis, reproduction, gene expression, and many other physiological processes. The micronutrients generally recognized as essential for higher plants are: Fe, Mn, Zn, Cu, B, Mo, Cl, Ni In this section: 1. Iron (Fe) 2. Zinc (Zn) 1. IRON (Fe)

Iron is an essential micronutrient required mainly for: - electron transport, - photosynthesis, - respiration, - chlorophyll formation, - nitrogen metabolism, - enzyme activity, - iron-sulfur proteins, - redox reactions. Although plants need iron in very small amounts, iron deficiency can severely reduce photosynthesis and growth. The central concept is: Fe→Electron Transport→Photosynthesis+Respiration→Growth 1.2 Definition of Iron Iron is an essential plant micronutrient that functions primarily in redox reactions and electron-transfer systems through iron-containing proteins and cofactors, thereby supporting photosynthesis, respiration, chlorophyll formation, nitrogen metabolism, and enzyme activity. Exam-ready definition Iron is an essential micronutrient involved in electron transport, redox reactions, chlorophyll formation, photosynthesis, respiration, nitrogen metabolism, and the functioning of iron-containing enzymes and proteins. 2. MODULE 13 — Fertilizers & Manures Module 13 deals with how nutrients are supplied to crops through organic materials, chemical fertilizers, biofertilizers, and different application methods. The central idea is: Nutrient Source+Right Rate+Right Time+Right Place+Right Method→Efficient Crop Nutrition + + + + A complete nutrient-management system does not simply mean “adding fertilizer.” It means supplying the right nutrients in the right chemical form and amount, at the right growth stage and location, while minimizing nutrient losses and maintaining soil health. 1. Fundamentals of Fertilizers and Manures 1.1 What is a fertilizer? A fertilizer is a material, natural or manufactured, that is applied to soil, plants, or irrigation water to supply one or more essential plant nutrients in a form available or potentially available to plants. FYM does not have one fixed nutrient composition. Its nutrient content depends on: - animal species - feed - bedding material - storage method - decomposition - moisture content - urine collection - age of manure - handling losses Therefore: FYM composition is highly variable 2.3 Major functions FYM supplies: - nitrogen - phosphorus - potassium - sulfur - secondary nutrients - small amounts of micronutrients - organic carbon But its major value is broader than nutrient supply. It can improve: Physical properties - aggregation - structure - water retention - infiltration - aeration - bulk density Chemical properties - nutrient supply - buffering - CEC-related nutrient retention - nutrient cycling Biological properties - microbial activity - decomposition - soil biological processes 2.4 Nutrient release from FYM Most nutrients in FYM are initially present in organic forms.
