Green manure refers to a crop or plant biomass grown primarily to be incorporated into the soil while it is still green or relatively succulent, with the purpose of improving soil fertility, organic matter and nutrient cycling. Core: Green Manure=Grow Crop→Biomass Production→Soil Incorporation 5.2 Common green-manure crops Important examples include: - sunn hemp (Crotalaria juncea) - dhaincha (Sesbania spp.) - sesbania - sunhemp - certain legumes and other suitable cover crops Legumes are especially valuable because of biological nitrogen fixation. 5.3 Nitrogen contribution Legume: N2→RhizobiaNitrogen FixationNH3/NH4+N 2 [ ] Nitrogen\ Fixation NH 3/NH 4 + The plant incorporates nitrogen into biomass. After incorporation: Organic N→NH4+→NO3−Organic\ N NH 4 + NO 3 Thus green manure can contribute nitrogen to subsequent crops.

Nutritional - nitrogen contribution - nutrient recycling Physical - aggregation - organic matter - infiltration - water retention Biological - microbial activity - soil biodiversity - decomposition Weed management A dense green-manure crop can suppress weeds through: - competition - shading - ground cover Erosion protection Living vegetation protects soil from: - raindrop impact - runoff - wind erosion

- Requires land/time. - Biomass production requires water and nutrients. - Decomposition can temporarily immobilize N if material has a high C:N ratio. - Incorporation requires appropriate machinery/labor. - Poorly selected species may harbor pests or diseases. - Timing is important. 5.6 Green manure vs cover crop They can overlap. Cover crop emphasizes soil cover and ecosystem functions. Green manure specifically emphasizes biomass incorporation into soil. Therefore: Some green-manure crops are cover crops, but not every cover crop is used as green manure. 6. Crop Residues

Crop residues are plant materials remaining in the field after harvesting the economically important portion of a crop. Examples: - rice straw - wheat straw - maize stalks - leaves - husks - roots - stems - pods - sugarcane trash 6.2 Residue management options Crop residues can be: 1. retained on soil surface 2. incorporated 3. chopped 4. mulched 5. composted 6. used as livestock feed 7. used for bioenergy 8. used for other industrial purposes 6.3 Nutrient recycling Residues contain nutrients absorbed during crop growth. After decomposition: Residue→Microbial decomposition→Mineralization→Nutrients→CropResidue Microbial\ decomposition Mineralization Nutrients Crop Important nutrients include: - N - P - K - S - micronutrients Potassium in some crop residues can become relatively available rapidly because much of it is present in soluble/ionic forms. 6.4 Carbon-to-nitrogen ratio A major factor is: C:N High C:N residue: N immobilization tendency Low C:N residue: Faster N mineralization tendency The exact behavior depends on residue quality, soil and environment. 6.5 Benefits of residue r

Poor residue management can cause: - temporary N immobilization - pest/disease carryover - planting difficulties - slower soil warming in some situations - residue accumulation - machinery problems Burning Residue burning can rapidly remove biomass but may cause: - carbon loss - nutrient loss - air pollution - greenhouse gas emissions - loss of biological habitat - fire risk Therefore, residue management should be based on the crop, soil, climate and production system rather than assuming complete removal or burning is always appropriate.

A biofertilizer is a preparation containing living microorganisms that, when applied appropriately to seed, soil, roots or planting material, can contribute to plant nutrient availability or nutrient acquisition through biological processes. Important distinction: Biofertilizer≠Organic manure Biofertilizers are primarily microbial inoculants. 7.2 Major types Nitrogen-fixing organisms Examples: - Rhizobium / related rhizobia - Azotobacter - Azospirillum - cyanobacteria in appropriate systems Phosphate-solubilizing microorganisms PSB/PSM-type inoculants can help mobilize poorly available phosphorus. Mycorrhizal inoculants Especially arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF). Potassium-solubilizing microorganisms Certain microbes can contribute to mobilization of mineral-associated potassium. 7.3 Rhizobium and legumes Classic symbiosis: Legume+Rhizobium→Root Nodules→Biological N Fixation Atmospheric nitrogen: N2→NH3/NH4+N 2 NH 3/NH 4 + Nitrogen is then incorporated into plant compounds.

Azotobacter is a free-living nitrogen-fixing bacterium associated mainly with non-leguminous cropping systems. Its effectiveness depends on: - soil environment - carbon availability - population establishment - crop - formulation - management

Azospirillum is associated with plant roots and can contribute to biological nitrogen fixation and plantgrowth-promoting effects. It is commonly discussed in relation to: - cereals - grasses - other non-leguminous crops 7.6 Phosphate-solubilizing microorganisms Some microorganisms produce: - organic acids - enzymes - chelating compounds These can increase mobilization of poorly available phosphorus. Conceptually: Fixed/insoluble P→Microbial activityMore available P

Mycorrhizal fungi form associations with plant roots. General relationship: Plant Root↔Mycorrhizal Fungus Plant supplies carbon to fungus. Fungus can expand the effective soil-exploration network and improve acquisition of nutrients, especially phosphorus, and sometimes water.

Biofertilizers can: - contribute to nutrient availability - support biological N fixation - mobilize phosphorus - improve nutrient acquisition - support root growth - interact with rhizosphere microbes - reduce dependence on some external nutrient inputs in suitable situations

Effectiveness depends strongly on: - microbial strain - crop - soil pH - temperature - moisture - organic matter - salinity - native microbial community - inoculant quality - storage - application method Therefore: Biofertilizer performance is environment-dependent Biofertilizers should not automatically be treated as complete replacements for mineral fertilizers.

Urea is a widely used nitrogen fertilizer containing approximately: 46%N by mass. Chemical formula: CO(NH2)2 8.2 Nitrogen supply After application, urea undergoes hydrolysis: CO(NH2)2+H2O→NH3+CO2CO(NH 2) 2+H 2O NH 3+CO 2 In soil, ammonia/ammonium chemistry then proceeds through: NH3+H2O↔NH4++OH−NH 3+H 2O NH 4 ++OH Ammonium can subsequently be nitrified: NH4+→NO2−→NO3−NH 4 + NO 2 - NO 3 Thus: Urea→NH4+→NO3− 8.3 Nitrogen losses from urea Volatilization Especially important when urea remains on the soil surface under favorable conditions. Urea→NH3↑Urea NH 3 Leaching After conversion to nitrate: NO3−→LeachingNO 3 - Leaching particularly where drainage is high. Denitrification Under waterlogged/low-O₂ conditions: NO3−→N2O→N2NO 3 - N 2O N 2
- High N concentration. - Easy to transport. - Widely available. - Suitable for many crops. - Can be used in split applications. - Suitable for fertigation where appropriate.

- No P or K. - N losses can occur. - Surface application can increase volatilization risk under suitable conditions. - Excess N can cause: - excessive vegetative growth - lodging - delayed maturity - pest/disease susceptibility in some situations - environmental losses 8.6 Urea calculation For: 100 kg N/ha100\ kg\ N/ha theoretical urea: 1000.46=217.4 kg/ha 0.46 =217.4\ kg/ha Actual fertilizer recommendation depends on the crop and nutrient-management plan. 9. DAP

DAP = Diammonium phosphate Chemical formula: (NH4)2HPO4 It is a concentrated fertilizer supplying: N+P A commonly marketed grade is approximately: 18−46−0 meaning: - 18% N - 46% P2O5P 2O 5 - 0% K2OK 2O Fertilizer grades are conventionally expressed as: N−P2O5−K2O

DAP supplies: Nitrogen Supports: - chlorophyll - proteins - enzymes - vegetative growth Phosphorus Supports: - ATP/energy transfer - root development - reproductive development - nucleic acids - early establishment 9.3 Soil reaction DAP dissolves and creates an initially alkaline zone around fertilizer granules. This can influence: - ammonia concentration - nutrient interactions - seed safety if placed too close to seed Therefore placement matters.
- Concentrated N + P source. - Useful where both nutrients are required. - Convenient handling. - Suitable for basal/placed applications in appropriate systems.

- Does not supply K. - Not appropriate if soil P is already excessive. - Poor placement can injure seeds. - P availability is strongly influenced by soil pH/mineralogy. - Nitrogen losses can occur depending on management. 10. MOP

MOP = Muriate of Potash It is: Potassium chloride (KCl) It is a major potassium fertilizer. Common fertilizer analysis is approximately: 60%K2O though actual product specifications can vary. 10.2 Nutrient supplied Mainly: K and chloride: Cl−Cl is also supplied. 10.3 Potassium functions K supports: - stomatal regulation - water relations - enzyme activation - carbohydrate transport - protein synthesis - stress responses - lodging resistance - disease/stress tolerance processes 10.4 Chloride consideration Because MOP supplies chloride: KCl→K++Cl−KCl K ++Cl It may not be preferred in every situation, especially where: - crop is chloride-sensitive - irrigation water is already high in chloride - salinity is a concern However, chloride itself is also an essential micronutrient at appropriate concentrations.
- Contains chloride. - Not appropriate for every chloride-sensitive crop/soil situation. - Does not supply N or P. - Excessive application contributes to salt load. 11. SSP

SSP = Single Superphosphate It is a phosphorus fertilizer that also supplies sulfur and calcium. Typical composition is approximately: 16%P2O5 with sulfur commonly around: 11−12%S Exact grades vary by product. 11.2 Main nutrients P+S+Ca The main fertilizer value is phosphorus and sulfur. 11.3 Phosphorus functions P supports: - energy transfer - root development - nucleic acids - membrane components - flowering/reproductive processes - early plant establishment 11.4 Sulfur functions S is needed for: - cysteine - methionine - proteins - enzymes - chlorophyll-related metabolism - oil synthesis - N metabolism Thus SSP can be especially useful where both P and S are required. 11.5 SSP vs DAP Feature DAP SSP N Yes Essentially no significant N P High Moderate S No significant intentional S Significant S K No No Typical grade 18-46-0 16% P₂O₅ + S Main advantage Concentrated N+P P+S supply 12. NPK Fertilizers

Suppose a fertilizer is: 10−26−26 It contains approximately: - 10% N - 26% P2O5P 2O 5 - 26% K2OK 2O by mass. For 100 kg fertilizer: 10 kg N10\ kg\ N 26 kg P2O526\ kg\ P 2O 5 26 kg K2O26\ kg\ K 2O 12.3 Why NPK fertilizers are useful They can: - supply multiple nutrients - simplify application - provide balanced nutrient combinations - reduce separate fertilizer handling - support crop-specific nutrient programs

Straight fertilizers Supply primarily one major nutrient. Examples: - urea → N - MOP → K Complex/compound fertilizers Contain multiple nutrients chemically combined. Blended fertilizers Different fertilizer materials are physically mixed to produce a target grade. 12.5 Important misconception NPK does not mean every crop needs equal amounts of N, P and K. The correct ratio depends on: - crop - soil - yield target - growth stage - previous crop - nutrient removal - irrigation - management 12.6 Nutrient calculation Suppose 200 kg/ha of a 10-26-26 fertilizer is applied. N: 200×0.10=20 kg200 0.10=20\ kg P2O5P 2O 5: 200×0.26=52 kg200 0.26=52\ kg K2OK 2O: 200×0.26=52 kg200 0.26=52\ kg Therefore: 20 kgN+52 kgP2O5+52 kgK2O 12.7 Important distinction: P₂O₅ and elemental P Fertilizer labels conventionally report phosphorus as: P2O5P 2O 5 rather than elemental P. Approximate conversion: P=P2O5×0.436P=P 2O 5 0.436 Similarly, potassium fertilizer is commonly reported as: K2OK 2O rather than elemental K. Approximate conversion: K=K2O×0.830K=K 2O 0.830 These are label-convention conversions, not ad
Micronutrient fertilizers are materials used to supply essential micronutrients required in relatively small quantities. Important micronutrients: Fe, Zn, B, Mn, Cu, Mo, Cl, Ni

Nutrient Example fertilizer/source Zinc Zinc sulfate Iron Ferrous sulfate, iron chelates Boron Borax, boric acid Manganese Manganese sulfate Copper Copper sulfate Molybdenum Sodium/ammonium molybdate Chlorine KCl and other chloride salts Nickel Nickel-containing specialized formulations 13.3 Important principle A micronutrient is required in a small amount, but that does not mean it is unimportant. Small requirement≠Small importance 13.4 Deficiency correction General pathway: Soil/Tissue Diagnosis→Identify Deficiency→Select Source→Determine Rate→Apply→MonitorSoil/ Tissue\ Diagnosis Identify\ Deficiency Select\ Source Determine\ Rate Apply Monitor 13.5 Application methods Micronutrients may be supplied through: - soil application - foliar spray - fertigation - seed treatment - coating - localized placement The appropriate method depends on: - nutrient - crop - deficiency severity - soil pH - soil chemistry - crop growth stage - fertilizer formulation

14. Basal Application Definition Basal application is the application of fertilizer before sowing/planting or at the time of sowing/planting so that nutrients are available during early crop establishment. Basal = Before or at planting

Provides nutrients during: - germination - root establishment - early vegetative growth Especially useful for nutrients that support early development, depending on soil/crop. 14.2 Typical nutrients Phosphorus is often strategically applied near planting because: - it is relatively immobile in soil - early root development can be important Potassium may also be applied basally depending on soil/crop. Nitrogen may be partly basal but often needs splitting because of mobility and loss risks.
- Early nutrient availability. - Supports establishment. - Efficient placement possible. - Useful for immobile nutrients.

Too much fertilizer close to seed can cause: Salt injury / ammonia injury / poor germination Therefore: Seed + fertilizer placement must be managed carefully 15. Top Dressing Definition Top dressing is the application of fertilizer to an established crop after emergence, generally on or near the soil surface. Top Dressing = Fertilizer applied after crop establishment 15.2 Main purpose Most commonly used for nutrients requiring additional supply during crop growth, particularly nitrogen. For example: Urea→N supplyUrea N\ supply during active vegetative/reproductive growth.
- Matches nutrient supply with crop demand. - Reduces excessive early nutrient availability. - Can improve N-use efficiency. - Allows adjustment based on crop condition/weather.

Surface-applied urea may experience: NH3 volatilization if conditions favor loss. Rain or irrigation may help move nutrients into the soil, but excessive rainfall can increase other losses. 16. Foliar Application Definition Foliar application is the application of nutrients directly onto plant leaves in a suitable spray solution. Leaf surface→Nutrient absorption 16.1 Common uses Especially useful for: - micronutrients - rapid correction of certain deficiencies - situations where soil availability is poor - supplementary nutrition Examples: - zinc - iron - boron - manganese - copper Crop-specific formulations are important. 16.2 Absorption pathway Nutrients can enter through: - cuticle - stomatal regions - other surface pathways Then: Leaf surface→Absorption→Cellular transportLeaf\ surface Absorption Cellular\ transport
- Rapid nutrient delivery. - Useful for correcting some deficiencies. - Can bypass certain soil limitations. - Requires relatively small quantities.

Foliar application is not always suitable for supplying the entire nutrient requirement. Potential problems: - leaf burn - concentration injury - poor absorption - wash-off by rain - environmental effects - limited mobility of some nutrients within phloem For example, calcium has limited phloem mobility, so foliar Ca may not reliably supply all developing tissues.

Definition Fertigation is the application of soluble or suitably formulated fertilizers through irrigation water. Fertilizer+Irrigation Water→Root Zone 17.2 Commonly associated systems - drip irrigation - micro-irrigation - sprinkler systems - certain other pressurized irrigation systems

- precise nutrient delivery - frequent small applications - nutrient placement near roots - efficient water-nutrient management - automation possible - useful for high-value crops 17.4 Nutrients commonly fertigation-compatible Depending on formulation and water chemistry: - N - K - some P sources - micronutrients 17.5 Important compatibility issue Some fertilizers can react in concentrated stock solutions. For example: Ca2++SO42−→CaSO4Ca 2+ +SO 4 2- CaSO 4 - r phosphate reactions can create precipitates under unsuitable conditions. Therefore: Fertilizer compatibility + water quality must be checked 17.6 Fertigation management Important parameters: - fertilizer solubility - irrigation water quality - pH - EC - concentration - injection rate - system pressure - filtration - flushing - crop stage - root-zone moisture 18. Band Placement Definition Band placement means applying fertilizer in a concentrated strip or band near the crop row rather than uniformly across the entire field. Band = Localized fertilizer strip

Row band Fertilizer placed alongside crop rows. Side dressing Fertilizer placed beside growing plants after establishment. Deep placement Fertilizer placed below/near the root zone at a suitable depth.

- Places nutrients near roots. - Can reduce fertilizer-soil contact for certain nutrients. - Useful for phosphorus in some systems. - Can improve nutrient-use efficiency. - May reduce fertilizer requirement relative to uniform broadcasting in some conditions. 18.4 Important precaution Fertilizer should not be placed excessively close to seed. Fertilizer band≠direct seed contact High salt concentration can damage germinating seeds.
Definition Broadcasting is the uniform spreading of fertilizer over the soil surface or field area. Broadcasting = Uniform spreading over an area
- Simple. - Fast. - Suitable for large areas. - Useful for certain nutrient sources and crops. - Can be combined with incorporation.

- Less localized than banding. - Greater soil contact for some nutrients. - Potential losses if surface-applied. - Uniform distribution depends on spreader calibration. - Less precise than localized application. 19.5 Broadcasting vs banding Feature Broadcasting Banding Distribution Whole area Localized Nutrient concentration Lower spatial concentration Higher near band Precision Lower Higher Labor Often lower More placement requirement Root proximity Variable Greater Risk of seed injury Usually lower if separated Higher if too close 20. Split Application Definition Split application means dividing the total fertilizer requirement into multiple applications at different times rather than applying the entire quantity at once. Total Fertilizer=Application1+Application2+Application3+⋯ = Application 1+ Application 2+ Application 3+ 20.1 Why split fertilizer? Particularly useful for mobile nutrients such as nitrogen. It helps synchronize: Nutrient Supply≈Crop Demand

Suppose a crop requires: 120 kgN/ha120\ kgN/ha A management plan could theoretically divide it into: 40+40+40=120 kgN/ha40+40+40=120\ kgN/ha The actual split should be crop- and recommendation-specific.
- Reduces nutrient surplus at one time. - Can improve nutrient-use efficiency. - Reduces some loss risks. - Matches crop demand. - Allows adjustment based on weather and crop condition.

- More labor/operations. - Requires good timing. - Difficult if machinery/access is limited. - Poor timing can still cause losses. 20.5 Split application vs top dressing These are not synonyms. Top dressing Describes how/when fertilizer is applied to an established crop. Split application Describes dividing the total fertilizer dose into multiple applications. Therefore: A top-dressed fertilizer can be one part of a split application program. 21. Integrated Nutrient Management (INM)

Integrated Nutrient Management (INM) is the coordinated use of organic, inorganic/mineral, biological and other nutrient sources to supply crops with balanced nutrients while maintaining or improving soil fertility, nutrient-use efficiency, productivity and environmental sustainability. Core: INM=Organic Sources+Chemical Fertilizers+Biofertilizers+Efficient Application+Soil Testing 21.2 Why INM is required Using only one nutrient source has limitations. Only chemical fertilizer May supply nutrients efficiently but does not by itself replace the functions of organic matter management. Only organic manure May have: - low nutrient concentration - slow release - large application requirements - variable nutrient content Only biofertilizer May not provide sufficient quantities of all required nutrients. Therefore: Integrated Sources>Single Source where “>” means broader nutrient-management capability, not necessarily higher yield in every situation. 21.3 Components of INM 1. Soil testing Soil Test→Nutrient DiagnosisSoil\ Test Nutrient\ Diagnosis 2. Organic sources - FYM - compost - vermic

- Rhizobium - Azotobacter - Azospirillum - phosphate-solubilizing microorganisms - mycorrhiza 5. Crop rotation Especially: Cereal↔LegumeCereal Legume 6. Residue recycling Residue→Soil Organic Matter+NutrientsResidue Soil\ Organic\ Matter+Nutrients 7. Efficient application - basal - top dressing - banding - fertigation - foliar - split application 21.4 INM nutrient cycle A simplified system: Organic Inputs→Decomposition→Mineralization→Available Nutrients→Plant Uptake Alongside: Mineral Fertilizer→Available Nutrients→Plant Uptake And: Biofertilizers→Biological Nutrient Mobilization/Fixation→Plant Nutrient Supply 21.5 INM and nitrogen For nitrogen: Organic N→NH4+→NO3−→Plant UptakeOrganic\ N NH 4 + NO 3 Plant\ Uptake Biological fixation: N2→NH3/NH4+→Plant/Soil NN 2 NH 3/NH 4 + Plant/Soil\ N Mineral fertilizer: Urea→NH4+→NO3−Urea NH 4 + NO 3 The goal is to synchronize these sources with crop demand. 21.6 INM and phosphorus Phosphorus may exist in: - soil solution - labile pools - organic pools - mineral-associated forms Microorganisms and organic matter can influence P cycling. Mineral P

Farmyard manure (FYM) is one of the most important traditional organic manures used in agriculture. It is primarily made from decomposed livestock dung, urine, bedding/litter material, and other farmyard organic wastes. FYM is important because it performs two functions simultaneously: Nutrient Supply+Soil Improvement + Unlike concentrated chemical fertilizers, FYM generally contains nutrients in relatively low and variable concentrations, but it contributes significantly to soil organic matter, nutrient cycling, soil structure, water retention, and biological activity.

Exam-ready definition Farmyard manure is a partially or well-decomposed mixture of livestock dung, urine, bedding material and other farm organic wastes that is applied to agricultural soil to supply plant nutrients and improve the physical, chemical and biological properties of the soil. In simple words: Animal waste + bedding + decomposition→FYM 3. What Does FYM Contain? FYM can contain: - cattle dung - urine - straw - crop residues - bedding material - fodder residues - shed-cleaning materials - small amounts of soil and other farm organic materials Its exact composition depends heavily on how it is collected and stored. Important principle FYM does not have one fixed nutrient composition Its nutrient content depends on: - animal species - animal diet - type of bedding - amount of urine retained - moisture - storage duration - decomposition - handling - exposure to rain - method of storage 4. Major Components of FYM Conceptually: FYM=Dung+Urine+Bedding+Organic Residues+Microbial Biomass Dung Contains: - organic carbon - nitrogen - phosphorus - potassium - sulfur - micronutrients -

Improved aggregation and pore structure can promote infiltration. Better Structure→Better Infiltration 14. Effect on Soil Chemical Properties FYM can influence: Nutrient availability Provides multiple nutrients and supports nutrient cycling. CEC Organic matter contains negatively charged sites that can contribute to cation retention. Organic Matter→Exchange Sites→CEC ContributionOrganic\ Matter Exchange\ Sites CEC\ Contribution Buffering Organic matter can contribute to soil's buffering capacity. Nutrient retention Improved organic matter can help retain some nutrients and reduce losses under appropriate conditions. 15. Effect on Soil Biological Properties FYM is an important source of organic substrates for soil organisms. It can stimulate: - bacteria - fungi - actinomycetes - earthworms - other soil organisms General pathway: FYM→Organic Substrate→Microbial Activity→Nutrient Cycling 16. FYM and Microbial Activity Microorganisms use organic carbon as an energy source. Therefore: Organic C→Microbial GrowthOrganic\ C Microbial\ Growth Microbial activity contributes to: - decomposition
N+P+K+Ca+Mg+S+MicronutrientsN+P+K+Ca+Mg+S+ 2. Organic matter Organic Matter→Structure+Water Retention+CEC ContributionOrganic\ Matter Structure+Water\ Retention+CEC\ Contribution

Organic Substrate→Microbial Activity→Nutrient CyclingOrganic\ Substrate Microbial\ Activity Nutrient\ Cycling 47. Final One-Read Summary Farmyard manure (FYM) is a decomposed mixture of livestock dung, urine, bedding and other farm - rganic wastes used as an organic nutrient source and soil amendment. Its most important functions are: FYM=Nutrient Supply+Organic Matter+Soil Improvement+Microbial Support + + + The nutrient pathway is: Organic Nutrients→Decomposition→Mineralization→Available Nutrients→Root Uptake The soil pathway is: FYM→Organic Matter→Aggregation+Water Retention+Biological Activity+Nutrient Cycling Its effectiveness depends on: Quality+Decomposition+Rate+Timing+Placement+Soil+Crop+Climate And its proper role in modern agriculture is: FYM is usually a component of Integrated Nutrient Management, not simply a replacement for all fertil izers. Ultimate memory FYM = Organic manure from livestock/farm wastes that feeds BOTH the crop and the soil. Compost

Compost is a stabilized organic material produced by the controlled biological decomposition of - rganic wastes under suitable conditions of moisture, oxygen, temperature, microorganisms, and time. It is one of the most important organic amendments in agriculture because it performs two functions: Nutrient Supply+Soil Improvement + Unlike a concentrated chemical fertilizer such as urea, compost generally contains nutrients in lower and variable concentrations, but it contributes substantially to: - soil organic matter - soil structure - water retention - microbial activity - nutrient cycling - aggregation - waste recycling

Exam-ready definition Compost is a stabilized organic material produced through the controlled biological decomposition of plant, animal, and other biodegradable organic wastes under suitable conditions of moisture, aeration, temperature, and microbial activity. In simple form: Organic Waste→Controlled Decomposition→Stabilization→Compost 3. What Is Compost Made From? Compost can be prepared from many biodegradable materials. Plant materials - crop residues - straw - leaves - weeds - grass - vegetable wastes - fruit wastes - husks - stalks Animal materials - livestock manure - bedding material - animal waste Other biodegradable materials - garden waste - food-processing residues - suitable biodegradable organic wastes The feedstock must be appropriate and reasonably free from contaminants. 4. Compost vs Raw Organic Waste Raw organic waste is not necessarily compost. For example: Fresh crop residue≠Mature compost The material becomes compost through: Decomposition→Stabilization→MaturationDecomposition Stabilization Maturation During this process: - easily decomposable compounds decreas

Temperature is both a process indicator and a factor controlling microbial populations. General pattern: Temperature↑→Thermophilic Phase→Temperature↓→Maturation Temperature depends on: - pile size - moisture - oxygen - feedstock - C:N ratio - microbial activity - ambient temperature 19. Particle Size Particle size influences decomposition. Smaller particles provide: Greater surface area which can increase microbial access. Therefore: Particle Size↓→Surface Area↑→Potential Decomposition Rate↑Particle\ Size Surface\ Area Potential\ Decomposition\ Rate But excessively fine material can reduce air-filled pore space and restrict aeration. Therefore: Optimal particle size is better than simply making everything very fine. 20. Moisture + Oxygen + C:N + Temperature The most important composting conditions can be summarized as: Feedstock+C:N+Moisture+Oxygen+Temperature+Time→Compost Quality + + + + + 21. Compost Maturity Maturity refers to the degree to which compost has undergone sufficient decomposition and stabilization to be suitable for its intended use. A mature compost generally shows:

Vermicompost is a stabilized organic material produced through the biological processing of organic wastes by earthworms together with microorganisms. Earthworms consume, fragment, mix and transform organic material, while microorganisms carry out much of the actual biochemical decomposition. The core idea is: Organic Waste+Earthworms+Microorganisms→Vermicompost Vermicompost is used in agriculture primarily as an organic manure and soil amendment. It can contribute nutrients while improving soil biological and physical properties.

Exam-ready definition Vermicompost is a stabilized, finely divided organic material produced through the biological processing and decomposition of suitable organic wastes by earthworms and associated microorganisms. In simple terms: Earthworms + organic waste + microorganisms → Vermicompost 3. What Is Vermicomposting? Vermicomposting is the process. Vermicompost is the product. Therefore: Vermicomposting=Process = Vermicompost=Final product = 4. Basic Principle Vermicomposting combines two major biological processes: Earthworm processing Earthworms: - consume organic material - fragment it - mix it - increase surface area - produce casts - alter microbial habitats Microbial decomposition Microorganisms: - decompose organic compounds - mineralize nutrients - stabilize organic matter - transform carbon and nitrogen compounds Thus: Earthworm Activity+Microbial Decomposition→Stabilized Organic Material 5. Role of Earthworms Earthworms are the central biological agents in vermicomposting. They process organic material through their digestive system. A simplified pathway is: Organic Waste

Earthworms are sensitive to excessive temperature. Vermicomposting generally works best under moderate temperatures suitable for the selected worm species. Excessive heat can cause: Temperature↑→Earthworm Stress→Activity↓→Mortality Risk↑Temperature Earthworm\ Stress Activity Mortality\ Risk This is one reason fresh manure should not necessarily be placed directly into a worm bed.

Vermicomposting requires adequate air movement. Poor aeration can cause: - anaerobic conditions - bad odor - reduced worm activity - slower processing Therefore: Good Porosity+Adequate Moisture+Aeration→Healthy Vermicomposting Turning should be handled carefully because excessive disturbance can harm earthworms. 23. pH Earthworms generally prefer a near-neutral to mildly suitable pH environment, though exact tolerance depends on species and feedstock. Extreme acidity or alkalinity can reduce worm activity. Therefore: Extreme pH→Earthworm Stress Feedstock selection and decomposition before worm introduction help stabilize the material.

Earthworms generally avoid strong light. Therefore vermicomposting units are commonly maintained in: - shade - covered structures - protected beds This also helps regulate: - temperature - moisture and protects worms from environmental extremes. 25. Earthworm Casts One of the important products of earthworm activity is earthworm casts. Casts are processed organic material excreted by earthworms. They can contain: - organic matter - microorganisms - plant nutrients - transformed organic compounds A simplified concept is: Organic Material→Earthworm Gut→Casts→Microbial Stabilization 26. Vermicompost Nutrients Vermicompost can contain: Macronutrients - nitrogen - phosphorus - potassium - calcium - magnesium - sulfur Micronutrients Potentially: - iron - zinc - manganese - copper - boron - other trace elements However: Nutrient concentration varies with feedstock and processing. There is no single universal vermicompost nutrient composition. 27. Nitrogen in Vermicompost Nitrogen exists in multiple forms. A simplified pathway is: Organic N→NH4+→NO3−Organic\ N NH 4 + NO 3 Earthworm activity

Vermicomposting can influence phosphorus transformation. Organic phosphorus can undergo microbial mineralization: Organic P→Available POrganic\ P Available\ P Earthworm activity and associated microorganisms can modify the chemical and biological environment. However, soil pH and mineral interactions still strongly determine actual plant availability.

Potassium can be released from organic materials during decomposition. Organic Residues→Decomposition→K+ releaseOrganic\ Residues Decomposition K + Therefore vermicompost can contribute potassium, but the amount depends on the feedstock. 30. Secondary Nutrients Vermicompost may supply: - calcium - magnesium - sulfur The actual amount depends on the materials used.

Vermicompost may contain: - Fe - Zn - Mn - Cu - B - other trace elements However: Presence of a nutrient≠guaranteed plant availability Availability depends on soil and chemical conditions. 32. Vermicompost and Soil Organic Matter One major agricultural role is contributing organic material to soil. Vermicompost→Organic Matter→Soil Organic Carbon Some carbon is decomposed: Organic C→CO2Organic\ C CO 2 while some may contribute to more stable soil organic matter. 33. Effect on Soil Structure Vermicompost can contribute to aggregation and structural improvement. Organic Matter+Microbial Products→Soil Aggregation Improved aggregation can influence: - infiltration - aeration - root penetration - water retention - resistance to crusting 34. Effect on Soil Water-Holding Capacity Organic matter can increase water retention. Vermicompost→Organic Matter↑→Water Retention Potential↑Vermicompost Organic\ Matter Water\ Retention\ Potential This can be useful especially in soils with low organic matter. But: Vermicompost≠Irrigation It improves the soil's capacity to use and retain water; it does no

Potential predators include: - ants - birds - rodents - other organisms Protection of the vermicomposting unit may be required. 58.5 Toxic feedstock Some materials may contain: - pesticides - heavy metals - salts - harmful chemicals These can affect worms and contaminate the final product. 59. Signs of Good Vermicompost A suitable finished product generally tends to be: - dark brown to dark in color - fine or granular - relatively uniform - earthy smelling rather than strongly putrid - relatively stable - free from obvious undecomposed waste in excessive amounts - free from visible contaminants However: Color and smell alone cannot fully certify quality. Laboratory testing is preferable when quality is important. 60. Quality Parameters Important quality parameters can include: Physical - moisture - texture - particle size - uniformity Chemical - pH - EC - organic carbon - total N - available/total P - K - C:N ratio - secondary nutrients - micronutrients Biological - maturity - stability - microbial activity - phytotoxicity Safety - pathogens - heavy metals - plastics - chemical conta

Green manure is a crop or plant biomass that is grown specifically for incorporation into the soil while it is still relatively green and succulent, rather than being harvested primarily for grain, food, or sale. Its main purpose is to improve: - soil organic matter - nutrient cycling - nitrogen supply, especially when legumes are used - soil structure - microbial activity - water infiltration and retention - soil fertility - long-term soil productivity The fundamental concept is: Grow Biomass→Incorporate into Soil→Decomposition→Nutrient Recycling + Soil Improvement d

Exam-ready definition Green manure is a crop or plant biomass grown and incorporated into the soil while green and relatively succulent, primarily to improve soil fertility, organic matter, nutrient cycling and soil physical and biological properties. In simple words: Grow a crop mainly to feed the soil 3. Why Is It Called "Green" Manure? It is called green manure because the plant material is generally incorporated while it is: - green - succulent - actively growing - relatively rich in easily decomposable organic compounds It does not necessarily mean the crop must be literally bright green at the exact time of incorporation. The important idea is: Fresh/green biomass→soil incorporation 4. Green Manure vs Green Manure Crop These terms are closely related but useful to distinguish. Green manure crop The crop specifically grown for biomass incorporation. Green manure The biomass/material incorporated into the soil. For example: Sesbania grown→cut/incorporated→green manure 5. Major Types of Green Manure Green manure can broadly be classified into: 1. Leguminous green manure 2. Non-leg

text: OIL And the key principle for agriculture is: A good green-manure system balances biomass and nutrient benefits against the land, time and water re quired to grow it. Crop Residues

Crop residues are the plant materials that remain in the field or are generated during harvesting, threshing, processing, or other operations after the economically useful portion of a crop has been harvested. Examples include: - straw - stalks - stems - leaves - husks - shells - cobs - pods - roots - stubble - chaff - processing residues Crop residues are not simply waste. They are an important source of: - organic carbon - nutrients - soil cover - animal feed - bedding - compost material - bioenergy feedstock - industrial raw material The basic agricultural concept is: Crop Residues=Remaining Plant Biomass After/From Crop Production = 2. Exam-Ready Definition Crop residues are the plant materials remaining after harvesting or processing a crop, including straw, stalks, leaves, roots, husks, cobs, pods, shells, stubble and other nonmarketable or unused plant parts. In simple terms: Crop harvested→useful product+remaining biomass + The remaining biomass is the crop residue. 3. Crop Residue Is Not the Same as Agricultural Waste The word waste can be misleading. A crop residue may have
The major stems remaining after harvesting. Examples: - maize stalk - cotton stalk - sorghum stalk - pearl millet stalk - sunflower stalk
The lower portion of stems remaining attached to the soil after cutting the crop. For example: Harvested Stem→Lower Stem Remaining=Stubble
Roots remaining underground after crop harvest. They are often overlooked but are important contributors to soil organic matter. Root Biomass→Soil Organic Matter
The central structure remaining after maize kernels are removed. Maize grain+maize cob + 5.8 Pods and Shells Examples: - groundnut shells - pulse pods - soybean residues

Bagasse is the fibrous residue remaining after sugarcane juice extraction. Sugarcane→Juice+Bagasse Bagasse has applications in: - energy generation - paper/pulp - boards - composting - other industrial uses 6. Crop-Wise Examples Crop Major residues Rice Straw, husk, bran, stubble Wheat Straw, chaff, stubble Maize Stalks, leaves, cobs Sugarcane Bagasse, tops, trash Cotton Stalks, leaves, bolls/residues Groundnut Haulms, shells Soybean Stems, leaves, pods Pulses Straw, stems, pods Sorghum Stalks, leaves Pearl millet Stalks, leaves Mustard Stems, leaves, pods Sunflower Stalks, leaves, heads The exact amount and composition depend on variety, yield, harvesting method and environmental conditions. 7. Residue-to-Product Relationship A crop produces both economically useful material and residue. Conceptually: Total Crop Biomass=Economic Product+Crop Residues For example: Maize plant→grain+stalks+leaves+cob+roots + + + + This is important because agricultural production does not end with the harvested grain. 8. Composition of Crop Residues Crop residues mainly contain: Carbon Major structura

Cellulose is a major structural carbohydrate. It is composed mainly of glucose units linked into long chains. Simplified: Cellulose→Microbial Decomposition→Simpler Carbon Compounds Cellulose can be decomposed by specialized microorganisms and enzymes.

Fertilizer application means placing or delivering a fertilizer nutrient into the soil, onto the plant, - r through irrigation water in a way that allows the crop to obtain the nutrient efficiently while minimizing losses. The two fundamental timing-based methods are: 1. Basal application 2. Top dressing These methods are especially important for understanding when a fertilizer should be supplied.

Basal application is the application of fertilizer before sowing/planting or at the time of sowing/planting, so that nutrients are available to the crop during early establishment and subsequent growth. In simple terms: Basal application = Fertilizer supplied at the beginning of crop establishment It may be applied: - Before sowing - During sowing - At planting - During transplanting - Just before planting 1.2 Purpose of basal application The major purpose is to ensure that essential nutrients are available in the root zone when the young crop begins active growth. The sequence is: Fertilizer application→Nutrient availability→Root uptake→Early crop establishment Basal fertilizer can support: - Root establishment - Early vegetative growth - Initial nutrient supply - Seedling establishment - Early crop vigor - Early reproductive preparation 1.3 Why is basal application important? Immediately after germination or transplanting, the plant begins developing its root system. If an essential nutrient is unavailable during this period, early growth can be restricted. Therefore: Good early nu

Top dressing is the application of fertilizer after the crop has emerged and started growing, usually by placing fertilizer on or near the soil surface close to established crop rows. In simple terms: Top dressing = Fertilizer supplied after crop establishment It is commonly used to provide nutrients during periods of high crop demand. 2.2 Why is top dressing used? The crop's nutrient requirement changes as it grows. For example: Seedling→Vegetative growth→Flowering→Grain/Fruit fillingSeedling Vegetative\ growth Flowering Grain/Fruit\ filling Nutrient demand can increase substantially during active growth. Therefore, fertilizer can be supplied when the crop needs it. Crop demand→Top dressing→Nutrient availability 2.3 Nitrogen and top dressing Nitrogen is the classic nutrient associated with top dressing. Why? Because N is dynamic in soil and can be lost. Split application is the practice of dividing the total required fertilizer dose of a nutrient into two or more applications at different times during the crop-growing period, rather than applying the entire quantity at once. Exam-Ready Definition Manual weeding is the physical removal of weeds from a crop field by hand or using simple handoperated tools such as hoes, khurpis, hand cultivators and digging tools. It is particularly useful in small fields, nurseries, vegetable crops, orchards and around individual crop plants where selective weed removal is required. Timely manual weeding reduces competition for water, nutrients, light and space and can also reduce future weed populations when weeds are removed before seed production. 37. Final Memory R

Mechanical weeding is the control or removal of weeds using mechanical force generated by tools, implements, machines, or farm equipment rather than manually removing individual weeds or applying herbicides. In simple terms: Mechanical weeding=Controlling weeds using mechanical tools or machinery = The mechanical operation may: - Uproot weeds - Cut weeds - Bury weeds - Break weed stems - Disturb weed roots - Cover weeds with soil - Physically separate weeds from crop plants The central principle is: Mechanical force→Weed damage/removal→Reduced competition→Crop yield protection 2. Why Mechanical Weeding Is Important Weeds compete with crops for: - Water - Nutrients - Light - Space - Carbon dioxide and other resources Mechanical weeding reduces this competition without requiring herbicides. It is especially important in: - Row crops - Organic farming - Herbicide-resistance management - Small and medium farms - Crops where inter-row machinery can operate - Situations where chemical weed control is unsuitable 3. Intercultivation means cultivation between established crop rows. It can: - Remove young weeds - Loosen surface soil - Break soil crust - Improve soil surface condition in some systems - Reduce weed competition However, excessive soil disturbance can have negative effects. 7. Tine Cultivator A cultivator equipped with tines can disturb soil and uproot young weeds. The tines pass through the soil: Tines→Weed root disturbance→Weed death It is generally most effective when weeds are small. 8. Blade Hoe / Sweep A blade or sweep cuts weeds near the soil surface. The basic action is: Blade→Cut weed→Weed desiccation/death It can be useful for inter-row weed control. 9. Rotary Weeder A rotary weeder uses rotating elements to disturb soil and remove weeds. It is used in suitable crops and row configurations. The rotating mechanism can: - Uproot weeds - Bury weeds - Disturb young weeds 10. Rotary Hoe A rotary hoe uses rotating wheels/tines to disturb the soil surface. It can be particularly useful against very young weeds. The principle is: Small emerging weed→Mechanical disturbance→Desiccatio

Mowing cuts weeds above the soil surface. It is useful in: - Orchards - Pastures - Roadsides - Field margins - Non-crop areas Its major role is often: Prevent excessive weed growth and seed production Repeated mowing may weaken some weeds, but the response depends on species. 15. Flame Weeding Flame weeding uses heat from a flame to damage weed tissues. Heat→Cell membrane/protein damage→Weed death or severe suppression It is a thermal rather than conventional soil-disturbance method, but is commonly discussed with physical/mechanical weed-management approaches. It can be useful in certain crops and situations, especially when weeds are small. 16. Harrowing for Weed Control Harrowing can disturb and destroy young weeds. It may be used: - Before planting - Between certain crop stages - As part of seedbed preparation However, harrowing can also move weed seeds within the soil profile. Therefore: Harrowing=Potential weed control+Potential seed redistribution = + 17. Tillage as a Weed-Management Tool Tillage can control weeds by: - Uprooting - Cutting - Burying - Exposing - Drying weeds.

Exam-Ready Definition Mechanical weeding is the physical control or removal of weeds using mechanical tools, implements - r powered machinery. It works by uprooting, cutting, burying or otherwise physically damaging weeds. Common methods include inter-row cultivation, hoeing, tine cultivation, rotary weeding, mowing and tractor-mounted cultivation. Mechanical weeding is particularly effective against young weeds and is useful in row crops, organic farming and herbicide-resistance management. Excessive or poorly timed mechanical weeding can cause crop injury, soil disturbance and exposure of buried weed seeds. 46. Final Memory Remember:

Mulching is the practice of covering the soil surface around or between crop plants with a layer of - rganic or inorganic material to modify the soil environment and suppress weeds. The material may be: - Organic - Inorganic - Living Examples include: Organic mulches - Straw - Hay - Crop residues - Leaves - Grass clippings - Compost - Wood chips - Bark - Sugarcane trash - Coconut husk/coir materials Inorganic/synthetic mulches - Black polyethylene - Transparent poly

Cultural weed control is the management of weeds by modifying crop production practices so that the crop becomes more competitive and weeds become less able to germinate, establish, grow, reproduce, and replenish the weed seed bank. In simple terms: Cultural weed control=Manage the cropping system so that the crop outcompetes weeds = Unlike manual or mechanical weeding, cultural control does not primarily attack weeds directly. Instead, it changes the environment and management conditions in favor of the crop. The basic principle is: Better crop establishment+Better crop competition+Less favorable conditions for weeds→Reduced we ed pressure + + 2. Why Cultural Weed Control Is Important Weeds succeed when they obtain sufficient: - Light - Water - Nutrients - Space - Time - Suitable temperature - Suitable moisture - Opportunities for reproduction Cultural practices can alter these conditions. For example: Fast crop establishment→Earlier canopy development→Less light reaching weeds Therefore: Strong crop competition→Weed growth↓ 3. Main Principle of Cultural Weed Control The central con

Intercropping means growing two or more crops together in a planned spatial arrangement. For example: Main crop + legume The combined canopy can occupy more space and intercept more light. Intercropping→Resource capture↑→Available resources for weeds↓ 25. Smother Crops A smother crop is a vigorous crop grown specifically or partly to suppress weeds through rapid growth and canopy formation. It may: - Shade weeds - Occupy space - Consume water/nutrients - Reduce weed establishment Conceptually: Rapid biomass production→Weed suppression 26. Cover Crops Cover crops are grown primarily to cover and protect the soil between or before main crops. They can suppress weeds by: - Occupying space - Blocking light - Using resources - Producing residues - Sometimes releasing allelochemicals After termination: Cover crop→Residue mulch→Further weed suppression Thus: Cover crop=Living competition + potential residue mulch =

Some plants release biochemical compounds that can influence the germination or growth of neighboring plants. This is called allelopathy. Conceptually: Plant residues/root exudates→Biochemicals→Possible weed inhibition However, allelopathic effects are highly dependent on: - Plant species - Compound - Concentration - Soil - Microorganisms - Environmental conditions Therefore: Allelopathy is a potential mechanism, not a guaranteed field-level effect. 28. Mulching as Cultural Weed Control Mulching is often included among cultural/physical weed-management practices because it modifies the crop environment. Mulch→Light reduction+Physical barrier+Microclimate modification→Weed emergence↓ + + Organic mulch also contributes to soil health. 29. Stale Seedbed Technique The stale seedbed technique uses cultural management to encourage weeds to emerge before crop planting. Sequence: Prepare seedbed→Encourage weed germination→Destroy weed flush→Plant crop The purpose is to reduce the number of weeds emerging with the crop. 30. Biological weed control is the management or suppression of weeds by using living organisms or their biological interactions to reduce weed growth, reproduction, establishment, or population. The organisms used may include: - Insects - Plant pathogens - Grazing animals - Fish - Competitive plants - Microorganisms - Other organisms capable of damaging or suppressing weeds The fundamental principle is: Biological agent→Weed damage/competition→Weed population↓ Unlike mechanical weeding, which physically removes weeds, biological control uses living - rganisms as the control mechanism.

Exam-ready definition Biological weed control is the deliberate use or management of living organisms and biological interactions to suppress weed populations and reduce their growth, reproduction, or competitive effects below economically damaging levels. The key word is suppression, not necessarily complete eradication. 3. Basic Principle Every biological weed-control program depends on an interaction between: Biological agent↔Target weed↔Environment A biological agent must be able to survive and function under the conditions of the production system. Therefore: Agent effectiveness=f(Agent+Weed+Environment+Management) = f( + + + ) 4. Why Biological Weed Control Is Used Biological control can help: - Reduce persistent weed populations - Suppress invasive weeds - Reduce dependence on herbicides - Manage weeds that are difficult to remove mechanically - Provide long-term suppression - Reduce repeated control costs in suitable systems - Contribute to integrated weed management It is particularly interesting for weeds that are: - Persistent - Invasive - Difficult to control mechanically

A mycoherbicide is a biological weed-control product based on a fungal pathogen used to suppress a target weed. The general process is: Fungal pathogen→Application→Infection→Disease→Weed suppression The term is analogous to "bioherbicide."

A bioherbicide is a biological agent or biological product used specifically to suppress weeds. It may contain: - Fungi - Bacteria - Other biological organisms - Biologically derived active substances in some contexts The important distinction is: Chemical herbicide=Chemical active ingredient = whereas: Bioherbicide=Biological basis for weed suppression = 16. Examples of Microbial Weed Control Some fungi have been investigated or used against specific weeds. Examples of organisms used or studied include species of: - Colletotrichum - Alternaria - Phytophthora - Puccinia Their effectiveness is highly target-specific. Therefore: A pathogen effective against one weed≠automatically effective against another weed 17. Host Specificity Host specificity is one of the most important requirements in biological weed control. The ideal biological agent should strongly affect the target weed while causing little or no unacceptable damage to: - Crops - Native plants - Beneficial plants - Ecologically important species The desired relationship is: Target weed damage↑Non-target damage↓ 18. Herbicides are substances used to prevent, suppress, or kill unwanted plants (weeds). They are one component of weed management and are particularly useful when weeds cannot be controlled efficiently by hand or mechanical methods. The basic concept is: Herbicide→Specific physiological/biochemical effect→Weed injury→Weed suppression or death d Herbicides do not all work in the same way. Different herbicides interfere with different plant processes such as: - Photosynthesis - Amino-acid synthesis - Lipid synthesis - Cell division - Pigment formation - Plant hormone function - Cell membrane function - Respiration - Growth regulation

Exam-ready definition A herbicide is a chemical substance or formulation used to inhibit the germination, growth, development, or reproduction of unwanted plants or to kill them. The word herbicide comes from: - herbi → plant - cide → killing However, in agriculture, a herbicide does not necessarily kill every weed. Some herbicides merely suppress growth or prevent reproduction. 3. Why Herbicides Are Used Herbicides are used because weeds compete with crops for: Water+Nutrients+Light+Space+CO2 Uncontrolled weeds can cause: - Reduced crop yield - Poor crop quality - Difficult harvesting - Increased harvesting cost - Increased irrigation demand - Increased nutrient consumption - Pest and disease habitat - Contamination of harvested produce - Reduced efficiency of farm machinery Therefore: Effective weed control→Reduced crop-weed competition→Higher crop productivity potential 4. Glyphosate is generally considered a systemic, non-selective herbicide when used according to its registered use. 20. Conceptually: PSII inhibition→Electron transport disruption→Photosynthesis↓→Oxidative damage Examples of active ingredients in this broad group include atrazine and some related herbicides. 21. Glutamine Synthetase Inhibitors Glutamine synthetase is important in nitrogen metabolism. A well-known herbicide in this group is glufosinate. Conceptually: Glutamine synthetase inhibition→Ammonium detoxification disrupted→Cellular damage Glufosinate is generally a non-selective herbicide in its conventional applications. 22. Inhibition can result in: Pigment synthesis disruption→Bleaching→Plant death/suppression Typical visual symptoms can include whitening or bleaching of new growth. 24. VLCFA Inhibitors VLCFA means: Very-long-chain fatty acids These are important components of plant membranes and surface structures. Inhibition can interfere with: - Cell growth - Membrane development - Seedling development They are especially important in some soil-applied pre-emergence programs. 25. They are particularly important for controlling many broadleaf weeds. Conceptually: Auxin-like activity→Abnormal growth regulation→Vascular/metabolic disruption→Plant death 26. Pigment Inhibitors Some herbicides disrupt pigment formation. The characteristic symptom can be: Green tissue→Yellow/white tissue because chlorophyll or related pigment systems are disrupted. 27. Mode of Action vs Mechanism of Action These terms are often confused. Mode of action The overall biological process/pathway through which a herbicide produces its effects. Site of action The specific biochemical target. For example: Herbicide→Target enzyme→Biochemical pathway disruption→Physiological injury→Death Understanding mode of action is extremely important for herbicide resistance management. 28. Herbicide Absorption Before a herbicide can work, it generally has to reach and enter the target plant. Possible routes include: Foliar absorption Leaf surface→Cuticle→Plant tissue Root absorption Soil solution→Root→Plant Shoot absorption Some soil-applied herbicides can be absorbed through emerging shoots. 29. They can be classified according to selectivity, timing, movement, application method and mode of action. Based on selectivity they may be selective or non-selective; based on movement they may be contact or systemic; and based on timing they may be pre-plant, pre-emergence or postemergence. Pre-emergence herbicides are herbicides applied before the emergence of the target weed or crop, depending on the specific use and label definition, primarily to control weeds during their germination and early seedling establishment. Their main purpose is to prevent weeds from becoming established and competing with the crop. The basic sequence is: Herbicide application→Weed germination/emergence→Herbicide uptake→Seedling injury→Weed sup pression They are especially important for controlling early-season weed flushes.

Exam-ready definition Pre-emergence herbicides are herbicides applied before the emergence of the target weed, or at a specified crop stage before weed emergence, to prevent or suppress weed germination and early seedling development. Important clarification "Pre-emergence" is a timing term. It does not automatically mean that the herbicide must always be applied before sowing. For example, depending on the registered use, a pre-emergence herbicide may be applied: - Immediately after sowing - Before crop emergence - Before weed emergence The specific product label and crop recommendation determine the correct timing. 3. Why Pre-Emergence Herbicides Are Important The early stage of crop growth is often highly sensitive to weed competition. Early weed emergence→Competition begins→Crop growth/yield potential can be reduced Therefore: Prevent early weed establishment→Reduce early crop-weed competition This is closely related to the critical weed-free period. 4. Pendimethalin is a widely known soil-applied herbicide used in various crops for control of susceptible annual weeds. It primarily affects: Cell division and microtubule-related processes It is particularly associated with pre-emergence weed control. Typical targets can include susceptible: - Grasses - Some broadleaf weeds The actual weed spectrum depends on the crop, dose, formulation and use conditions.

Atrazine is a photosystem II inhibitor and is used selectively in certain crops and weed-management programs. Conceptually: Atrazine→PSII inhibition→Photosynthetic electron transport disrupted It can provide soil residual activity and is particularly important in certain maize and related cropping systems where registered.

Pretilachlor is a soil-applied herbicide used in certain rice production systems. It is particularly associated with early-season control of susceptible weeds. Its activity is related to disruption of lipid-related processes in developing seedlings.

Butachlor is another soil-applied herbicide historically and currently used in certain rice systems where registered. It is particularly associated with early control of susceptible annual grasses and some other weeds.

Oxyfluorfen is a PPO-inhibiting herbicide that can be used in certain crops and situations. Its activity can result in: PPO inhibition→Reactive oxygen-related membrane damage→Rapid tissue injury Its registered uses and timing must be followed carefully because crop safety depends strongly on application conditions. 18. Post-emergence herbicides are herbicides applied after the target weeds have emerged from the soil to control existing weeds. Unlike pre-emergence herbicides, which primarily target germinating or emerging weeds, postemergence herbicides are applied when weeds are already visible above the soil surface. The basic sequence is: Weed emerges→Herbicide application→Absorption→Mode of action→Weed injury→Suppression/ death They are particularly useful when the actual weed population can be identified after emergence.

Herbicide resistance is one of the most important challenges in modern weed management. When the same herbicide or the same mode of action (MOA) is repeatedly used, susceptible weeds are controlled while naturally less-sensitive individuals survive. If those survivors reproduce, resistance traits can become more common in the weed population. The basic process is: Herbicide use→Susceptible weeds die→Less-sensitive weeds survive→Reproduction→Resistance freq uency increases

Exam-ready definition Herbicide resistance is the inherited ability of a weed population to survive a herbicide dose that would normally control a susceptible population of the same species. The key words are: Inherited + Weed population + Survival + Normally effective herbicide 3. Herbicide Resistance vs Herbicide Tolerance These terms are often confused. Herbicide tolerance A plant species naturally survives a herbicide because it was never sufficiently susceptible. Natural insensitivity→Tolerance Herbicide resistance A weed population that was previously susceptible develops or becomes dominated by individuals capable of surviving the herbicide. Selection→Survival→Inheritance→Resistance Therefore: Tolerance≠Resistance 4. Simple Example Imagine a field contains 10,000 weeds. Initially: - 9,990 are susceptible - 10 have a naturally occurring resistance trait After herbicide application: 9,990→controlled9,990 while: 10→survive10 If the survivors produce seeds: 10→many offspring10 Repeated selection can result in a much larger proportion of resistant weeds. Spray timing is the selection of the correct time or growth stage for applying a herbicide so that weeds are controlled effectively while crop injury, environmental losses, and unnecessary herbicide use are minimized. The basic principle is: Correct herbicide+Correct timing+Correct dose+Correct application→Effective weed management ed + + + Even a suitable herbicide can perform poorly if it is applied too early, too late, or under unsuitable environmental conditions.

Herbicide safety refers to the practices used to protect farm workers, applicators, crops, livestock, consumers, beneficial organisms, soil, water, and the environment from unnecessary exposure or harm during the handling, mixing, transport, application, storage, and disposal of herbicides. In agriculture, plants are continuously exposed to insects, mites, pathogens, weeds, rodents, birds, nematodes and other organisms. Not every organism found in a field is a pest. An organism becomes a pest when its presence or activity causes enough damage or economic loss to justify management. The central idea is: Organism+Crop damage+Economically important loss→Pest + + This is one of the most important concepts in pest management. 2. Definition of Pest Simple definition A pest is an organism that causes damage to crops, livestock, stored products, humans, or other valuable resources. Agricultural definition An agricultural pest is an organism that damages a crop or agricultural product sufficiently to reduce its yield, quality, economic value, or usability. Exam-ready definition A pest is any organism that causes or has the potential to cause economically significant damage to a crop, agricultural product, livestock system, or other human resource. The word economically significant is important. 3. The Most Important Concept: Not Every Insect Is a Pest Suppose a farmer sees 100 i

But: Color alone≠reliable identification because color can vary with: - Life stage - Temperature - Nutrition - Sex - Geographic population - Lighting Use multiple characteristics. 29. Host Plant Association Different pests have different host preferences. Therefore: Pest identity=f(organism features+host crop+damage) = f( + + ) Knowing the crop can significantly narrow the possible pest list. 30. Location on the Plant Where the pest occurs is diagnostically useful. For example: Location Possible pest groups Roots Nematodes, root-feeding insects Soil surface Termites, cutworms and other soil pests Young shoots Aphids, borers, thrips Leaf underside Aphids,

55. Pest Identification vs Pest Diagnosis These terms are related but slightly different. Pest identification Answers: What organism is this? Pest diagnosis Answers: What is causing the observed crop problem? Diagnosis may require distinguishing among: - Pest - Disease - Nutrient deficiency - Environmental stress - Herbicide injury Therefore: Identification⊂Diagnosis in many practical crop-protection situations. 56. Pest Identification vs Pest Monitoring Identification Determines what pest is present. Monitoring Determines: - How many are present - Where they are present - Whether numbers are increasing - Whether damage is increasing Therefore: Identification=WHO? = Monitoring=HOW MANY? WHERE? HOW FAST? = 57. Pest Identification vs Pest Management Identification What is the pest? Management What should we do about it? The logical order is: Identify→Monitor→Assess→Manage 58. Then: IDENTIFY→MONITOR→ASSESS→DECIDE→MANAGE Final memory line Pest identification is not simply finding an insect; it is proving which organism is responsible for the observed crop damage. And the golden rule: IDENTIFY FIRST — MANAGE SECOND

Insect anatomy is the study of the structure and organization of an insect's body. Understanding insect anatomy is essential for pest management because the body structure helps us: - Identify insects correctly - Distinguish insects from mites, spiders and other arthropods - Identify insect orders and families - Understand feeding behavior - Understand movement and reproduction - Determine how insecticides enter or affect insects - Identify different life stages - Understand why different pests cause different types of crop damage The most fundamental feature of insects is: Insect body=Head+Thorax+Abdomen = + + 2. Definition of an Insect An insect is an arthropod belonging to the class Insecta, characterized in the adult stage generally by: - A segmented body divided into head, thorax and abdomen - Three pairs of jointed legs - One pair of antennae - Usually one or two pairs of wings, although some insects are wingless - An external skeleton made mainly of chitin-containing cuticle The key identifying feature is: 3 pairs of legs = 6 legs 3. Unlike humans, insects do not have an internal skeleton like vertebrates. They have an exoskeleton, also called the integument. It forms the outer covering of the body. Major functions include: - Protection - Body support - Muscle attachment - Prevention of excessive water loss - Protection from physical damage - Formation of specialized structures - Support for movement Conceptually: Exoskeleton=Protection+Support+Muscle attachment = + + 5. Composition of the Insect Exoskeleton The cuticle contains: - Chitin - Proteins - Lipids - Other structural components The cuticle is not simply a rigid shell; it is a complex, layered structure. 6. Layers of the Integument From outside to inside, important layers include:

A living cellular layer underneath the cuticle. It produces components of the cuticle. General arrangement: Epicuticle→Exocuticle→Endocuticle→Epidermis 7. Why the Exoskeleton Matters in Pest Management The insect cuticle is important because many insecticides can enter through the insect's body surface. Conceptually: Insecticide→Cuticle penetration→Internal tissues The properties of the cuticle can influence: - Absorption - Penetration - Water loss - Insecticide susceptibility This is one reason insect anatomy is relevant to pesticide action.
The insect body is composed of repeated segments that have become specialized. These segments are organized into: Head+Thorax+Abdomen + + The specialization of body segments is called tagmatization.
The head is primarily responsible for: - Sensory perception - Feeding - Receiving environmental information Major structures include:

Most adult insects have one pair of antennae. Antennae are important sensory organs. They detect: - Odors - Chemical signals - Touch - Air movement - Humidity - Temperature and other environmental cues in some insects Basic structure: Scape+Pedicel+Flagellum + + Scape The first segment, attached to the head. Pedicel The second segment. Flagellum The remaining distal portion, often composed of multiple segments. 11. Antennal Forms Antennae can have different shapes. Examples include: - Filiform - Setaceous - Moniliform - Serrate - Pectinate - Plumose - Clavate - Capitate - Geniculate - Aristate These shapes can help in insect identification. For example, some male mosquitoes have highly plumose antennae that are associated with sound detection. 12. Compound Eyes Most adult insects have a pair of compound eyes. A compound eye consists of many visual units called ommatidia. Conceptually: Compound eye=Many ommatidia = Functions include: - Detecting movement - Detecting light - Detecting shapes - Visual orientation

Many insects also have simple eyes called ocelli. They are generally associated with: - Light detection - Detecting changes in illumination - Orientation They differ from compound eyes in structure and function.

Mouthparts are extremely important in agricultural entomology. They determine how an insect feeds. Different insect groups have evolved different mouthpart structures. Major feeding types include: Chewing Piercing-sucking Raspingsucking Siphoning Sponging Chewing-lapping 15. Basic Components of Insect Mouthparts A generalized chewing mouthpart includes: - Labrum - Mandibles - Maxillae - Hypopharynx - Labium These structures have been modified in different insect groups. 16. Chewing Mouthparts Chewing mouthparts are adapted for biting and cutting solid plant material. Important structures include strong: Mandibles Examples include: - Caterpillars - Grasshoppers - Many beetles Typical crop damage: - Holes - Defoliation - Leaf margins eaten - Missing tissue Conceptually: Chewing mouthparts→Tissue removal→Visible feeding damage 17. Piercing-Sucking Mouthparts These mouthparts are adapted to penetrate plant tissues and suck fluids. Common among: - Aphids - Whiteflies - Leafhoppers - Scale insects - Mealybugs - Many true bugs They contain elongated stylet-like structures. Typical damage: -

The thorax is the middle region of the insect body. It is divided into three segments: Prothorax+Mesothorax+Metathorax + + The thorax is primarily responsible for: - Locomotion - Leg movement - Wing movement

Each thoracic segment bears one pair of legs: 3 thoracic segments×1 pair legs=3 pairs Therefore: 3 pairs=6 legs This is one of the easiest ways to distinguish insects from spiders. 24. Basic Insect Leg Structure A generalized insect leg consists of: Coxa→Trochanter→Femur→Tibia→Tarsus The distal end may include: - Pretarsus - Claws - Other specialized structures
The tibia lies between the femur and tarsus. It can contain specialized structures such as: - Spines - Spurs - Sensory structures

The tarsus is the distal portion of the leg. It is often divided into smaller segments called tarsomeres. The terminal region contains structures involved in gripping surfaces. 30. Types of Insect Legs Legs are modified according to function. Walking legs Used for ordinary locomotion. Jumping legs Highly developed for jumping. Example: - Grasshoppers Digging legs Adapted for burrowing. Example: - Mole crickets Swimming legs Adapted for movement through water. Grasping/predatory legs Adapted to capture prey. Example: - Praying mantis Pollen-collecting legs Specialized in some bees. Thus: Leg structure reflects function

Many adult insects have wings. Typically: Mesothorax and/or metathorax→Wing-bearing segments However, wing development varies among insect groups. Some insects are: - Winged - Partially winged - Wingless - Wingless only in particular castes or life stages 32. Wing Structure An insect wing is an extension of the body wall rather than a limb with bones like a vertebrate wing. It contains a network of veins. Wing veins provide: - Structural support - Passage for nerves and tracheae during development - Useful taxonomic characters 33. Wing Venation Wing venation refers to the arrangement of veins. It can be useful for: - Identifying insect groups - Distinguishing species - Understanding evolutionary relationships Therefore: Wing venation→Important identification character

The abdomen is the posterior region of the insect. It contains important systems associated with: - Digestion - Excretion - Respiration - Reproduction The abdomen is generally more flexible than the thorax. 35. Abdominal Segments The abdomen is composed of multiple segments. The exact number visible can vary among insect groups and life stages. Segments contain structures associated with: - Spiracles - Reproductive organs - External genital structures - Terminal appendages

Insects generally breathe through a tracheal system. Air enters through openings called: Spiracles Spiracles are typically located along the thorax and abdomen. General pathway: Atmosphere→Spiracle→Trachea→Tracheoles→Tissues 37. Tracheal System Unlike vertebrates, insects do not primarily transport oxygen through blood like humans do. Their tracheal system delivers gases directly toward tissues. Major components: - Spiracles - Tracheae - Tracheoles - Air sacs in some insects 38. Insect Respiration The basic process is: O2→Spiracles→Tracheae→Tracheoles→CellsO 2 and: CO2→Tracheoles→Tracheae→SpiraclesCO 2 This system is important in understanding some insect-control methods. 39. Digestive System The insect digestive system processes food and absorbs nutrients. It can broadly be divided into: Foregut+Midgut+Hindgut + +
The foregut is associated with: - Food intake - Storage - Initial mechanical processing Structures may include: - Mouth - Pharynx - Esophagus - Crop - Proventriculus in some insects
The midgut is a major site of: - Digestion - Nutrient absorption It is especially important in insect physiology and some insecticidal modes of action.

The hindgut is involved in: - Water and ion recovery - Waste processing - Formation of fecal material It includes structures such as: - Ileum - Colon - Rectum 43. Malpighian Tubules Insects generally use Malpighian tubules as major excretory structures. They help regulate: - Nitrogenous waste - Water - Ions Conceptually: Malpighian tubules→Excretion + Osmoregulation 44. Circulatory System Insects have an open circulatory system. Their circulatory fluid is called: Hemolymph The hemolymph circulates through the body cavity rather than being confined entirely to a closed network of blood vessels. 45. Dorsal Vessel The main pumping structure is the dorsal vessel. It includes: - Heart - Anterior aorta The heart generally pumps hemolymph toward the anterior region. 46. Nervous System The insect nervous system coordinates: - Movement - Feeding - Sensory information - Behavior - Internal functions It includes: - Brain - Ventral nerve cord - Ganglia Conceptually: Sensory input→Nervous system→Behavioral/physiological response 47. Insect Brain The insect brain processes sensory information and

Oviposition means the laying of eggs by a female insect. The location of eggs is important in pest management. Eggs may be deposited: - On leaves - On stems - In soil - Inside plant tissue - On fruits - In stored products Understanding oviposition behavior helps locate early infestations. 50. Insect Sensory Organs Insects possess numerous sensory receptors. They can detect: - Smell - Taste - Touch - Sound/vibration - Light - Temperature - Humidity - Chemical signals Important sensory structures include: - Antennae - Compound eyes - Ocelli - Sensilla - Specialized sensory organs

Sensilla are specialized sensory structures. They may detect: - Chemicals - Touch - Temperature - Humidity - Mechanical stimuli They are found on: - Antennae - Legs - Mouthparts - Wings - Other body surfaces 52. Insect Cuticle and Molting The exoskeleton does not expand continuously like an internal skeleton. Therefore, insects must periodically shed their old cuticle. This process is called: Ecdysis The process associated with development through molts is called: Molting 53. Why Molting Is Necessary As the insect grows: Body size↑ but the old exoskeleton cannot expand indefinitely. Therefore: Old cuticle→Shedding→New cuticle This creates vulnerable developmental periods. 54. Insect Growth and Development Insects generally develop through one of two major patterns. Complete metamorphosis Egg→Larva→Pupa→Adult Example groups include many: - Butterflies/moths - Beetles - Flies Incomplete metamorphosis Egg→Nymph→Adult Example groups include many: - Grasshoppers - Cockroaches - True bugs 55.
