A drought-resistant variety is a crop variety that possesses inherited characteristics allowing it to maintain survival, growth, reproduction, yield, or yield stability better than susceptible varieties when exposed to water-deficit conditions. Drought resistance is not one single trait. It is a combination of mechanisms that help plants cope with: - low rainfall, - prolonged dry periods, - low soil moisture, - high atmospheric water demand, - intermittent drought, - drought during sensitive growth stages. The central concept is: Drought-Adapted Genetics→Better Water-Stress Response→Improved Survival/Growth/Yield Stabilit y

A drought-resistant variety is a crop variety possessing inherited traits that enable it to maintain physiological function, growth, reproduction, survival and/or yield relatively better than susceptible varieties under defined water-deficit conditions. The term resistant should be interpreted relatively. Drought Resistance≠Complete Drought Immunity A drought-resistant variety can still suffer damage when drought becomes sufficiently severe. 3. What Is Drought? Drought is a condition in which water availability is insufficient to meet the water requirements of plants over a period of time. Agricultural drought can involve: Low Rainfall→Soil Moisture Deficit→Reduced Root Water Uptake→Plant Water Stress Drought can result from: - low rainfall, - delayed monsoon, - prolonged dry spell, - high temperature, - high evapotranspiration, - low soil-water storage, - inadequate irrigation. 4. Drought Resistance vs Drought Tolerance These terms are often used interchangeably, but they can be distinguished conceptually. Drought resistance Broad ability of a plant to maintain performance under wat

Recover after drought stress is relieved. 7. Deep Root System One important drought-adaptation trait is the ability to access water from deeper soil layers. Deep/Extensive Roots→Greater Soil Volume Explored→Potentially Greater Water Access Important root traits include: - rooting depth, - root length, - root density, - root branching, - root angle, - root hydraulic properties. However, deep roots are useful only where deeper soil contains accessible water. 8. Root-to-Shoot Balance Under drought, plants may alter biomass allocation. Drought→Root/Shoot Allocation Changes A greater root investment can potentially improve water acquisition, although excessive root investment also has carbon costs. Therefore: More Roots≠Automatically Better Root effectiveness depends on: - soil depth, - soil moisture distribution, - root conductivity, - soil compaction, - nutrient availability. 9. Stomatal Regulation Stomata control: - CO₂ entry, - water vapor loss. During drought: Soil Moisture↓→ABA Signaling→Stomatal Closure This reduces water loss but also reduces CO₂ entry. Therefore: Stomatal Closure

A high-yielding variety (HYV) is a crop variety that has been developed or selected to produce relatively high economic yield under suitable environmental conditions and appropriate crop management, compared with relevant existing varieties or standards. The important point is that “high-yielding” is a comparative and management-dependent concept. High-Yielding Variety→High Yield Potential+Suitable Environment+Good Management + + A high-yielding variety does not automatically produce high yield everywhere.

A high-yielding variety is a genetically improved crop variety selected or bred for high yield potential and capable of producing relatively high economic yield when grown under suitable environmental conditions and appropriate management. The term HYV is therefore mainly associated with yield potential/performance, rather than a particular seed class or reproductive system. 3. What Does "High Yield" Mean? Yield is the quantity of economically useful product obtained per unit area. Examples: - wheat → grain, - rice → grain, - maize → grain, - potato → tubers, - cotton → lint, - groundnut → pods/seeds, - sugarcane → cane/stalk biomass, - tomato → marketable fruit. A simplified yield relationship is: Yield=Yield Components×Environmental/Management Effects For cereals: Yield≈Plants/area×Grains/plant×Average grain weight 4. Yield Potential vs Actual Yield This is one of the most important concepts. Yield potential The maximum yield a genotype can approach under defined favorable conditions without major limitations from: - water, - nutrients, - pests, - diseases, - weeds, - temperature a

Seed purity refers to the extent to which a seed lot contains the desired seed of the stated crop and variety, free from unwanted materials such as: - inert matter, - seeds of other crops, - weed seeds, - other varieties, - diseased or damaged material, depending on the testing framework. Seed purity is a major component of seed quality. Seed Quality=Genetic Quality+Physical Quality+Physiological Quality+Seed Health = + + + Seed purity mainly concerns physical purity and genetic/varietal purity, which must be distinguished from germination and seed vigor.

Seed purity is the degree to which a seed lot consists of the intended crop seed and conforms to the required physical and varietal identity standards, with minimal contamination by other crop seeds, weed seeds, inert matter, or other unwanted components. In seed testing, the exact meaning of "purity" depends on the applicable testing and certification standard. 3. Why Is Seed Purity Important? Pure seed helps ensure that the farmer plants the intended crop rather than a mixture of: - unwanted crop species, - weeds, - other varieties, - foreign material. Poor purity can lead to: Poor Seed Purity→Unwanted Plants→Competition→Management Problems→Potential Yield/Quality Loss 4. Seed Purity Is Not the Same as Germination This is one of the most important distinctions. Seed purity What is actually present in the seed lot? Germination How many seeds produce normal seedlings under a defined test? Therefore: Purity≠Germination A seed lot can have: - high purity + poor germination, - high purity + high germination, - poor purity + high germination, - poor purity + poor germination. 5. Major Co
Remove plants that differ from the desired variety. 4. Controlled multiplication Maintain proper seed production procedures.
Prevent mechanical mixing during harvest and processing. 6. Proper storage Keep different seed lots separately identified.

Rouging is the removal of plants that are: - genetically off-type, - diseased where relevant, - otherwise undesirable, from a seed-production field. Conceptually: Off-Type Plant→Identification→Removal This helps maintain genetic/varietal purity. 18. Field Isolation Cross-pollinating crops can receive pollen from nearby fields. Therefore: Isolation→Unwanted Cross-Pollination↓→Genetic Purity↑ Isolation requirements depend on: - crop, - reproductive biology, - seed class, - applicable regulations. 19. Self-Pollinated Crops Self-pollinated crops generally have lower risk of pollen-mediated contamination than strongly crosspollinated crops. However, genetic purity can still decline through: - mechanical mixing, - residual off-types, - seed handling errors, - occasional outcrossing. Therefore self-pollinated does not mean: 20. Cross-Pollinated Crops Cross-pollinated crops have greater risk of genetic contamination through pollen. Therefore they may require stronger measures such as: - isolation, - controlled pollination, - male sterility systems, - removal of off-types. 21. Hybrid Seed Pur

Germination percentage is one of the most important indicators of the physiological quality of seed. It tells us what proportion of seeds in a tested sample are capable of producing normal seedlings under the prescribed germination test conditions. In simple terms: Germination percentage tells us how many seeds successfully germinate and produce normal seedlings out of the total number of seeds tested. The basic formula is: Germination (%)=Number of normal seedlingsTotal number of seeds tested×100 100

Germination percentage is the percentage of seeds in a sample that produce normal seedlings under specified test conditions within the prescribed testing period. The words normal seedlings, specified conditions, and prescribed period are important because germination is measured using a defined testing procedure rather than simply counting any seed that shows a root. 3. Basic Formula GP=NT×100 T 100 Where: - GPGP = germination percentage - NN = number of normal seedlings - TT = total number of seeds tested

Suppose: - Seeds tested = 100 - Normal seedlings = 85 Then: GP=85100×100GP= 100 100 GP=85% This means that 85% of the tested seeds produced normal seedlings under the specified test conditions. It does not mean that exactly 85% will necessarily emerge in a farmer's field. 5. Another Example Suppose 400 seeds are tested and 348 produce normal seedlings. GP=348400×100GP= 400 100 GP=87% Therefore, the germination percentage is 87%. 6. What Is a Normal Seedling? A normal seedling is a seedling that has the essential structures needed for continued development into a healthy plant, according to the applicable seed-testing rules. Depending on the crop, this generally involves properly developed: - root system, - shoot, - primary structures, - necessary supporting tissues. A seed that begins germinating but produces a severely abnormal seedling may not be counted as a normal germinating seedling. Therefore: Radicle Emergence≠Automatically Normal Seedling 7. Germination Process The biological process can be represented as: Viable Seed→Imbibition→Metabolic Activation→Reserve Mobilization→Radi

Seeds are often divided into multiple replicates. For example: - Replicate 1 → 100 seeds - Replicate 2 → 100 seeds - Replicate 3 → 100 seeds - Replicate 4 → 100 seeds Total: 400 seeds400 Replicates help assess consistency and reduce the influence of random variation. 17. Germination Test Conditions A germination test controls important environmental conditions such as: Temperature Maintained within the appropriate range for the crop. Moisture Adequate moisture is supplied. Oxygen Seeds must have adequate gas exchange. Substrate Examples can include: - paper, - sand, - other standardized germination media. Light Some species require specified light conditions. The exact requirements are crop- and method-specific. 18. Germination Count During testing, seedlings are evaluated at prescribed counting times. There may be: - first count, - final count. First count Provides information about early germination. Final count Determines the final germination percentage under the specified test. The exact counting schedule varies by crop and testing standard. 19. First Count vs Final Germination

Seed vigor describes the overall ability of a seed lot to germinate rapidly, emerge uniformly, establish strong seedlings, and perform well across a range of environmental conditions. It is different from simply asking whether a seed can germinate. The key idea is: Vigor=Speed+Uniformity+Strength+Stress Tolerance = + + + A seed lot can have high germination percentage but low vigor.

Seed vigor is the sum of those properties of a seed or seed lot that determine its potential for rapid, uniform emergence and development of normal seedlings under a broad range of environmental conditions. The exact wording and test methods can vary among seed-testing frameworks, but the central concept is performance beyond final germination percentage. 3. Why Seed Vigor Is Important Seed vigor strongly affects early crop establishment. High Seed Vigor→Rapid Germination→Uniform Emergence→Strong Seedlings→Better Stand Establi shment Low-vigor seed may: - germinate slowly, - emerge unevenly, - produce weak seedlings, - be more sensitive to stress, - deteriorate faster during storage, - establish poorly under unfavorable field conditions. 4. Seed Vigor vs Germination Percentage This is the most important distinction. Germination percentage asks: How many seeds produce normal seedlings under specified test conditions? Seed vigor asks: How rapidly, uniformly and robustly can those seeds perform, especially under lessthan-ideal conditions? Therefore: High Germination≠High Vigor

Consider two seed lots: Characteristic Lot A Lot B Germination 95% 95% Germination speed Fast Slow Emergence Uniform Uneven Stress performance Strong Weak Seedling growth Strong Weak Both lots have: 95% germination But Lot A may have substantially greater vigor. This demonstrates why germination percentage alone cannot fully describe seed quality. 6. Germination vs Vigor vs Viability Property Main question Viability Is the seed alive? Germination % Can it produce a normal seedling under specified test conditions? Vigor How rapidly, uniformly and robustly does it perform? A useful relationship is: Viability→Germination Capacity→Vigor/Performance But these are different measurements, not interchangeable quantities. 7. Seed Vigor Is a Seed-Lot Characteristic Vigor is commonly evaluated at the seed-lot level. Two lots of the same variety can have different vigor because of differences in: - maturity, - harvesting, - drying, - mechanical damage, - storage, - temperature, - moisture, - seed health. Therefore: Same Variety≠Same Seed Vigor 8. Components of Seed Vigor Important aspects includ

Whether seeds germinate and emerge at approximately the same time. 4. Seedling strength Ability to produce strong seedlings. 5. Stress tolerance Ability to perform under unfavorable conditions. 6. Storage potential Ability to retain quality during storage. 9. Seed Vigor During Germination High-vigor seeds generally proceed efficiently through: Imbibition→Membrane Repair→Metabolic Activation→Reserve Mobilization→Radicle Emergence - xed Imbibition Membrane\ Repair Metabolic\ Activation Reserve\ Mobilization Radicle\ Emergence Low-vigor seeds may have greater physiological deterioration and slower recovery after hydration. 10. Seed Aging and Vigor Seed vigor often declines before a large decline in final germination becomes obvious. A conceptual deterioration sequence is: Seed Aging→Membrane Damage→Metabolic Dysfunction→Vigor↓→Germination↓→Seed Death ed Seed\ Aging Membrane\ Damage Metabolic\ Dysfunction Vigor Germination Seed\ Death This is why vigor can act as an early indicator of seed deterioration. 11. Membrane Integrity Dry seeds undergo substantial physiological changes during re

Seed viability refers to whether a seed is alive and capable of developing into a normal plant under suitable conditions. It is one of the fundamental properties of seed quality. The simplest way to remember it is: Viability asks: “Is the seed alive?” This is different from: - Germination → Can it produce a normal seedling under specified test conditions? - Vigor → How rapidly, uniformly, and strongly can it perform? - Purity → What proportion of the seed lot is the intended seed?

Seed viability is the capacity of a living seed to remain physiologically alive and capable of germination and development into a normal seedling when suitable conditions are provided. A seed may be viable but dormant, meaning it is alive but does not germinate immediately under the conditions provided. 3. Basic Concept The relationship can be represented as: Living Seed→Viable Seed→Potential to Germinate→Normal Seedling But an important distinction is: Viability≠Germination because dormancy or unsuitable test conditions can prevent a viable seed from germinating. 4. Viability vs Germination This is one of the most important concepts in seed science. Viability Asks: Is the seed alive? Germination Asks: Does the seed produce a normal seedling under specified test conditions? Therefore: A viable seed may fail to germinate because it is dormant. For example, imagine 100 seeds: - 95 are alive, - 5 are dead, - but 10 of the living seeds are dormant. The viability may be approximately: 95%95\% while observed germination under the particular test may be lower. The exact relationship depends

Seed storage is the process of maintaining seeds under suitable environmental and handling conditions between harvest and sowing so that they retain their: - viability, - germination capacity, - vigor, - genetic identity, - physical quality, - seed health. The main objective is not simply to keep seeds physically present—it is to slow physiological deterioration and preserve planting value. The basic principle is: Good Storage→Deterioration↓→Viability&Vigor retained

Seed storage is the controlled preservation of seed from harvest until planting or longterm conservation under conditions that minimize deterioration and maintain viability, germination, vigor, genetic integrity and seed health. 3. Why Seed Storage Is Necessary Seeds may need to be stored: - between harvest and the next planting season, - between production and marketing, - for emergency reserves, - for breeding programs, - in seed banks, - for long-term genetic conservation. Without proper storage: Time+Moisture+Temperature+Oxygen+Pests/Pathogens→Seed Deterioration 4. Main Objectives of Seed Storage Good seed storage aims to: 1. maintain viability, 2. maintain high germination, 3. preserve seed vigor, 4. prevent insect damage, 5. prevent fungal growth, 6. prevent excessive moisture absorption, 7. prevent mechanical damage, 8. maintain genetic identity, 9. prevent contamination and mixing, 10.extend seed longevity. 5. The Most Important Storage Principle For many orthodox seeds, a fundamental storage principle is: Low Seed Moisture+Low Temperature+Suitable Packaging→Longer Storage Li

Temperature strongly affects the rate of many biological and chemical processes. Generally for many orthodox seeds: Temperature↓→Metabolic Activity↓→Deterioration Rate↓ Therefore, cool storage can extend longevity when combined with appropriate moisture and packaging. However, cold alone does not make poor storage safe. 13. Temperature + Moisture These two factors are especially important. A conceptual relationship is: High Temperature+High Moisture→Rapid Deterioration while, for many orthodox seeds: Low Temperature+Low Appropriate Moisture→Longer Longevity The actual safe values depend on: - species, - seed type, - packaging, - storage duration, - intended use. 14. Relative Humidity Seed moisture interacts strongly with the relative humidity (RH) of the surrounding air. Seeds can exchange moisture with the atmosphere until they approach an equilibrium moisture condition. Conceptually: RH changes↔Seed Moisture changes Therefore, even properly dried seeds can absorb moisture if stored in humid air using unsuitable packaging. 15. Seed Moisture Equilibrium The relationship can be repres

Packaging protects seed from: - moisture, - insects, - rodents, - contamination, - mechanical damage, - environmental fluctuations. Packaging can broadly be: Moisture-permeable Allows exchange with surrounding air. Moisture-resistant/hermetic Greatly restricts moisture exchange. The appropriate packaging depends on: - seed type, - initial moisture, - storage environment, - storage duration, - intended use. 17. Hermetic Storage Hermetic storage uses sufficiently moisture- and gas-tight packaging to isolate seed from external environmental changes. Its major principle is: External Humidity Fluctuation→Seed Moisture Change↓ When properly designed and used with appropriately dried seed, hermetic systems can help maintain quality. However: Hermetic packaging does not rescue seed that was stored too wet. If wet seed is sealed, deterioration can continue inside the package.

Oxygen is required for normal respiration. Reducing oxygen availability can slow certain biological processes, but seed storage should not be reduced to simply "remove all oxygen." The practical goal is to create an appropriate storage atmosphere and prevent harmful deterioration. Modified-atmosphere and controlled-atmosphere systems may be used in specialized applications.

Light can influence seed longevity and germination behavior depending on the species. Some seeds are light-sensitive for germination. During storage, protection from excessive light can help prevent unwanted environmental exposure, but temperature and moisture are generally more central to storage longevity for many orthodox seeds. 20. Seed Storage Types Seed storage can be divided broadly into: 1. Short-term storage Usually between harvest and the next planting season. 2. Medium-term storage Seeds are maintained for longer periods under controlled conditions. 3. Long-term storage Used for: - genetic conservation, - breeding materials, - germplasm, - seed banks. 21. Farm-Level Seed Storage Farmers may store seed for the next planting season. Important requirements include: - properly dried seed, - clean seed, - suitable containers, - cool and dry storage, - insect protection, - rodent protection, - labeling, - periodic inspection. A simple chain is: Harvest→Cleaning→Drying→Testing→Packaging→Storage→Periodic Monitoring 22. Commercial Seed Storage Commercial seed storage requires great

Good storage hygiene includes: - cleaning storage rooms, - removing old seed residues, - controlling spills, - cleaning equipment, - inspecting containers, - controlling pests. A simple principle is: Clean Storage→Lower Contamination/Pest Risk 35. Seed Lot Identification Every seed lot should be properly identified. Useful information includes: - crop, - variety, - seed lot number, - production date/year, - source, - treatment, - moisture, - germination, - testing information, - storage date. This prevents mixing and improves traceability. 36. Seed Mixing Different varieties or lots should not be mixed accidentally. For example: Variety A+Variety B→Loss of Lot Identity This is particularly important for: - certified seed, - foundation seed, - breeder material, - hybrid seed, - breeding populations. 37. Genetic Integrity During Storage Proper storage should preserve the identity and quality of the seed lot. Storage itself generally does not create new genetic variation in the same way breeding does, but deterioration, contamination or accidental mixing can compromise the usefulness an

Seed treatment is the process of treating seed before sowing to protect the seed and emerging seedling, improve establishment, and sometimes enhance germination or early growth. It is one of the most important practices in seed technology because the seed is particularly vulnerable during the period from sowing → germination → seedling establishment. The basic concept is: Seed Treatment→Seed Protection/Physiological Enhancement→Better Establishment Seed treatment may involve: - physical treatment, - chemical treatment, - biological treatment, - physiological treatments such as priming, - combinations of these.

Seed treatment is the application of physical, chemical, biological or physiological treatments to seed before sowing to protect the seed and seedling from pests and pathogens, improve germination and establishment, or enhance early plant performance. The exact treatment depends on: - crop, - seed type, - target pest/pathogen, - environmental conditions, - farming system, - treatment objective. 3. Why Is Seed Treatment Needed? After sowing, seeds encounter: - soil-borne fungi, - bacteria, - insects, - nematodes, - unfavorable moisture, - temperature stress, - salinity, - competition from other organisms. A vulnerable seed can therefore suffer: Seed→Pathogen/Pest Attack→Poor Germination→Poor Emergence→Poor Stand Seed treatment attempts to interrupt this pathway. 4. 14. What Is Grafting? Grafting is a method of vegetative propagation in which parts of two compatible plants are joined so that they heal together and grow as one plant. The two major components are: Scion+Rootstock + Scion The upper portion selected for desirable characteristics such as: - fruit quality, - variety/cultivar identity, - yield characteristics, - flowering/fruiting characteristics. Rootstock The lower portion that provides: - root system, - anchorage, - water and nutrient uptake, - and potentially tolerance/resistance traits.

Grafting is a vegetative propagation technique in which a scion from one plant is joined to a compatible rootstock of another plant so that their tissues unite and form a functional composite plant. Field clearing is the first major operation in land preparation in which unwanted vegetation, crop residues, stones, debris, obstacles, and other materials that interfere with crop production are removed, managed, or incorporated appropriately. The objective is not simply to make the field look clean. Field clearing prepares the land for subsequent operations such as: - tillage, - leveling, - irrigation, - drainage, - sowing or transplanting, - mechanization, - pest and disease management. The basic sequence is: Existing Field→Clearing→Accessible Field→Tillage/Bed Preparation→Planting

Field clearing is the planned removal, management, or incorporation of unwanted vegetation, crop residues, weeds, stones, debris, and other physical obstructions from a field before subsequent land-preparation and crop-establishment operations. A crucial point is that clearing does not always mean removing everything from the field. For example, useful crop residues may be: - retained as surface mulch, - incorporated into soil, - chopped, - baled and removed, - or otherwise managed according to the production system. Therefore: Field Clearing≠Complete Removal of All Biomass 3. Objectives of Field Clearing The major objectives are: 1. Remove physical obstructions Such as: - stones, - branches, - stumps, - plastic, - wire, - old infrastructure, - large debris. 2. Manage weeds and unwanted vegetation Reduce competition and facilitate subsequent field operations. 3. Manage previous crop residues Residues may be: - retained, - chopped, - incorporated, - removed, - burned where legally permitted and agronomically justified. 4. Facilitate machinery Clearing provides safer movement of: - tra

Primary tillage is the first major soil-working operation performed after field clearing, when tillage is part of the production system. It involves deep or relatively deep mechanical manipulation of the soil to break, loosen, invert, lift, shatter, or disturb the soil profile as needed for the next crop. Its main purpose is to create a suitable soil condition for: - root development, - water infiltration, - aeration, - weed management, - residue management, - subsequent seedbed preparation. The basic sequence is: Field Clearing→Primary Tillage→Secondary Tillage→Seedbed Preparation→Planting However, not every farming system requires conventional primary tillage. Reduced-tillage and no-till systems may minimize or eliminate it.

Primary tillage is the first principal soil-tillage operation used to break, loosen, shatter, invert, or otherwise modify the soil to the required depth and condition before subsequent seedbed preparation and planting. In simple words: Primary tillage = First major soil-working operation 3. Why Is Primary Tillage Done? The exact objective depends on the soil, crop and production system. Major objectives include: 1. Soil loosening Dense soil can be mechanically loosened. Compacted Soil→Tillage→Looser Soil 2. Breaking large clods Primary tillage can break and rearrange soil aggregates. 3. Improving root-zone conditions A suitable soil structure can allow roots to explore the soil. 4. Incorporating or managing residues Crop residues may be: - incorporated, - partially incorporated, - left on the surface, - or otherwise managed. 5. Weed management Tillage can uproot or bury some weeds. 6. Incorporating amendments Where appropriate, materials such as: - lime, - manure, - compost, - some fertilizers may be incorporated. 7. Breaking restrictive layers Deep tillage or subsoiling may address

Subsoiling is deep tillage intended to disrupt a compacted or restrictive layer below the normal tillage depth. It is generally justified only when a genuine restrictive layer exists. Compacted Layer→Subsoiler→Mechanical Disruption It can improve: - root penetration, - water movement, - soil physical conditions, when compaction is actually limiting. But: Deep Tillage without a Limitation≠Automatically Better 12. Secondary tillage consists of the soil-working operations performed after primary tillage to refine and condition the soil for planting. While primary tillage mainly breaks, loosens, shatters, or inverts the soil, secondary tillage focuses on: - breaking remaining clods, - leveling and smoothing the soil, - creating a suitable seedbed, - improving seed–soil contact, - controlling emerging weeds, - incorporating or distributing residues and amendments, - preparing beds, ridges, or furrows where required. The basic sequence is: Field Clearing→Primary Tillage→Secondary Tillage→Seedbed Preparation→Planting However, in reduced-tillage and no-till systems, conventional secondary tillage may be reduced or completely absent.

Secondary tillage is the series of relatively shallow soil-working operations performed after primary tillage to break clods, level and refine the soil, manage weeds and residues, and create suitable conditions for crop establishment. In simple words: Secondary Tillage = Refine the soil for planting 3. Primary vs Secondary Tillage — Core Difference This is one of the most important distinctions in land preparation. Primary tillage Secondary tillage First major soil-working operation Follows primary tillage Usually deeper Usually shallower Breaks/loosens/inverts soil Refines and conditions soil Handles major soil disturbance Handles clods and surface condition May incorporate major residues Distributes/refines residues Creates rougher initial soil condition Creates finer planting condition Examples: plow, chisel Examples: harrow, cultivator, rotary tiller Easy memory Primary = Break Secondary = Refine 4. Main Objectives of Secondary Tillage 4.1 Clod Breaking Primary tillage may leave large soil clods. Secondary tillage breaks them into smaller aggregates. Large Clods→Secondary Tillage

Harrowing is one of the most common secondary tillage operations. It can: - break clods, - level soil, - control small weeds, - mix residues, - refine the seedbed. Different harrows have different actions. 12. Disc Harrow Disc harrows use rotating concave discs. They can: - break clods, - mix soil, - cut residues, - level the surface. Compared with a heavy disc plow, a disc harrow generally performs a more refining operation. 13. Spike-Tooth Harrow Spike-tooth harrows use rigid teeth. They can be used for: - surface smoothing, - light clod breaking, - shallow weed control. They generally produce relatively shallow disturbance. 14. Spring-Tooth Harrow Spring-tooth harrows have flexible teeth. They can: - loosen shallow soil, - break clods, - uproot weeds, - handle certain residues. The flexibility allows the teeth to respond to field conditions.

Cultivators are used for shallow-to-moderate soil manipulation depending on design. They can perform: - weed control, - soil loosening, - residue management, - seedbed preparation. Cultivators can be used both before and after crop establishment, depending on the implement and farming system. 16. Rotary Tiller A rotary tiller uses rotating blades to intensely mix and break soil. It can create a fine seedbed rapidly. However: Very Fine Seedbed≠Always Better Seedbed Excessive rotary tillage can: - destroy stable aggregates, - increase pulverization, - increase erosion risk, - consume significant energy, - contribute to compaction below the tilled layer in some conditions.

A roller can be used to: - firm the soil, - crush clods, - improve surface uniformity, - create suitable seedbed conditions. Firmer soil can sometimes improve seed placement, but excessive compaction is undesirable.

Planking involves dragging a plank or similar implement across the field to: - level the soil, - crush clods, - smooth the surface. It is a simple seedbed-finishing operation. 19. Secondary Tillage Depth Secondary tillage is generally shallower than primary tillage. Conceptually: Dsecondary<Dprimary <D primary in many conventional systems. But there is no universal numerical depth because the appropriate depth depends on: - crop, - soil, - moisture, - implement, - residue, - seed placement, - farming system. 20. Soil Moisture During Secondary Tillage Moisture strongly affects the quality of the operation. Too wet Wet Soil→Smearing + Compaction Too dry Dry Soil→Large Clods + High Energy Requirement Appropriate moisture Better Aggregation + Better Seedbed 21. Secondary Tillage and Soil Structure The goal should be to create an appropriate aggregate structure rather than destroy all aggregates. Good soil structure supports: - water infiltration, - aeration, - root growth, - microbial habitat. Excessive secondary tillage can: Aggregate Breakdown→Structural Degradation 22. Secondary Tilla

Ploughing is the operation of cutting, lifting, breaking, loosening and, depending on the plough, turning or inverting a layer of soil to modify the soil condition for crop establishment and management. Main Purpose of Ploughing Ploughing may be performed to: 1. loosen soil, 2. break compacted soil, 3. invert or turn soil, 4. bury or incorporate selected residues, 5. uproot weeds, 6. expose some weed roots, 7. improve initial seedbed conditions, 8. incorporate certain amendments, 9. improve root-zone conditions, 10.prepare the field for secondary tillage. The actual purpose depends on the soil and production system. 4. Ploughing as Primary Tillage In conventional agriculture: Ploughing≈Primary Tillage But they are not identical concepts. Its main purpose is to break soil clods, refine the seedbed, level the soil surface, control young weeds, and create suitable conditions for sowing or planting. Harrowing is a relatively shallow soil-working operation performed mainly after primary tillage to break clods, loosen and refine the surface soil, level the seedbed, control small weeds, and prepare suitable conditions for planting. Rotavation is a tillage operation performed using a rotary tiller (rotavator) fitted with powered rotating blades. The rotating blades cut, break, mix, and pulverize soil and can incorporate or mix crop residues and other materials into the surface layer. Unlike a conventional plough, which is primarily pulled through the soil, a rotavator uses PTOdriven rotating blades to actively work the soil. The basic concept is: Rotavation=Powered Rotation+Cutting+Breaking+Mixing = + + + A conventional sequence may be: Field Clearing→Primary Tillage→Rotavation→Seedbed→Sowing But rotavation can sometimes be used as a primary or secondary tillage operation, depending on the machine, soil condition and farming system.

Rotavation is the mechanical tillage operation in which PTO-powered rotating blades cut, break, loosen and mix soil and residues to prepare or refine the soil for crop establishment. In simple words: Rotavation = Powered rotating blades used to work and refine soil 3. What Is a Rotavator? A rotavator, also called a rotary tiller, is an agricultural implement containing rotating blades/tines mounted on a rotor. The rotor is generally driven by: Tractor PTO The PTO transfers mechanical power from the tractor to the rotating rotor. Simplified power flow: Tractor Engine→Transmission→PTO→Rotor→Blades→Soil 4. Basic Working Principle The rotating blades enter the soil and perform several actions.

Repeated blade action can produce a relatively fine soil condition. Therefore: Cut→Lift→Break→Mix→Refine 5. Rotavation and Primary/Secondary Tillage Rotavation is important because it does not fit into only one fixed tillage category. Depending on the system, a rotavator may be used for: - primary tillage, - secondary tillage, - seedbed preparation, - residue incorporation, - inter-row cultivation with specialized equipment. Therefore: Rotavation≠Only Secondary Tillage It can serve different functions. 6. Rotavation After Ploughing One common application is: Ploughing→Large Clods→Rotavation→Fine/Refined Seedbed This can reduce the number of separate operations in some situations. 7. Soil amendments are materials added to soil primarily to improve its physical, chemical, or biological properties and thereby create a more favorable environment for plant growth. The central idea is: Problematic Soil+Appropriate Amendment→Improved Soil Condition + Examples include: - lime, - gypsum, - organic manure, - compost, - biochar, - elemental sulfur, - crop residues, - certain mineral amendments, - specially formulated conditioners.

A soil amendment is a material added to soil to modify and improve one or more physical, chemical, or biological properties of the soil for better soil functioning and plant growth. In simple words: Soil Amendment = Material Used to Improve Soil Properties 3. Why Are Soil Amendments Needed? Soils can have limitations such as: - excessive acidity, - excessive alkalinity/sodicity, - poor structure, - low organic matter, - poor water retention, - poor infiltration, - compaction, - salinity-related problems, - low biological activity, - nutrient-related limitations. An appropriate amendment can address a specific limitation. The basic decision pathway is: Soil Problem→Diagnosis→Amendment Selection→Application→Monitoring 4. Organic matter incorporation is the practice of adding organic materials to soil and mixing them into the soil profile using suitable tillage or other incorporation methods. The organic material may include: - crop residues, - farmyard manure (FYM), - compost, - green manure, - plant residues, - properly processed organic wastes. The objective is to improve soil functioning, nutrient cycling, soil structure, water relations and biological activity.

Organic matter incorporation is the agricultural practice of incorporating organic materials such as crop residues, manure, compost or green manure into the soil to promote decomposition, nutrient cycling and improvement of soil physical, chemical and biological properties. text: SEED STORAGE Source-derived content SEED STORAGE Purpose of Seed Storage: The purpose of seed storage is to maintain the seed in good physical and physiological condition from the time they are harvested until the time they are planted. Stages of Seed Storage: The seeds are considered to be in storage from the moment they reach physiological maturity until they germinate, or until they are thrown away because they are dead or otherwise worthless. The entire storage period can be conveniently divided into following stages. 1. Storage on plants (Physiologically maturity until harvest) 2. Harvest, until processed and stored in a warehouse. 3. In storages (Warehouses). 4. In transit ( rail wagons , trucks, carts, railway sheds , etc) 5. In retail stores. 6. On the user’s farm. The seed quality, i.e germination and vigour, can be considerably affected at any of the stages mentioned above , unless sound principles involved in seed storage are practised and the seeds properly handled. Soil compaction, causes, effects and management causes and forms of compaction COMPACTED SOILS Compacted soils cannot function healthily, resulting in poor crop establishment and lower crop yields. There is also less infiltration of rainfall, increased runoff and soil erosion. Causes of soil compaction Soil compaction occurs when soil density is increased by an energy input into moist or wet soil. The force may be exerted by tyres, tillage tools or animal hooves. In conventional tillage systems, most of the surface area of a paddock receives at least one wheel pass during a fallow. The first pass of a tractor wheel can create 90 per cent of the damage cau sed by five passes. effects on soil and crops Most compaction occurs in the top 20 −30 centimetres of the soil. Repeated tillage at the same depth can form a hardpan a dense, impenetrable layer beneath the tilled soil. The most important factor determining the extent and severity o f soil compaction is the moisture content at the time of tyre or implement passage. Soil erosion, degradation and conservation definition and extent ERODED SOILS Soil erosion is defined as the wearing away of topsoil. Topsoil is the top layer of soil and is the most fertile because it contains the most organic, nutrient-rich materials. Such soils are called as Eroded soils . Soil erosion is the displacement of the upper layer of soil, one form of soil degradation. causes and factors A low level of erosion of soil is a naturally occurring process on all land. The agents of soil erosion are water and wind, each contributing a significant amount of soil loss each year. Soil erosion may be a slow process that continues relatively unnoticed, or it may occur at an alarming rate causing a serious loss of topsoil. The loss of soil from farmland may be reflected in reduced crop production potential, lower surface water quality, and damaged drainage networks. types and effects Human activities have increased by 10-40 times the rate at which erosion is occurring globally. Rainfall and surface runoff Rainfall, and the surface runoff which may result from rainfall, produces four main types of soil erosion: splash erosion, sheet erosion , rill erosion , and gully erosion . Splash erosion is generally seen as the first and least severe stage in the soil eros ion process, which is followed by sheet erosion, then rill erosion and finally gully erosion (the most severe of the four). In splash erosion, the impact of a falling raindrop creates a small crater in the soil, ejecting soil particles. The distance these soil particles travel can be as much as 0.6 m (two feet) vertically and 1.5 m (five feet) horizontally on level ground. If the soil is saturated, or if the rainfall rate is greater than the rate at which water can infiltrate into the soil, surface runoff occurs. Biomass definition, sources and availability. Source-derived points Photosynthesis is a naturally occurring process which derives its energy requirement from solar radiation. The plants may be grown on land (terrestrial plants) or grown on water (aquatic plants). Biomass also includes forest crops and residues after processing. The residues include crop residues (such as straw, stalks, leaves, roots etc.,) and agro-processing residues (such as oilseed shells, groundnut shells, husk, bagasse, molasses, coconut shells, saw dust, wood chips etc.,). The term biomass is also generally understood to include human waste, and organic fractions of sewage sludge, industrial effluents and household wastes. The biomass sources are highly dispersed and bulky and contain large amounts of water (50 to 90%). Thus, it is not economical to transport them over long distances, and conversion into usable energy must takes place close to source, which is limited to particular regions. 3.1 Availability of biomass The total terrestrial crop alone is about 2 × 1012 metric tones. These include sugar crops, he

Biomass conversion routes and products. Source-derived points (i) Collection of urban and industrial wastes as supplementary fuel in boilers and as a feed stock for producing methane and some liquid fuels. (ii) Collection of agricultural and forest residues to produce fuels, organic manures and chemical feed stock. (iii) Growth of some specific energy plants for use as energy feedstock and cultivation of commercial forestry, aquatic and marine plants for different products. Thermo-chemical conversion includes processes like combustion, gasification and pyrolysis. Combustion refers to the conversion of biomass to heat and power by directly burning it, as occurs in boilers. Gasification is the process of converting solid biomass with a limited quantity of air into producer gas, while pyrolysis is the thermal decomposition of biomass in the absence of oxygen. The products of pyrolysis are charcoal, condensable liquid and gaseous products. Biochemical conversion includes anaerobic digestion to produce biogas and fermentation to obtain alcohol fuels, The third approach is oil extraction.

Practically the combustion process is an interaction amongst fuel, energy and the environment. Fuel may be defined as a combustible substance available in bulk, which on burning in presence of atmospheric air generates heat that can be economically utilized for domestic and industrial purposes. The common fuels are compounds of carbon and hydrogen in addition, variable percentages of oxygen and small percentages of sulphur and nitrogen are also present. Biomass fuels are normally thermally degradable solids. Combustion of organic materials not only generates natural components of air such as carbon dioxide and water but also produces carbonaceous residues, smoke and tar and gases of carbonyl derivatives, and carbon monoxide. Energy from the Sun, in the form of sunlight, supports almost all life on Earth via photosynthesis, and drives the Earth’s climate and weather. The Sun has an effective black-body temperature TS of 5777 K and it is the largest member of the solar system. The Sun is a sphere of intensely hot, gaseous matter with a diameter of 1.392*109 m and is, on average, 1.496*1011 m (Astronomical Unit) away from the Earth. The Sun is, effectively, a continuous fusion reactor. It is estimated that 90% of the Sun’s energy is generated in the region 0 to 0.23R (R being the radius of the Sun=6.95*108 m) the average density (ρ) and the temperature (T) in this region are 105 kg m-3 and about 840*106 K respectively. At a distance of about 0.7R from the centre, the temperature drops to about 1.3*105 K and the density to 70 kg m-3. Hence for r>0.7R convection begins to be important and the region 0.7R<r<R is known as the convective zone. The outer layer of this zone is called the photosphere.

Soil conservation is the control of soil erosion in order to maintain agricultural productivity. Causes of Soil Erosion Soil erosion is often the effect of many natural causes, such as water and wind. There are also human factors which increase the rate of soil erosion such as construction, cultivation and other activities. Why Soil Conservation? Conservation is not just the responsibility of soil and plant scientists, hydrologists, wildlife managers, landowners, and the forest or mine owner alone. All citizens should be made aware about the importance of natural resources as our lives depend on that and everyone should be involved in the process of caring of these resources properly and using them intelligently.

The loosening of the soil from its place and its transportation from one place to another, resulting in the detachment, transportation, and deposition of soil particles. What is Soil Erosion? Soil erosion is the process of detachment, transportation, and deposition of soil particles. It occurs when wind or water dislodges soil particles from their place and transports them to another location. Phases of Soil Erosion Detachment: The dislodging of the soil particle from the soil mass by erosive agents. Transportation: The entrainment and movement of detached soil particles (sediment) from their original location. Soil conservation is crucial in India due to the large area subjected to soil degradation, which threatens the country's food security. Causes of Soil Degradation India loses about 150 M-ha to water or wind erosion, and an additional 4 M-ha through ravines and gullies. This accounts for 53.3% of the country's total geographical area. Effects of Soil Degradation Soil degradation threatens India's food security, with a projected population of two billion by 2100 and stagnant food grain production at 211 million tons for the last five years. Strategies for Soil Conservation Maintain vegetation cover in vulnerable areas to prevent erosion. Use partial harvesting forests and seasonally dry or wet areas for pasture instead of arable land. Implement crop rotation to prevent soil exhaustion. Use contour ploughing in vulnerable areas. Carefully manage irrigation to reduce soil salinity development. Manage livestock grazing to prevent overgrazing. Restrict construction and urbanization to lower agricultural potential areas. Secure pledges to restore land to its former condition before granting

Soil degradation may result from natural causes and human-induced causes. Natural Causes Topographic and climatic factors such as steep slopes, frequent floods and tornadoes, storms and high-velocity wind, high-intensity rains, leaching in humid regions, and drought in dry regions are among the natural causes. Anthropogenic Causes Deforestation and overexploitation of vegetation, shifting cultivation, soil desurfacing, overgrazing, indiscriminate use of agrochemicals and lack of soil conservation practices, and overextraction of ground water are some anthropogenic causes of soil degradation. Main Causes of Human-Induced Soil Degradation deforestation overgrazing mismanagement of agricultural land overexploitation bio-industrial activities

The conversion of a forest into a non-forest use such as farmland, ranches, pasture, industrial complexes, and urban areas. Causes and Effects Deforestation is expanding and accelerating into the remaining areas of undisturbed forest, and the quality of the remaining forests is declining. Deforestation processes include industrial logging, clear felling, indiscriminate cutting, forest fires, shifting cultivation, and encroachment. Environmental Impacts The effects of deforestation are loss of forest, loss of biodiversity, climate change, and natural disasters such as cyclones, flood and drought, disruption of water cycle, decline in water quality, soil erosion, and sedimentation. Consequences for Soil Cutting trees in large tracts results in the climate getting drier in that area. Forest clearance exposes the bare soil to the scorching effect of the sun and the beating action of the rains. Significant amount of top soil is lost by erosion. Consequences for Climate Deforestation increases the carbon dioxide emission into the atmosphere. Tropical forests account for about 20 % of total

Shifting cultivation or slash-and-burn agriculture is an ancient farming system usually practiced by the indigenous people in the hilly areas of the humid tropics. Characteristics of Shifting Cultivation In this system, a patch of forest, usually on gentle slopes or on summits of hills, is cleared, vegetation is slashed and burned, holes are dug in soil with elementary tools, and seeds of assorted crops are sown before monsoon. Seeds germinate and grow rainfed, and the crops are harvested after 6–8 months. Then the land is left fallow. Farmers clear a new patch of forest for cultivation in the next season. Effects on Soil and Water The effect of burning is, however, temporary. Rains following burning remove bases rapidly by erosion and leaching. Growing evidence suggests that shifting cultivation in its distorted form leads to an adverse effect on soil and water. Changes in Rotation Period Overpopulation Settlement of plain landers to hills Scarcity of available land for cropping

Overgrazing is a major cause of soil degradation worldwide. Causes and Effects Livestock are the main source of income in many arid and semiarid countries. Domestic stocks are widely diverse and consist of camels, donkeys, horses, cows, sheep, and goat. Consequences of Overgrazing The forage and overgrazing of livestock cause a chain of degradation, critically reducing vegetation cover and soil fertility, as well as increasing erosion. Mechanisms of Erosion Domestic animals rapidly clear vegetation, placing stress on a land that already has a low vegetation cover. They also move in large groups and have sharp hooves that easily break up the soil, leaving it susceptible to erosion. Impact on Soil Fertility Erosion decreases fertile organic content of the soil. The lack of organic matter can lead to desertification through reduced nutrient availability for plant growth.

Soil desurfacing refers to the removal of a layer of surface soil for many different purposes, including construction of road and railroads and making of bricks. Importance of Surface Soil The surface soil is the most fertile part of the soil; it contains the highest organic matter and nutrients and possesses the most suitable physical and chemical conditions for plant growth. Effects of Soil Desurfacing decreases organic matter decreases nutrients reduces available water exposed subsoil is more compact significantly reduces soil quality and crop yields

The practice of growing a single crop year after year on the same land, in the absence of rotation through other crops. Effects on Soil Fertility The roots of the crop draw the same kind and proportion of nutrients from the soil for a long period of time. The nutrient status of the soil becomes imbalanced after a prolonged period of cropping. Impact on Ecosystems Particular types of insects and pests proliferate. Farmers become increasingly dependent on pesticides.

Irrigation in arid lands can further enhance desertification through salinization and alkalinization. Causes of Mismanagement of Irrigation It is not possible for farming to occur without artificial irrigation in arid lands where there is a deficiency of moisture. However, irrigation in arid lands can further enhance desertification through salinization and alkalinization. Effects of Mismanagement of Irrigation Salinization occurs when irrigation water evaporates quickly, leaving natural salts at the surface of the soil. Over a long time, excessive quantities of salts accumulate at or near the soil surface, making it increasingly difficult for plants to extract water from the soil. Importance of Leaching Requirement Irrigation water must consider the leaching requirement (extra water to leach the salts) of the soil.

Heavy farm machineries are used in mechanized agriculture by developed countries. Impact on Soil Degradation The impact of heavy farm machineries on soil degradation is discussed in more detail in connection with soil compaction.

Soil erosion is the detachment and transportation of soil material from one place to another through the action of wind, water in motion or by the beating action of rain drops. Factors Influencing Soil Erosion Energy group: potential ability of rainfall, runoff and wind to cause erosion (termed erosivity) Resistance group: erodibility of the soil, depending on its mechanical and chemical properties Protection group: plant cover, intercepting rainfall and reducing velocity of runoff and wind Rate of Soil Loss The rate of soil loss is normally expressed in units of mass or volume per unit area per unit of time. Under natural conditions, annual rates are of the order of 0.0045 t ha for areas of moderate relief and 0.45 t ha for steep relief. Impacts of Soil Erosion Excessive or enhanced soil erosion due to poor land management can result in both on-site and off-site impacts that are detrimental to a whole range of receptors. Where soil erosion occurs, the soil resource can be severely depleted if the rate of erosion exceeds the rate of natural soil formation.

Soil erosion is the removal of soil from the land's surface by natural forces such as water, wind, or ice. Agents of Soil Erosion Water erosion is the removal of soil from the land's surface by running water, including runoff from melted snow and ice. Sheet erosion occurs when thin layers of soil are removed from sloping land due to overland flows. Rill and gully erosion occur when water removes soil from small channels or streams. Types of Wind Erosion Saltation: Soil particles are carried away by wind in the form of small leaps. Suspension: Smallest soil particles are thrown into the air and transported by wind to long distances. Surface creep: Heavier soil particles are pushed or spread along the surface by wind. Gully Erosion Gully erosion is an advanced stage of sheet erosion. The rate of gully erosion depends on various factors such as runoff producing characteristics, drainage area, soil characteristics, and alignment.

The hydraulic pressure caused by heavy rains increases the weight of the rocks at cliffs, which come under the gravitational force and finally slip or fall off. Landslides Sometimes entire hillock may slide down. In this type of erosion, water and gravity act together. Stream Bank Erosion The rivers during floods splash their water against the banks and thus cuts through them. Particularly at curves, water strikes with great speed and the bank caves in alongside.

section: Water Erosion: Forms of Water Erosion
text: Soil detachment, transport, and deposition are the three main processes of water erosion. Forms of Water Erosion Water erosion occurs through three main processes: soil detachment, transport, and deposition. Soil Detachment Soil detachment occurs after the soil adsorbs raindrops and pores are filled with water. Raindrops loosen up and break down aggregates. Weak aggregates are broken apart first. Detached fine particles move easily with surface runoff. When dry, detached soil particles form crusts of low permeability. Transport Detached soil particles are transported in runoff. Smaller particles (e.g., clay) are more readily removed than larger (e.g., sand) particles. The systematic removal of fine particles leaves coarser particles behind. The selective removal modifies the textural and structural properties of the original soil. Eroded soils often have coarse-textured surface with exposed subsoil horizons. Deposition Transported particles deposit in low landscape positions. Most of the eroded soil material is deposited at the downslope end of the fields. Placing the deposited mater

The three main processes of water erosion are detachment, transport, and deposition. Detachment Soil detachment occurs after the soil adsorbs raindrops and pores are filled with water. Raindrops loosen up and break down aggregates. Weak aggregates are broken apart first. Detached fine particles move easily with surface runoff. When dry, detached soil particles form crusts of low permeability. Transport Detached soil particles are transported in runoff. Smaller particles (e.g., clay) are more readily removed than larger (e.g., sand) particles. The systematic removal of fine particles leaves coarser particles behind. The selective removal modifies the textural and structural properties of the original soil. Deposition Transported particles deposit in low landscape positions. Most of the eroded soil material is deposited at the downslope end of the fields. Placing the deposited material back to its origin can be costly. Runoff sediment transported off-site can reach downstream water bodies and cause pollution.

Sheet erosion is the removal of a thin layer of soil from the whole slope, primarily by raindrop impact and shallow surface flow. Causes and Effects Soil particles are detached primarily by raindrops and secondarily by frost, hooves of farm animals, tillage, and mechanical action of farm machines. Detached particles are transported by runoff water as overland flow. Types of Sheet Erosion Raindrop erosion Laminar erosion Rillet erosion Layer erosion Characteristics and Processes Surface becomes smoother Intensity of accumulation of runoff water depends on the height of the water stream, the coarseness of the surface, vegetation, or crop distribution.

Rill erosion occurs when rainfall exceeds the rate of infiltration, causing water to accumulate on the surface and move along sloping lands, concentrating in tiny channels called rills. Causes and Effects Rill erosion is caused by large amounts of material released and transported for variable distances in concentrated areas. It can lead to high soil loss, but the small channels do not usually interfere with tillage implements. Formation and Characteristics Rills are less than 30 cm deep and are formed by the cutting action of flowing water detaching soil particles. The amount of soil loss may be high, but the small channels do not usually interfere with tillage implements. Factors Influencing Rill Erosion Precipitation intensity and frequency Soil permeability and resistance Land slope and surface roughness Tillage lines, rows of crops, and exposed roots Types of Rill Erosion Ridge formation with sharply cut rillets and gullies Impermeable or still heavier material Crack erosion Narrow rillets resembling cracks Tunnel erosion or hollow erosion Material of varying resistance, vertica

The main feature of gully erosion is the volume and velocity of water at the lowest level. Characteristics of Gullies Gullies may grow into gorges and canyons in high altitudes and very steep slopes. Gullies may be flat, narrow, broad, and round. Types of Gully Forms Flat forms occur mostly on shallow soil or in connection with a specific lithic structure of the slope. Narrow, acute forms are created with a narrow V-section, the breadth of the gully usually being equal to its depth or smaller. Broad gullies have a wide bottom and are U shaped. Active Gullies Active gullies maintain steep or even perpendicular sides. It happens frequently that recent forms replace older forms so that their origin and age cannot be assessed from superficial observation.

The process of erosion that occurs along the banks of rivers and streams, characterized by the formation of gullies, canyons, and other landforms. Characteristics of Gully Erosion Gullies may grow into gorges and canyons in high altitudes and very steep slopes. Gullies may be flat, narrow, broad, and round. Types of Gullies Flat forms occur mostly on shallow soil or in connection with a specific lithic structure of the slope. Narrow, acute forms are created with a narrow V-section, the breadth of the gully usually being equal to its depth or smaller. Broad gullies have a wide bottom and are U shaped. Factors Influencing Gully Erosion The main feature of gully erosion is the volume and velocity of water at the lowest level. The energy of flowing water increases its cutting and smashing power and often results in bank erosion.

A channel or miniature valley cut by concentrated runoff through which water commonly flows only during and immediately after heavy rains. Characteristics of Gully Erosion Any concentration of surface runoff is a potential source of gully erosion. A gully is too large to be filled by normal tillage practices. Types of Gullies Dendritic Branching Linear Distinction between Ravine, Gully and Rills A gully is too large to be filled by normal tillage practices. A ravine is a deep narrow gorge.

The main processes in the development of gullies are waterfall erosion and channel erosion. Process of Development Gullies usually start with channel erosion. When an overfall develops at the head of the gully, the gully continues to develop by waterfall erosion. Types of Erosion Waterfall erosion extends the gully head Channel erosion enlarges the depth and width of gullies

Minimizing surface runoff is essential in gully control. Factors Affecting Gully Erosion The rate of gully erosion depends primarily on the runoff producing characteristics of the watershed, the watershed area, soil characteristics, size-shape and slope of gully etc. Causes of Watershed Deterioration Misuse of land (man made changes) Short intensive rainstorms Prolonged rains of moderate intensity Rapid snow melts Methods for Gully Control Improvement of gully catchments to reduce and regulate the runoff rates (peak flows) Diversion of surface water above the gully area Stabilization of gullies by structural measures and accompanying re-vegetation

Preventing the formation of gully is much easier than controlling it once it has formed. Planning for Gully Control One of the major steps in a gully control programme is to plan the control of runoff from the drainage area. The various methods employed for controlling runoff may be considered in the following order:

section: Retention of Runoff on the Drainage Area
text: Retention of runoff on the drainage area can be achieved through good crop management and applicable conservation practices. Methods for Reducing Runoff crop management and applicable conservation practices such as contouring, strip cropping, bunding, terracing etc. Where contour bunds are used, runoff is greatly reduced. On cultivated areas, small and medium sized gullies can also be reclaimed by placing a series of earthfills across the gully.

section: Diversion of Runoff Around the Gullied Area: The most effective
text: control of gullies is by complete elimination of runoff from the gullied area. Methods for Diverting Runoff Terraces and diversion ditches are generally used for diverting runoff from its natural outlet. Use of Terraces Terraces are very effective in the control of small gullies on cultivated fields or even medium size shallow gullies. Alternative Methods for Diversion Ditches If the slope above a gully is too steep for terracing, or if the drainage area is pasture or woodland, diversion ditches may be used to keep the runoff out of the gully. Conveyance of Runoff through the Gully If it is not possible to either retain or divert the runoff, then runoff must be conveyed through the gully itself.

A sod flume is a type of structure used to control overfall in gullies, providing a protected surface for runoff to flow into the gully. Design Considerations The design of sod flume serves the purpose of preventing further waterfall erosion by providing a protected surface over which the runoff may flow into the gully. Slope varies with the soil type, size of watershed, height of overfall and type of sod used. Design Parameters Slope: varies with soil type, watershed size, overfall height, and sod type. Maximum depth of flow: 30 cm. Design Guidelines The flume should be wide enough to maintain a non-erosive velocity. A slope of 4:1 is considered the steepest for its design.

TGCS have a life span of 3 to 8 years and they are pretty effective where the amount of runoff is not too large. Types of TGCS Woven wire check dams Brush dams Loose rock dams Plan or slab dams Log check dams Boulder check dams Purpose and Function These are made of locally available materials. Basic purposes they serve are to retain more water as well as soil for proper plant growth and prevent channel erosion until sufficient vegetation is established on the upstream side of the gully.

section: Design Criteria for Temporary Check Dams
text: The overall height of a temporary check dam should not exceed 75 cm, with an effective height of about 30 cm being sufficient. Design Considerations Life of the check dams under ordinary conditions should be in between 3 to 8 years. Spillway capacity of check dams is generally designed to handle peak runoff that may be expected once in 5 to 10 year return period. Spacing and Apron Check dams should be spaced so that the crest elevation of one dam is at the same level as the bottom elevation of the adjacent dam upstream. An apron or platform must be provided at the down-stream end to catch water falling over the top.

Used in gullies of moderate slopes (not more than 10 percent) and small drainage areas that do not have flood flows which carry rocks and boulders. Help in the establishment of vegetation for permanent control of erosion. Dam Construction Dam is built in half-moon shape with the open end up- stream. Optimum Curvature The amount of curvature is arbitrary: but an off-set equal to 1/6 of the width of gully at the dam site is optimum.

A row of posts is set along the curve of a proposed dam at about 1.2 m intervals and 60-90 cm deep. Setting up the Dam To construct a woven-wire dam, a row of posts is set along the curve of the proposed dam at about 1.2 m intervals and 60-90 cm deep. Heavy gauge woven wire is placed against the post with the lower part set in a trench (15-20 cm deep), and 25-30 cm projected above the ground surface along the spillway width. Rock, brush or sod may be placed approximately up to a length of 1.2 m to form the apron. For sealing the structure, straw, fine brush or similar material should be placed against the wire on the upstream side upto the height of spillway. Sealing the Structure straw fine brush similar material

A structure, such as a dam, is constructed by covering the sides and bottom of a gully with straw or fine mulch, followed by the placement of stakes and brushes to hold it in place. Construction Process For a distance of 3-4.5 m along the site of the structure, sides and bottom of the gully are covered with thin layer of straw or similar fine mulch. Brushes are then packed closely together over the mulch to about one half of the proposed height of dam. Stake Placement Several rows of stakes are driven crosswise in the gully, with rows 60 cm apart, and stakes 30-60 cm apart in the rows. Heavy galvanized wire is used to fasten the stakes in a row, as well as to firmly compress the brushes in places. Additional Support Sometimes large stones are also placed on top of brush to keep it compressed and in close contact with the bottom of the gully. Maintenance Requirements Major weakness is the difficulty of preventing the leaks and constant attention is required to plug openings of appropriate size with straw as they develop.

Suitable for gullies with small to medium size drainage area, used in areas where stones or rocks of appreciable size and suitable quality are available. Materials Flat stones are the best choice for dam making. Stones can be laid in such a way that the entire structure is keyed together. Construction If round or irregular shaped stones are used, structure is generally encased in woven-wire so as to prevent outside stones from being washed away. If the rocks are small, they should be enclosed in a cage of woven- wire.

A trench is made across the gully to a depth of about 30 cm, forming the base of the dam on which stones are laid in rows. Designing the Dam The center of the dam is kept lower than the sides to form spillway. Apron Construction Several large flat rocks may be countersunk below the spillway. Extending about 1 m down-stream from the base of the dam. Trench Depth A trench is made across the gully to a depth of about 30 cm.

The process of building a dam using planks placed across the gully. Dam Construction The planks are placed across the gully to form the dam. If the planks are not close fitting, straw or grass may be used for sealing purposes. Spillway Notch A suitable opening for the spillway notch is made over the headwall. Up-Stream Face On the up-stream face, a well tempered earth fill is made. Down-Stream Face The apron may be made of loose rock brush sod or planks

They are used to stabilize incipient, small and branch gullies generally not longer than 100 m and with catchment areas of less than two hectares. Construction Materials Logs and posts used for the construction are placed across the gully. They can also be built of planks, heavy boards, slabs, poles or old railroad ties. Objectives and Applications to hold fine and coarse material carried by flowing water in the gully to stabilize gully heads Design Specifications Maximum Height 1.5 m Spillway Shape Rectangular Spillway Dimensions Length: 1-2 meters,Depth: 0.5-0.6 m

Boulder check dams are used to control channel erosion and stabilize gully heads in gully systems. Design Considerations The maximum total height of the dam is 2 m. Foundation depth must be at least half of the effective height. Spillway Design The thickness of the dam at spillway level is 0.7 to 1.0 m (average 0.85 m). The inclination of its downstream face is 30 percent (1:0.3 ratio); Spillway Design (continued) The form of the spillway is generally trapezoidal. Not specified

section: Soil Loss Estimation by Universal Loss Soil Equation Introduction
text: The Universal Soil Loss Equation (USLE) is a widely accepted method to predict average annual soil loss caused by sheet and rill erosion. Limitations of the USLE While it can estimate long-term annual soil loss and guide conservationists on proper cropping, management, and conservation practices, it cannot be applied to a specific year or a specific storm.

The most widely used empirical model worldwide for estimating soil loss, developed in the USA. Limitations of the USLE The USLE makes simplified assumptions in the processes of soil erosion and has limited consideration of complex factors. Advantages of the USLE The USLE is simple, easy to use, and does not require numerous input parameters or extensive data sets for prediction. Equation Components R: rainfall and runoff erosivity index K: erodibility factor LS: topographic factor C: cover and management factor P: support practice factor Equation Formula A = R*K*LS*C*P, where A is average annual soil loss (Mg ha)

The EI is computed as the product of total storm energy times the intensity of the rain. Computing the EI The USLE uses the annual EI which is computed by adding the EI values from individual storms that occurred during the year. Relationship to Soil Loss According to Wischmeier and Smith (1978), the EI corresponds closely to the amount of soil loss from a field. Limitations of the USLE-Computed EI The USLE-computed EI is only valid for rain intensities ≤ 63.5mm h. Modifications for Tropical Regions Modifications to EI have been proposed for tropical regions (Lal, 1976). EI Values and Region Type Values of EI below 50 (mm h) correspond to dry regions. Values of EI above 500 (mm h) correspond to humid regions.

The product of the raindrop and the maximum intensity of rainfall over kinetic energy, used as an estimator of soil loss. History and Development Wischmeier and Smith (1958) found that the product of the raindrop and the maximum intensity of rainfall over kinetic energy was the best estimator of soil loss. Calculation and Application EI = E × I(5.1) The USLE uses the annual EI which is computed by adding the EI values from individual storms that occurred during the year. The EI corresponds closely to the amount of soil loss from a field. Limitations and Modifications The USLE-computed EI is only valid for rain intensities ≤ 63.5mm h1. Modifications to EI have been proposed for tropical regions (Lal, 1976). Interpretation of EI Values EI30 Region <50 mm h Dry Regions >500 mm h Humid Regions
